ROBERT A . CRIGLER
Grand Master October 18, 1968-0ctober 17. 1969
Robert Arthur Crigler (Bob). the 103rd Grand Master to serve as
Grand Master of Masons in California and Hawaii, has laid down a
path during his years of service and. particularly. during his year as
Grand Master, which future Grand Masters may well emulate.
Bob was born in Denver, Colorado. the son of Robert 0. Crigler and
Mary Frances Crigler. The Criglers moved to the Los Angeles area
and Bob attended Huntington Park High School. graduating in the
class of 1933, Los Angeles City College and U.C.L.A. He is also a
graduate of the Los Angeles Stock Exchange Institute.
Our Grand Master's business career has been both varied and successful. Starting as a stock and bond trader in 1938, the war in 1942
interrupted, and through 1943 he served as Technical Representative,
U.S. Air Force, in the African war theatre. Returning to civilian life.
Bob spent two years with Hydraulic Engineering Company as General
Manager before establishing his own business in Insurance and Industrial Land Development. His keen business sense and awareness of
value, as well as a talent for organization, brought an increasing flow
of clients. both local and Eastern who have relied on his judgment in
the purchase of land and the development of buildings in the expanding
industrial complex which is the West Coast.
The young stock broker of 1938 found time for romance as well and
on August 5. 1939. Dena Davis became his bride. Two children. Robert
A . Crigler, Jr., now a member of Redondo Lodge No. 328. and Karen
Cristine, now a stewardess with Continental Airlines, together with
granddaughter, Denettee Crigler, and Bob's mother complete the immediate family. As would be expected of such an ardent Mason. the
family has been religiously active as well. Bob and Dena are longtime
members of Plymouth Congregational Church where Bob has s erved
as Lay Leader, Moderator and President of the Board of Trustees.

ROBERT A . CRIGLER
Grand Master
O ctober 18. 1968-0ctober l 7, 1969

Robert 0. Crigler was made a Mason in Angeles Mesa Lodge No.
625 in 1942 and it was quite natural that Bob should follow in his
father's footsteps. Upon the acceptance of his application and election
to receive the degrees of Freemansonry, our Grand Master was raised
in John Marshall Lodge No. 636 on March 12, 1945, rising through
advancing offices to serve as its Worshipful Master in 1953 and there-

after as Officers Coach from 1954. He was appointed a member of the
Columbia Temple Committe e in 1960. and, as Inspector of District No.
522 in 1961. In 1963, to fill the vacancy crea ted by the death of Assistant Grand Lecturer Ralph W . Collins, the then Grand Master Ira W.
Coburn wisely chose this devoted Brother. The s trong ties of respect
and brotherly love forged during the past years were evidenced in the
loyalty and leadership which Bob gave to the Fifth Division and recognition of his service spreading beyond that area led the representa tives
assembled at the 1966 Communi cation to elect him to the office of
Junior Grand Warden.
Other Masonic affiliations have added to Brother Crigler's understanding of the wider responsibilities of his office. He is a member of
Signet Chapter No. 57 Royal Arch Masons, and Command ery No. 9,
Knights Templar. A member of and Past Wise M aster of Los Angeles
Scottish Rite Bodies. he was decorated with the rank of K.C.C.H. He
is a member of St. Gabriel Conclave, Red Cross of Constanti ne. He
was honored by the Award of Legion of Honor by the Order of De
Malay. He has served the Grand Lodge of India as its Official Representative near the Grand Lodge of California .
Civically, our Grand Master has been recognized by the John F .
Kennedy Award for outstandin g and long-term service as Chairman
of the Beverly Hills Draft Board and by the Gold Salute Award of the
Los Angeles Junior Chamber of Commerce.
This has been a year marked by turmoil and dissent on our campuses and by a seemingly growing inclination on the part of public and
private officials to shun responsibility. Robert A. Crigler has exhibited
the leadership and courage not only to speak to the issues, but, by his
actions. to demand of himself and others the standards of conduct and
selfless devotion to the duties of a Master Mason learned at the altar of
Masonry. This will, in the results of this year, establish a high mark for
future Grand Masters to emulate as their goal.

The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge was opened in ample form,
following which the Flag of our Country was received.
There were 1482 officers and representatives from 704 chartered
Lodges and one Lodge under dispensation, 1191 Past Masters and 22
disti?gu~shed guests from other jurisdictions present during this Communication.

APPOINTMENTS
The Deputy Grand Master announced the appointment of Henry D.
Oliphant, David H. Terry and John W. Swank as members of the Committee on Distribution.

Durin~ the Communication the Grand Master announced the temporary appomtment of William H. Price, Assistant Grand Lecturer, to
serv~ as Grand Chaplain at the Thursday afternoon and Friday morning
sessions.

TELEGRAMS
The Grand Master directed the Grand Secretary to send appropriate telegrams to each of the absent Past Grand Masters.
During the session the Grand Secretary read congratulatory messages received from other Grand Jurisdictions and concordant groups.

you take all of the people who go to sleep in church and lay them end

deep enough, you find there, interwov en in the human heart, some rainbows. For the great genius of America is that it has given to ordinary
men the capacity to become extraord inary citizens. And plain, ordinary ,
everyday individua ls can stand for great things and great ideas.
I think one of the most unusual stories in America n history has to do
with t~o little boys who decided at twelve and thirteen years of age that
America had no future and they were going to Europe to make a living
and build a life. They started down through the midwest with little packs
on their backs. They arrived in New Orleans on the 13th of the month,
expectin g to take a ship at one o'clock in the morning to go to Europe.
The Captain didn't know they were coming. the ship was loaded at
twelve thirty and, as the boys arrived on the dock, they saw the lights
of the boat taking off down the Mississip pi for the Gulf.
They sat there on the dock in utter disillusio nment and despair and
a few moments later a crusty old sailor happene d to come along and he
saw the two lads sitting there. dejected, disillusioned. youngste rs. He
engaged them in conversa tion, learned of the difficulty and he began
to sell them on the dream- a dream of the America that was yet to be.
and the boys decided they would give it a whirl. And they came back
home and today you remembe r these two boys in America n history. The
two boys who were going to Europe because America had no future.
and we honor them as great citizens, were Mark Twain and Thomas
Edison. Had it not been for the dream in the soul of a crusty old sailor
on the boardwa lk in New Orleans on the 13th of the month. America
would have lost two of its greatest potential citizens. Oh. you never
know what is going to happen in the mind or the soul of a boy or a girl
when you put there a dream.
Charles Brookfield had the unusual experien ce of getting up one
morning and reading his obituary in the newspap er. I get up every morning and check the obituary column and if my name isn't there. I get up.
But he had the experien ce of seeing his there. And he was rather surprised at what they said about him. One line caught his mind because it
read, ''Charles Brookfield, never a great actor. was invaluab le in small
parts." I like that. Never a great actor, he was invaluab le in small parts.
Oh. we can't all be a presiden t of the United States or a governor of the
state or the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge but every man can be
invaluab le in the part that he plays in the life of our Fraternit y and the
responsib ility that is his. For it is your loyalty and my loyalty to those
everyday responsibilities that comman d us and demand us that weave
the strange fab ric of this intangibl e somethin g we call democra cy and
our way of life. "For there is a spark in the souls of little people that
bursts into flame." John Steinbec k said that in "The Moon is down."
" There is a spark in the souls of little people that bursts into flame."

Masonry. We stress this in our Constitu tion Day observan ces, for the

have so many 'donkeys ' braying it is difficult to keep a sense of balance.
For there are multitud es of people who are crying for freedom of speech.
They want to be heard but they have not learned ho:". t.o listen. ~nd
one must always put alongsid e of freedom .. . respons1brl1ty ... for 1f a
country gives to one the right to speak, then it likewise imposes upon

I said to myself one day, "Well. Kenny Carlson. you talk a great
deal about liberty, freedom. What do you really mean by it? Supposi~g
you were to take a piece of paper at this moment and you were to write
down what freedom really means to you. What would you say?" I

please. I n the law court it is justice. In the home it i~ love. In the school

the right to say to a candidat e for political office, I may d1sagr~e with
everythin g you say but I would give my life to defend your right to
say it.'"
But we don' t s.ay that very much any more. We would rath er shoot
our opponen ts.
I was asked not too long ago. in a televis ion interview . whether I
thought there was more juvenile delinque ncy today than there was w?en
I was a boy. I'm not sure that there is, in relation to the total populatio n,
but I think the characte r of crime has changed .
Growing up there in midwest ern Canada, I certainly wasn't a.ny
angel as a youngste r and neither were you, although we would h~e
everybod y to think we were. I can remembe r we ?ad an old grouch 1.n
our neighbor hood. N o neighbor hood is complete without a grouch. This
fella' was really somethin g. He was so mean that when he walked down
the street even the sewers backed up! And I remembe r he planted a field
of carrots and never did know why the carrots didn't come up that
summer. We kids were in there every night at nine o'clock and we ate
them. But we didn't murder people. We didn't destroy schools. We
didn't do as a boy in London did-pok e out the left eye of eleven horses
just for fun. We didn't do as three teenager s did in Los Angeles a few
weeks ago--be at up an old gentlema n seventy-five years of age and almost left him for dead. The only reason offered, "We did it for fun-it
was kicks." No. the characte r of crime has changed . Somehow we have

lost out of America n life that fine line between that which is tolerable and

can you corrupt in a democra cy and still retain that democra cy?"
Still we are the inheritor s of freedom. We give to our young people
a great heritage of this freedom.
It was in 1764 that Christop her Gasden wrote to the agent of the
colony of South Carolina over London and said, "There ought to
be no 'New England er,' no 'New Yorker,' but all of us America ns."
And you remembe r that dramatic moment when Patrick Henry stood

your boundari es of colonies. I am not a Virginia n. I am an America n."
It brought the Assembl y to its feet, and there began to develop a deeper
sensitivi ty to the meaning of freedom, the freedom that is ours as Americans, and as Masons. Always. we must place alongsid e freedom •. .
responsibility.
The third well from which I have been privileged to drink all of my
life is the well of our flag. Now I am running the danger here of sounding
a little corny, because for some strange reason today. it does not seem

I must say to you that I remembe r those early days when we used to

Four hundred and sixty-five of our Brethren have been summoned
to the Lodge above. Among them, two Past Grand Masters, two veteran
Inspectors and many of the most dedicated members of our Craft.
One of the most beloved Masons in California left us on March 1,
when Ernest G. (Doc) Bashor. a Past Master of Sunset Lodge No. 352,
was called from this earthly life. A special eulogy in his memory was
prepared by Brother Ralph H. Head, also a Past Master of Sunset
Lodge and his close friend for many years. It was hoped that he could
deliver this eulogy this morning but circumstances beyond his control
render it impossible for him to arrive in time for this service. I will
deliver Brother Bashor's eulogy as Ralph wrote it.
Time being of the essence, does not permit more than a few eulogies
of our departed brothers. however, a complete list of their names will be
attached to and become a permanent part of the record of these proceedings.

1930's he was Governor of Bombay and later Under Secretary of State
for India and Burma. He was Lord Chamberlain of England from 1952
to 1963.
His Masonic career was indeed one of devotion, having served as
Grand Master of the United Grand Lodge of England for 18 years.
Many of you present this day will remember him as our guest at the
dedication of this Temple in 1958. at which time he addressed our Grand
Lodge at some length, concluding his remarks by presenting the Grand
Lodge of California, on behalf of the United Grand Lodge of England,
a silver and crystal ink stand made in 1783, during the reign of King
George III, to be used by future Grand Masters of Masons in California.
This is now on display in the central case on the second floor.
Roy Weiland, a native of Ohio where he was born March 17, 1896,
was a member of Crocker Lodge No. 454 of Daly City. He departed
this life on Christmas Day, 1968. He was raised November 3, 1937, in
Crocker Lodge and served as its Master in 1948. Immediately after relinquishing the Master's chair, he was elected Secretary of his Lodge,
serving continuously for ten years and, after an interval. again from
1964 to 1966.
He served Grand Lodge on its Distinguished Guest Committee from
1958 to 1965 and from 1967 to the time of his death, on the Grand Lodge
Week Activities Committee. He was a Past Patron of Crocker Chapter, Order of the Eastern Star, a member of the California Scottish Rite
Bodies, of San Francisco, Islam Temple of the Shrine, Royal Order of
Jesters and Honorary Member of the Temple Guard.
He is survived by his wife Rose as well as a son and daughter.

William F. Holman, Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Minnesota for two years, and a dual member of Silver Cord Lodge No. 505
of Santa Ana, passed away on August 10 in Santa Ana, California. at
the age of 86. He was raised in Cataract Lodge No. 1 in Minnesota and
was a charter member and Past Master of University Lodge in Minneapolis. A 33° Scottish Rite Mason, he led the Maundy Thursday services in Orange County last Easter. An honorary member of Zuhrah
Temple of the Shrine and a very active member of El Bekel Shrine
Temple of Long Beach, Past Patron Hermosa Chapter 105 O.E.S.
He initiated and guided the development of the Masonic Cancer
Hospital at the University of Minnesota and led in the endowment of
over a million dollars for this hospital. toward the care of the ill and the
infirm. He and his wife, Grace, gave unsparingly of themselves in
support of the Masonic Homes of California, in particular their work for
the Childrens Home at Covina.
A a scholar, he ranked with the highest. A native of Friend, Nebraska, he was a Phi Beta Kappa at the University of Nebraska and taught
there for seventeen years. Returning to Minnesota, he taught there for
forty-three years, finally assuming charge of the entire physical plant
of the University. He served under all but two of the University's
presidents.
A devoted family man, he and his wife, Grace, met on the campus
where he was teaching and to whom he was married for 57 years. Besides his devoted wife. he leaves a son, John, and a daughter, Jane.

George Morris Warner, our friend and Brother, was called without
warning from our midst on Friday, January 10, 1969, struck down by
an automobile as he left the Los Angeles Scottish Rite Temple. A dual
member of Menorah Lodge No. 623, where he was raised in 1942, and
John Marshall Lodge No. 636, where he had just concluded a brilliant
year as Master. George lived Masonry, every waking moment. Active
on many committees of Menorah Lodge where he served as its Treasurer
in 1945. He also was active in Al Malaikah Temple of the Shrine.
He joined the Los Angeles Scottish Rite Bodies in June, 1945, and
served on many of its committees and, most important, on its Welfare
Committee, serving without stint wherever and whenever called on. A
friendly, gregarious man who loved his fellow man and delighted in
demonstrating that affection when in the presence of the afflicted, the
destitute, the aged or ill Brother, the widow and the orphan. The distress
of a Brother, the tears of the widow and the hurt of a child were never
so muted as to escape his attention. In recognition of his service, the
Supreme Council was pleased to invest him with the rank and decoration
of Knight Commander of the Court of Honor on October 3, 1967.

office he held until shortly before his death. A member of Al Malaikah
Temple of the Shrine, Long Beach Scottish R ite Bodies and the Order
of the Eastern Star, he exemplified Masonry in its very finest sense.

Lawrence McCulley Judd was born in Honolulu, Hawaii, March 20,
1887. He came from a line of distinguished forebears.
His grandfather, Dr. Gerrit Parmek Judd, came to the Islands in
1829 as a medical missionary and for nearly fifty years served as statesman and adviser to Hawaiian kings.
His father, Albert Francis Judd, was a dis tinguished legislator,
lawyer and judge. A justice of the Supreme Court of Hawaii for 26
years, nineteen of them as Chief Justice.
Lawrence, in his own right, added fame and personal credits to the
family name.
He was educated in Punahou School, the Hotchkiss School and the
University of Pennsylvania; where he received his degree in business.
His business career was mostly in the merchandising field with Alexander & Baldwin, Ltd., as a Director of Theodore H. Davies & Company,
and as a Vice President and Director of the Hawaiian Meat Company.
Entering politics in 1920, he served six years in the Hawaiian Senate
(President of the Senate in 1923).
In 1929, at the age of 42, he was appointed the seventh Governor
of Hawaii by President Herbert Hoover. He served in this capacity
until 1934. Nineteen years later, in 1953, he was appointed Governor of
American Samoa, having been one of the few men ever to serve as
Governor of two territories. He subsequently resigned due to poor
health.
Over and above all of these honors, he will best be remembered for
his life long devotion to the welfare and health of the unfortunate victims
of H a nsen's disease. As a boy he watched people stricken with this
disease placed aboard ship in Honolulu Harbor for the sad trip to Kalupapa settlement on Molaki. Throughout his adult life his interest in their
welfare never ceased. He always worked toward more humane treatment for them. It was, in a great measure, due to his efforts that so many
changes for their betterment have taken place. At the age of 81 he was
still fighting for this cause. The state is now embarked on a re-examination of the handling of persons afflicted with this disease. They had
hoped to include him on the committee to make the review.

Ernest G . Bashor-The Roman philosopher, Seneca, wrote "Let us
see to it that our lives, like jewels of great price. be noteworthy not
because of their width, but because of their weight. Let us measure them
by their performance, not their dura tion."
Weighed by performance, the life of Brother Ernest G. Bashor would
total millions of carats, for few have lived so full a life and contrib uted
so greatly to the welfare of his fellow man as he.
Ernest Bashor was raised a Master Mason in Sunset Lodge N o. 352
on July 30, 1918, and guided his Lodge as Master in 1935. For twentytwo years he was a member of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board
and for fourteen years its Chairman. During his tenure the Endowment
Fund increased from one to seven million dollars.
Ernest Bashor was a complete man. Consider this: He was a practicing physician and surgeon for fifty years, specializing in Obstetrics
and Gynecology. senior on the staff of the Los Angeles County Hospital.
and founder-board member of Monte Sano Hospital.
As a member of Kiwanis, he served as President of the Los Angeles
Club, District Governor and International Trustee. For forty years he
was a member of. and past president of. the Los Angeles Breakfast Club.
For almost the same period of time Ernest Bashor was a member of the
Board of Directors of McKinley Home for Boys, serving as President
of the Board for nearly half that time.
When he died on March 1. 1969, California Freemasonry lost one of
its most stalwart and courageous members. His family lost a devoted

words of the poet " .. . showed the names whom love of God had blest
and lo: Ernest Bashor' s name led all the rest."

Lester George Bruno by Harold N. Richards, Grand Lecturer-We
who survive, we who ourselves are "only waiting 'til the shadows are a
little longer," pay now a last tribute of that respect and affection we
have for Lester George Bruno, who was summoned from our midst by
Our Supreme Grand Master quite suddenly on April 1, 1969. thus bringing to a close a brilliant Masonic career at its very zenith.
He was a powerful influence upon the youth and Masonic fabric of
his times. His virtues are engraved upon the hearts of those who knew
him best. Gifted with extraordinary natural abilities. directed by unswerving fidelity to his own convictions. matured by reflection and experience. he rose rapidly in his devotion to Masonry and humanity.
Starting with Sacramento Chapter Order of De Molay he became
Master Councilor. After reaching his majority year he still maintained
his interest, serving on the advisory council. chairmaning that group,
Chapter Dad Advisor for several years, rising to State Dad Advisor for
Northern California and finally. at the time of his death was an honorary
member of the International Supreme Council. Order of De Molay.
On this platform this evening it will be our pleasure to be entertained
by a wonderful group of boys and girls from our Youth Orders-the
Northern California De Molay Show and Band. Les Bruno was one of
the organizers of the De Molay Show and Band, serving as president
at the time of his death. He was a key figure in the development of this
nationally recognized and highly praised organization.
He was a strong supporter and offered much encouragement to the
young men of the Chapter. He was never too busy to sit down and
counsel or off er encouragement to a young chap with something on his
mind. Les's nature dictated these little acts of thoughtfulness, not for
public relations, not for personal acclaim, but simply because Les liked
young people. and was vitally interested in their welfare.
Born in El Dorado, his early years and school days were spent in
the Sacramento and San Joaquin Valleys. He was a successful vinyardist in his later years, retiring about two years ago.
Petitioning Capital City Lodge No. i99, F. & A.M. in 1929 he rose
through the chairs to grace the oriental chair in the East in 19i 1. He
remained an active participant in Blue Lodge Masonry throughout his
Masonic career and served as Master of the Northern California Past
Masters Association a few years ago.

Becoming a 32nd Degree Scottish Rite Mason in 1951, he immediately became active on the stage crew and later in ritualistic work.
He served the Sacramento Bodies of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite in many capacities: As Venerable Master of the Lodge of Perfection in both 1961 and 1962; as Director of the Temple Board for many
years. and more recently as Degree Administrator for all the Degrees.
In 1957 he received the honor and decoration of Knight Commander
of the Court of Honor and coroneted a 33rd Degree Inspector General
Honorary by the Supreme Council of the Southern Jurisdiction of the
Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite.
In 1968 he was designated the Sacramento Valley Representative
for the Sovereign Grand Inspector General of California for the Scottish
Rite.
In 1952 he became a member of Ben Ali Temple of the Shrine, and
worked diligently on the stage crew and on various committees. He was
appointed to the Divan three years ago, and at the time of his death he
was serving as Oriental Guide in the progressive line of Ben Ali Temple.
A champion and defender of freedom and the public schools. a gifted
leader of the good fight, a master of the "retort courteous," a wit and
lover of life, his was a powerful personality and a luminous mind. He
has left a lasting mark for good upon the men and events of his time.
The California Legislature. by Resolution of the Assembly Rules
Committee, recognized Lester G. Bruno's accomplishments in the areas
of service to youth, to Freemasonry. and to his community. and expressed
its regret at the passing of "a man of character and devotion to his
fellowman."
Another Mason, Edwin Markham, the poet, expressed a philosophy
subscribed to by many of us:
"There is a destiny that makes us brothers
None goes his way alone
All that we send into the lives of others
Comes back into our own."
Such was the life, philosophy. and purpose of Lester G. Bruno-And such was his reward!

Irvin Shulkin-A Life of Love and Harmony-We are taught that
"though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels and have not
love, I am become as sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal. . . . And now
abideth faith . hope and love, these three, but the greatest of these is
love; and ...
"As harmony is essential. so should harmony continue to be the
strength and support of all sm:ieties. esp.:cially of ours."
Irvin Shulkin's life is filled with love and ha rmony. Constantly displayed in his smile and in his every act, he led a joyous and happy life of
dedication and service to his God, his family, his neighbor and his friend.

22

PROCEEDIN GS OP THE

Irv was born in Sioux City. Iowa on March 17, 1906. The down-toearth simplicity of that typically Midweste rn town marked him throughout his whole life with us. Without pretense. without self-pride or ego,
he sought perfection in everything he did , and, having attained perfection, wore it with his characteri stic humility.
Harmony was exhibited in early youth. and through the medium of
music, he brought happiness to others. Having perfected himself in the
trumpet. Irv left the town of Sioux City behind. and in the 20s traveled
with the bands of that day, starting out with Red Nichols and graduatin g
to such big bands as Jimmy Greer, the Dorsey Brothers and Paul
Whiteman .
It was while playing with Phil Harris in San Francisco that Irv
met his life-long partner, Nora, then singing with Meredith Willson.
They met at the famous St. Francis Hotel and were married in I 933.
Their children , Katherine Kristine and Steffen, known as Kathy and
Steff to their family and friends. attest through the dose harmony of
the Shulkin family to Irv and Nora's virtuosity in family life.
With the coming of the children, a more settled life became the
family, and Irv settled into studio and radio work. It was in I 945 that
he became a Mason, and quite naturally. petitioned Silver Trowel Lodge
No. 415 in Hollywoo d.
Here, again, the harmony of Masonry captured Irv's imagination.
and in the rhythms of our ritual. he saw a challenge and reward. His
abilities soon found recognition, and he rose through the officer corps
to service as Master in 1954.
In 1962, the call to service again was heard and Irv was drafted to
serve as Inspector of the 568th Masonic District. The officers and
members of Benjamin Franklin. Ionic, Beverly Hills and John Marshall
Lodges present at his memorial service bear testimony of Irv's untiring
devotion to each of them. Through triumphs and defeats. through joy
and near despair, through all of the satisfactio ns and disappoin tments of
Lodge life, he guided them like the conductor of a great orchestra, calling
on each for all that could be given and blending in his own talents to
produce the harmony and perfection which was his own mark.
Irv's happiest years Masonica lly were spent in the lnspectora l Corps.
Here he met equally devoted and dedicated men, and, with them, practiced the art, making and giving friendship unselfishly.
Surely, no man could go to his Maker from a scene dearer to his
heart than that of Thursday night, October 2nd. Playing a role in the
raising of Robert A. Crigler. Jr.. son of our Grand Master, Irvin Shulkin
went with death the kind messenger sent to translate him from this imperfect to that all-perfect . glorious and celestial Lodge above, where the
Supreme Grand Master of the universe forever presides.
There love and harmony will also forever prevail for our departed
Brother.

Frank Wade Raddatz- Past Master. Meridian Lodge No. 667.
f. & A. M. Inspector. 524th Masonic District, Grand Lodge F. & A. M.
of California , February 18. 1899. to October 1. 1969.
"After the tempest-c alm,
After the shadow-l ight,
And the golden dawn breaks clearly
After the long, long night,
After the rain, the sunshine,
After the tears. the laughter,
And when this life is over,
Life eternal follows after."
A belief in God and immortalit y is a requireme nt for all who would
become members of the Masonic Fraternity and, possessing this b~lief.
frank Raddatz could accept the transition from life as we know 1t to
life eternal with understan ding and without fear.
On October 1, 1969, the Masons in the Glendale area were stunned
to learn that their beloved Inspector had suffered an unexpecte d, fatal
heart attack while on a short vacation just prior to this Communi cation
of Grand Lodge.
Frank was close to me in that he was an officer of Meridian Lodge
No. 667 during my years as Inspector of the old 86th Masonic D istrict
and it was my privilege to install him as Master of his Lodge in 1949.
Then it became my great pleasure to recommen d him to be my
successor in 1950 and to have him as my Inspector during the past 19
years.
•
.
Funeral services, including the Masonic service, were conducted m
the First Baptist Church in Glendale on October 4th in the presence of
675 friends including 225 Masons . Indicative of the esteem in which
Frank was held was the presence of the Grand M aster and the Assistant
Grand Lecturer of Division 5 who assisted as pall-beare rs . Also present
were the Senior Grand Warden , three Past Grand Masters and nu merous Grand Officers, Inspectors and Grand Lodge committeemen.
Frank was born in Stockton , Utah on February 18. 1899 and he
spent most of his adult years in Los Angeles County. Except for a six
months period in 1942, during which he was a member of the Un ited
States Air Force, Frank's business career was with the Purchasin g Department of the County. In February of this year, after '16 years of
service, he retired as Chief Deputy Purchasin g Agent and a testimonial
dinner at the Huntingto n-Sherato n Hotel in Pasadena , attended by a
large group of business associates and Masons. was evidence of the
esteem in which Frank was held.
In addition to a number of profession al societies to which he belonged, Frank was a member of the Los Angeles County Acacia Club and
the Los Angeles Bodies of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite in
which he had been an active member since 1955.

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

It was in the course of his business activities that Frank met the one
who was to be his loyal and faithful help-mate, H arriet, to whom he was
joined in marriage on October 12. 194 2. There can be no question but
that much of Frank's successes in business and fraternal life were due to
the inspiration he received from his devoted wife.
In addition to his wife, Frank is survived by two brothers-Otto . also
a Past Master of Meridian Lodge, and Richard. These and other relatives mourn his passing.
It is interesting to note that of 187 Inspectors presently serving the
Grand Lodge of California, Frank ranked ninth in seniority-trul y a
remarkable record of faithful service-solely for the betterment of
Masonry and his fellow man-and with no thought of personal gain.
Plain and unpretentious in his demeanor and habits, Frank was at
ease with all men- and they with him. Plain spoken and uncompromising when occasion required, yet he offered friendliness. compassion
and understanding -and his dry wit and humor were relished by his
friends.
Frank was a quiet man-a good listener-and a good thinker. When
he spoke it was with conviction. Frank was dependable-o ne of the
stalwarts so necessary to the success of whatever the project might be.
Frank meant much to the officers and members of the Lodges which
came under his care during his years as Inspector.
He was affectionately called "Mother" Raddatz because he helped
bring so many new Lodges into existence. Frank was also highly regarded by his fellow Inspectors. the Grand Lodge Officers and committeemen and by every Grand Master under whom he served because of
his capabilities, his devotion to Masonry and his willingness, always, to
serve whenever called upon.
And. most importa ntly, these attributes relating to Frank's character
carried over into his home life. He and Harriet shared their lives together as few couples are privileged to do. Notwithstandi ng his contributions for others, the ties of home and family always came first in the
scheme of life for Frank.
In bringing these remarks to a close. perhaps we can fasten on just
one of Fra nk's many attributes to place among our memories. I spea k
of his humbleness-n ot in the sense of a weakness but, rather, in his
a ppreciation of the many blessings he considered to be his.
This causes me to think of one illustrious in Masonic history, a man
called upon to help build a t em ple. A humble man, he did not bear the
title of king as did his two associates-he was the architect who drew
the designs upon the trestleboard whereby his Brethren might pursue
their labors. As a leader of Masonry in his community, Frank, too, was
an architect who drew designs upon the trestleboard that his Brethren
might fulfill their tasks. And to one so engaged, no greater honor can
come than to be known as a builder of men .

To the memory of Frank Raddatz, we speak these few words penned
by Winn MacCourt:
.
"Friends are treasures we receive as onward through our lives we go.
Ones to count on we believe-to share our happiness and woe.
A smile, a word, a friendly deed brings with it all that we do needto brighten up a cloudy day,
God bless our friend-for this we pray."

EULOGY
ARTHUR PAULSEN

By L. Harold Anderson
I am indeed indebted to our Most Worshipful Grand Master for the
privilege of devoting a few minutes in a service of loving memory and
deep appreciation for our Past Grand Master Arthur Paulsen. He was a
great and good man, a much beloved friend , a dedicated Masonic
Brother and a true Christian gentleman.
When I first became acquainted with Brother Paulsen and had the
opportunity to know him so well was when he and I were appointed as
two of the members of a Special Committee of three for the Masonic
Homes. At this time I was serving as President of the California State
Public Utilities Commission and Brother Paulsen was a Superior Court
Judge from Weaverville, having served in that capacity since 1933. His
kindly legal mind was of most importance in the work of the committee.
Arthur Paulsen was born in Weaverville May 4, 1890. the son of
Peter M. and Barbara Paulsen. California pioneers of Gold Rush days.
Peter Paulsen engaged not only in mining, the common pursuit of the
day, but also in the hotel business in Weaverville.
Arthur Paulsen received his early education in Weaverville, and
was admitted to the practice of law in California March 12, 1917. Elected
to the office of District Attorney of Trinity County in January 1923, he
filled the post with distinction. He became a judge of the Superior Court
of Trinity County in January 1933, a position in which he has distinguished himself. Judge Paulsen is recognized by his colleagues as being
possessed of a very fine legal mind, and much of his time was spent away
from Weaverville holding court in various parts of the state at the request and direction of the State Judicial Council.
·Responding to the call of bis country in 1917, he enlisted in World
War I. and served in the 144tb Field Artillery in F ranee.
Arthur Paulsen and Jennie Skinner were married in Sacramento
October 21, 1919, and to them was born a daughter, Gloria Evelyn.
His Masonic career has been one of service to Trinity Lodge No. 27,
where he was raised August 2, 1913. and to the Grand Lodge of California. His first position in Trinity Lodge No. 27 was that of Senior
Deacon and he became Master in 1924. He was appointed Junior Grand
Deacon of the Grand Lodge in 1941 and in 1943 very capably filled the
office of Grand Orator. He served as a member of the Committee on
Charters, the Committee on Jurisprudence, the Special Committee on
the Masonic Homes, and the Special Committee on Masonic Homes
Admissions. In 194 7 be was elected the Junior Grand Warden of Grand
Lodge, and served successively as Senior Grand Warden, and Deputy
Grand Master until his election as Grand Master in 1950.
Judge Paulsen was a member of Royal Arch Masons, serving as High

Priest of Trinity Chaper, later consolidated with Shasta Chapter No. 19.
As might be expected of a judge and an outstanding citizen of his
own county, Arthur Paulsen has been identified with all worthwhile
public services including the Red Cross, Tuberculosis Association, the
Boy Scouts, and crippled children's organizations. His other memberships include the American Legion, Veterans of Foreign Wars, the
Order of Odd Fellows, and the Native Sons of the Golden West. With
all his activity, he still found the time to serve on the Board of Trustees
of Trinity Congregational Church in Weaverville.
It has been well said that "It is the lot of many to rule; to rule
well is the fortune of but few" and no better single descriptive phrase
could be chosen for the term of Grand Master Paulsen. When it was
necessary to rule, he ruled well, with firmness and impartiality. Perhaps
it was the fact that he lived in a remote, mountainous county, far removed from the stress and strain of city life, that gave him such dear
objective thinking on the problems of the Grand Lodge, but whatever
it was, the depth of his understanding was matched only by his sincerity
in applying the principles of Freemasonry to the situations which confronted him. He will long be respected for meeting and talking with the
Brethren "on the level" and he will likewise be well remembered for his
intense interest in the program of Masonic education.
As time adds luster to the names of men who build well in organizations, the name of Arthur Paulsen will stand out in the long list of men
who have served the Grand Lodge of California during the past one
hundred twenty years.

EDGAR V . STEWART , JR.
By Ellsworth Meyer

the next two Grand Masters also chose him for that office, a distinction
indeed. Thereafter he was appointed an Inspector and reappointed
until, after five years, he was elected Junior Grand Warden. He advanced and in October, 1955. was elected Grand M aster.
D uring the ensuing year, his sense of humor prompted him to repeatedly point out another distinction. that, due to the changing of the
dates for the Annual Communication. he was bound to serve the shortest full term of any Grand Master, only forty-seven weeks. It was a
busy yea r, for he constituted seventeen newly chartered Lodges. laid
seventeen cornerstones and attended to all the receptions, breakfasts and
other affairs associated with the office. In February. he was elected
chairman of the Conference of Grand M as ters, hence he presided over
the 1956 conference and opened the 1957 session.
On the completion of his term as our Grand Master, he served for
two years on the Committee on Policy and General Purposes and then
was appointed to the Board of Trustees of our Masonic Homes. He
was reappointed for two additional terms of three years or the constitutional maximum of nine years. during the las t seven of which he was
president of the board. For the year I 968. he returned to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
I have enumerated these dates. offices and committee appointments
to recall to our minds that continuously for twenty-four years he was
serving this Grand Lodge as an officer, committeeman or board mem ~
ber and that, in succession , sixteen Grand Masters had found him
worthy and well qualified for different tasks. These official acts speak
more eloquently than any words I could conjure up, but do not completely delineate the man.
Of medium height, he was always impeccably attired. His voice was
pleasantly deep and carried well. During thirty-three years of contact
with him , from one to three times each week, never once did I hear his
voice raised in anger. Profanity he knew not. All his friends knew of
his religious devotion, but he never intruded it into conversations or the
affairs of others. He lived his faith, but did not expect all others to conform to the standards he set for himself. When it was his duty to be
somewhere, he invariably was there. When he had some task to per~
form, he punctually performed it without flurry or ostentation. His days
-his life, were of even tenor and of service to mankind . He builded
well.
Of Ned Stewart and the four hundred and s ixty-four other members of this Grand Lodge who have stepped across the Great Threshhold, we are confident that they are " happy in our Father's mansion,
busy in another room."

?n. M ay 22 of this year, another of our P ast Grand Masters gained
adm1ss1on to that celestial lodge which never. never closes, Brother
Edgar V . Stewart. Jr .. 90th Grand Master of this jurisdiction. He is
survived by his beloved wife, Marion.
Ned, as all his many friends affectionately called him. was born in
Brooklyn, New York, in 1901 and his parents brought him to Los Angeles at an early age. His education w as in the public schools of that
city and he was graduated from Manual Arts High School. He continued his education by attendance at a business college and through
university extension courses.
He first entered retail trade but then turned to what became his
life work, that of an insurance underwriter. In his chosen field, he was
indeed successful, but he devoted a substantial part of his years to the
service of others.
For more than twenty years, he was a member of the board of directors of the Midnight Mission. one of the largest charitable organizations in Los Angeles and twice served as president of the board. He was
an active, devoted member of the First Church of Christ. Scientist, in
Beverly Hills , served on its board of directors and a term as president
of the board.
On this occasion. we shall principally note his M asonic career, which
was long, distinguished and marked by several unusual features.
Ned received his degrees in Loyalty Lodge, Los Angeles; the first
but seven months after his twenty-first birthday and his third seven
months later in December, 1923. Distinction number one, he was appointed Chaplain for the ensuing year. He continued to advance in
office and five years later was elected M aster for the year 1929. Distincton number two, he was the first Master of Loyalty Lodge who
had received the degrees therein.
While he was advancing in his Lodge. he received the degrees of
the Scottish Rite in the Los Angeles Bodies. Being a good ritualist, he
was soon busy in several of the degrees of the Rite and was invested
with the rank and decoration of Knight Commander of the Court of
Honor in 1937 and coroneted with the Thirty-third Degree in 1943.
Two years later he was appointed a director of degree work and elected
Junior Warden of the Lodge of Perfection. He continued in the first
capacity for 18 years until 1961 and served as Junior or Senior Warden
for 25 years until 1968, when he was elected Venerable Master.

On Friday, October 14, 1966 you, my Brethren, representing all the
Masons in California and Hawaii designated me to represent you in
this great Grand Lodge by electing me to the station of Junior Grand
Warden. One year later on Friday, October 13, 1967 you continued
your mandate by electing me Deputy Grand Master and last October
18th you placed in my hands the highest honor and the greatest responsibility which is in your power to grant to any man, Grand Master of
Masons in C alifornia and Hawaii. On that day of installation one year
ago, which will live forever in my memory, I prayed that our Supreme
Grand Master would favor me with divine guidance and assistance
and that He would never let me forget that I represented all the Masons
in our jurisdiction.
As your Grand Master and your chief executive officer, you have
specifically charged me to exercise a general and careful supervision
over the Craft and see that the Constitution and regulations of the
Grand Lodge are strictly maintained, supported and obeyed.
In reporting to you the activities of your Grand Master during the
past year, I will echo the comments of my predecessor s, "It has been
a most active year."
The itinerary attached to this message chronicles the travels and
events in which the Grand Master or others representing him, participated. There were many outstanding Masonic events during the year
and though time and space prevent the delineation of all of them, the
following are deserving of special recognition.
ALL MASONIC FAMILY RECEPTION FOR THE GRAND MASTER

On Sunday, November 17, 1968, at 2:00 p.m. in the Los Angeles
Sports Arena, climaxing two years of preparation, the Inspectors of the
Fifth Division hosted a reception for the Grand Master unlike any
ever held before. They named it "The First All M asonic Family Reception for the Grand Master" and invited all the affiliated and concordant
bodies to participate. Among the more than thirteen thousand in attendance, the following distinguishe d members of the Masonic family paid
their respects to the office of the Grand Master and were most generous
with their kind remarks. Henry C. Clausen. Past Grand M aster of the
Grand Lodge of California and Deputy Grand Commander of the
Supreme Council of the Scottish Rite, Southern Jurisdiction; Lovell E.
Spurgeon, Grand Commander , Knights Templar; J. W. Combes, Grand
High Priest, Royal Arch Masons; Arthur B. Ledbetter, Illustrious Grand
Master of the Grand Council, Royal and Select Masters; Leo E. Anderson, Past Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of C alifornia and Potentate
of Al Malaikah Shrine Temple; Mrs. Florence Dunn, Worthy Grand

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

of having a daughter who is an airline stewardess is that the parents
receive greatly reduced fares. We availed ourselves of this unusual
opportun~ty and Mrs. Crigler and I left Los Angeles on December 30,
1968, flymg over the polar route on Scandinavian Airlines to Copenhagen. The connecting Hight took us to Zurich where we were delayed
at the airport for six hours because of a severe snowstorm. We continued on to New Delhi and then to Madras. a coastal city on the
southeastern tip of India where the Grand Festival Communication of
the Grand Lodge of India was held in Rajaji Hall. We were warmly and
~raciously received during our stay in this beautiful city whose climate
ts comparable to our city of San Diego.
The Grand Lodge of India was opened in a highly dignified and
colorful manner by Most Worshipful Bhogilal C. Shah, the Grand
Master, who then directed a special escort composed of the Deputy
Grand Master, the four Regional Grand Masters, the Deputy Grand
Directors of Ceremonies, the President of the Board of General Purposes, the Grand Secretary, the Grand Deacons and the two Assistant
Grand Directors of Ceremonies, to escort your Grand Master in to the
Grand Lodge. I was accorded a warm and enthusiastic reception and
was highly honored by being seated in the East on the right of the
Grand Master. Acting on your behalf. I presented to the Grand Lodge
of India, a beautiful baton which had been handcrafted in California
by one of our members. The workmanship on this baton was outstanding
and reflected the many hours of painstaking labor necessary to the
accomplishment. The Brother who performed this work of art wished
to remain anonymous but a letter thanking him for the unselfish donation of his remarkable talents was sent to him by your Grand Master.
During our brief stay, our constant guide and host was Sir Harold,
Lieutenant General Williams, former Deputy Grand Master and presently the Regional Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Northern
India. We are indebted to him for his many acts of kindness. The Grand
Lodge of India concluded its communication with the election and installation to the office of Grand Master of Most Worshipful M. S. Thacker.
Brother Thacker is a genial and learned man and has been awarded the
highest distinction and honor that can be conferred by the government
of India, the title of Padma Bhushan. He and his charming wife were
most gracious to us as were the Maharajah of Faridkot, the newly
installed Assistant Grand Master, and Z. R. Irani, the Senior Grand
Warden. Their hospitality and friendship will remain long in our hearts.

The intended recipient was delighted at the prospect of rece1vmg his
button and with the exception of his broken hip, was in fairly good
health. The button was forwarded to the Inspector by the Grand Secretary on May 21. 1969. On May 19, 1969 prior to the presentation date
but subsequent to his eligibility date, the Brother suffered a fatal stroke
and on May 30, 1969. died. The daughter has asked for the button.
Under our law, as presently constituted , I had to deny her request.
Under Section 150 j of the California Masonic Code, Grand Master
Warren ruled and Grand Lodge concurred that "the fifty-year button
may not be presented posthumously to the family." In 1957, Grand
Lodge approved the ruling of Grand Master L. Harold Anderson that
the "application for a fifty-year button should not be made where the
Brother is confined to a state hospital and has little contact with reality
since the ceremony would have no meaning." My Brethren, there have
been many instances where the recipient of a flfty-year button has passed
away shortly after the presentation. In some cases. within hours; in
others, within a few days or weeks. Some recipients. for personal reasons,
have had their fifty-year buttons mailed to them at their request, not
wishing to have a presentation ceremony. It is conceivable and probable
that in this latter category some may never have received or seen the
button personally. It, therefore, seems inconsistent to me that one
Brother can receive his button on the day of eligibility, pass to his eternal
reward shortly thereafter with his heirs retaining possession of the
button to do with as they please, while another Brother's family or
heirs are denied the same consideration because the Brother desired a
presentation ceremony but died before the event could become a reality.
It would seem to be discriminatory and not in keeping with our practice
of fair and equal treatment for all.

I'. therefo~e, recommend that the incoming Grand Master appoint a
special committee whose duty and responsibility it will be to continue
~o prepare a new. revised Code for the consideration of the Grand Lodge
m accordance with the mandate of Grand Lodge as outlined in Grand
Masters Dayton's recommendatio n No. 7 (amended) and Grand
Master Hopp's recommendatio n No. 6.

I recently received a request from an Inspector for direction and
guidance, in answering a letter he had received concerning a fifty-year
veteran's button. The facts are as follows. A Brother was eligible to
receive his fifty-year button on May 5, 1969. On that date he was
a pa tient in the Veterans' Home at Yountville, having suffered a broken
hip. The Veterans' Home was a considerable distance from the Brother's
Lodge and the Secretary of the Lodge corresponded with and endeavored to have the button presented by the Inspector of the district
nearest to the Veterans' Home. This Inspector paid a visit to the
hospital on May 1, J 969, and made arrangements for the presentation.

RECOMMENDAT ION No. 3

I. therefore, recommend that annotations j and I under Section l 50
of the California Masonic Code be repealed and that it be the policy
of this Grand Lodge to provide upon request, a fifty-year button to the
family or heirs of a deceased Brother, provided the Brother was eligible
for but had not received such a button prior to his death.

BOARD OP CONTROL

In order to assist the special committee on study of Sojourner Relief
and the Board of Relief system. I requested the Board of Control to
make a complete in-depth study of existing operations, practices and
procedures of all Boards of Relief. A detailed and comprehensive survey
was undertaken by the Board of Control. After reviewing the accumulated information, it was apparent that in order to properly assess our
problems and endeavor to solve them, it would be necessary to request
strict compliance of our laws and regulations from all Boards of Relief.
Only then could it be ascertained if our laws and regulations needed to
be changed or modified to meet our Masonic responsibility and commitments. At my request, the Board of Control endeavored to secure
compliance with our law from all Boards of Relief. In most instances,
their task was made easier by the wholehearted cooperation of the
Brethren in charge. On a few occasions when friendly persuasion failed,
sterner measures were needed. The Board of Control will present a
complete report to you and I wish to commend personally, each of the
members thereof for the time, the patience and the perseverance expended by them in discharging their duties.

DEc1s10N No. 1

I was asked if it would be proper for a Lodge to rent its facilities
to a clandesti ne lodge and also if it would be permissible for a Lodge to
rent a lodge facility from a clandesti ne lodge. The answer to both
question s is NO. It is not permissible for a Lodge to rent its hall to or rent
J hall from a clandesti ne lodge or organiza tion
which purports to be
Masonic in characte r. To permit the use of the same Masonic hall by
Loth a regular Lodge and a clandesti ne lodge might well be interpret ed
by those both in and out of the Craft as recognition o~ Ma~onic inte:course, clearly proscribe d by Section 319 of the Californ ia Masomc
Code.
DECISION No. 2
A Lodge was having financial problems and stated they ':'~re no
longer able to maintain or retain their hall. They as~ed permission to
form a commun ity hall associati on which would be incorpor ated as a
non-profit corporati on. The Lodge proposed to sell the hall to the nonprofit corporat ion for one dollar and then become a tenant. I held that
it would be illegal to sell the property to an association for one dollar.
It would be a gift of its property for the benefit of the associati on if
the reasonab le market value exceeded one dollar and a Lodge may not
thus dispose of an asset. It seemed to me that if the p:oposed c~m­
munity hall associati on could operate successfu lly by rentmg the build-

BROTHERLY LovE AND RELIEF

Two extraordinary events exemplifying the Masonic principles of
brotherly love and relief occurred in our jurisdiction which merit our
applause and approbation. In January. heavy and continued rains caused
severe damage and flooding in the community of Santa Paula. Many
families lost their homes and most of their possessions. Some were
stranded without food . shelter or clothing. The officers and members
of Santa Paula Lodge No. 291 opened their temple and proceeded to
care for and feed forty~eight refugees, men, women and children who
had been driven from their homes; a stirring testimonial of Masons
assuming their obligation toward their fellowmen.
On your behalf I sent a letter of commendation to the Masons of
Santa Paula Lodge No. 291 for their inspirational action.
In the summer of 1 968, seven teenage youths from California
journeyed thirteen hundred miles into Mexico for a vacation of sur.fing
at the seaside village of San Blas. Because of an abundance of mosqu1tos.
they forsook their campers and rented a house to sleep in. While playing
their musical tape recordings one night, the police came to investigate
the loud music which evidently had disturbed the neighbors. In searching
the premises, the police discovered two marijuana butts in an abandoned
chest of drawers. The boys denied knowledge of the marijuana but were
arrested and charged with possession of marijuana, a federal offense.
and placed in a Mexican state penitentiary. The parents of the boys
hired a prominent and highly regarded defense lawyer in Mexico to
represent the youths. In addition, a Congressman and a United States
Senator endeavored to intercede through the State Department. All
efforts met with failure and the boys were still in the penitentiary in
December. When Dallas Roose, our Senior Grand Steward from
Chula Vista, was apprised of the matter he journeyed across the border
to Tijuana to discuss the case with Joaquin Aguilar Robles. a Past
Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Baja California who had offered
his assistance. This good Brother from our sister jurisdiction across the
border effected the release of the boys on Christmas Day and arranged
to have them flown from Mexico City to San Diego for a joyous and
tearful reunion with their families.
On my recent visit to the Grand Lodge of Baja California, I had the
honor and privilege of meeting Past Grand Master Robles and personal-

INSURANCE

On assuming the office of Grand Master last October, I appointed
an Insurance Committee and charged them to study and evaluate the
entire insurance program of Grand Lodge and its entities and to make
recommendations thereon to the Grand Master. To this committee, I
appointed the very finest and most knowledgeable Master Masons I
could find. Samuel C. Levin, a Past Master of Pacific Lodge No. 136 and
long active in the insurance business as a broker in San Francisco was
Chairman. The committee also included Harry B. Keeling . Past Master
of Henry Knox Lodge No. 662. He heads his own firm. employing a
large staff with headquarters in the Wilshire District in Los Angeles
and is considered to be one of the foremost insurance agents and
brokers in Southern California. The other members of the committee
are William G. Deeble, a Past Master of All States Lodge No. 593
and a prominent, capable insurance man from Long Beach; Samuel E.
Harris. Past Master of Temple City Lodge No. 612. an insurance executiv~ .with the Continental Assurance Company. They worked long
and diligently and spent many hours away from their own businesses
in the pursuit of their assignment. They are men of the highest ethics
and moral integrity and did not receive nor would they accept remuneration of any kind for their services; choosing to serve in an advisory
capacity because of their love for the Fraternity. Their recommendations which were concurred in by your Grand Master have resulted
in our insurance coverages being increased and broadened for relatively
the same cost and in some instances, savings were effected.
I express to each of these Master Masons my commendation for the
excellence of their labors.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRANO LODGE ADMINISTRATION

The administrative duties of the Grand Master in recent years
have increased tremendously and this year has been no exception,
necessitating many hours of labor by the Grand Master in the Grand
Lodge office. In addition, your Grand Master has attended most of
the meetings of the Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial
Temple and the Trustees of our Masonic Homes. The activities of
these boards have also increased substantially.
The overall operation of our Grand Lodge and its entities involves
the expenditure of hundreds of thousands of dollars annually as well
as the employment of numerous personnel. As a businessman, I share
the concern of Past Grand Master Myron E. Smith who stated to this
Grand Lodge. "The funds of the Grand Lodge are trust funds and
their use should be regulated with precision and exactness." In these
days of inflation, rapidly rising costs and decreased purchasing power
of the dollar, it should be our constant endeavor to improve the administration and operation of our Grand Lodge by effecting such economies
as may from time to time be desirable or necessary. As most successful
and well organized businesses periodically survey their operations and
procedures, to see if any improvement could be made, so should we
do likewise.
RECOMMENDATION No. 4

It is, therefore, my recommendation that the incoming Grand Master
appoint a special committee, three of whose members shall consist of the
Deputy Grand Master, the Senior and Junior Grand Wardens who will
cause to be made, an in-depth study of the administration and operation
of our Grand Lodge and its entities with a view toward effecting
economies and improving efficiency. I further recommend that provision be made in the budget for the necessary expenses of the committee
and that the committee report its recommendations at our next Annual
Communication.

on the finger of my only son, Robert A. Crigler, Jr .. on the occasion of
my raising him to the sublime degree of Master Mason in Redondo
Lodge No. 328. Only those of you who have experienced this supreme
moment of fulfillment can know the joy in my heart. The intervening

CONCLUSI ON

Just three years ago you filled my cup to overflowing when you
elected me Junior Grand Warden and now as I am about to lay down
the gavel. I do so in the knowledg e that Masonry is the greatest force
for moral good in the world today and that you have accorded me an
honor which comes to but few men, that of leading the Craft in California
and Hawaii.
These years have been the most rewarding of my life. The opportunity to meet and enjoy Masonic fellowship with thousands of members
of the Craft and the pleasure of working with my Brothers in the advancemen t of our ideals and principles will always remain close to
my heart.
To you, my Brethren, I shall be eternally grateful.
These things I believe - That all Masons are equal and each,
regardless of station, rank or office must be treated equally. That
Masonry has no special privileges or special considerat ions to bestow
on any Mason or group of Masons except the privilege of service. In
the light of this knowledg e and belief it has been my constant endeavor
to perform these duties and all other duties delegated to the Grand
Master by you who are the Grand Lodge.
Those who have preceded us have given .us a priceless possession ,
Freemaso nry, and today the quality of the Craft in our jurisdictio n
has never been higher. It remains for you and me to continue to elevate
it toward the ultimate goal of all Masons, the Brotherho od of man under
the Fatherhoo d of God.
Almost two thousand years ago, the greatest of all teachers said, "A
new commandm ent I give unto you, that ye love one another." My
Brethren, in that short sentence we have been given the perfect definition of Freemaso nry. As Master Masons, it is given to us strictly in
charge, ever to walk and act.

RECOMME NDATION No. 3

The Committe e on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand M aster has recommen ded that annotation s j and 1 appearing under Section 150 of the California Masonic Code, which places
certain restrictions upon the presentati on of a fifty-year button if the
recipient dies after becoming eligible but before receiving the button
or if he is confined in a state hospital and is unable to comprehe nd the
presentati on.
The recommen dation arose from a case detailed by the Grand Master in his message. A Brother became eligible on May 5, 1969. He was
connned in a hospital a considerab le distance from bis home. Arrangements were completed for the presentati on but before the button reached
the area the Brother suffered a stroke from which he did not recover
and died eleven days later. H is daughter requested the button , but it
could not be presented under earlier decisions which had been approved
by the Grand Lodge.

56

57

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRANO LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that no
distinction should exist, to give one example, between two Brothers
both of whom become eligible but one of whom requests that the button be mailed to him instead of being formally presented and he dies
after it has been placed in the mails and another Brother, who is willing
to have the button formally presented but dies before the presentation
is made. The family of the first would receive the button but under existing law the family of the second would not.
Your Committee is cognizant, however, that such buttons have been
presented since 1928. If the recommended change in policy were adopted
without any limitation thereon as to retroactive opera tion, it is possible
that hundreds of requests might be made now as to Brothers who died
ten, twenty or thirty years ago. In changing our policy it does not appear to your Committee that it is desirable to make the change prior
to the start of the current year. We, therefore, recommend that the
change of policy in relation to deceased Brothers be limited to Brethren
whose eligibility occurs on or after January 1, 1969.
The Committee on Jurisprudence will present the proper implementation of the recommendation as so modified and we recommend a
"yes" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
To effect the implementation of the Grand Master's Recommendation Number 3, the Committee on Jurisprudence proposes the following:
RESOLVED, that annotations "j'' and ")'' under Section 150 of
the California Masonic Code be deleted and that an annotation to said
section be added as follows: "It is the policy of the Grand Lodge to
provide upon request a fifty-year button to the family or heirs of a deceased or incompetent brother who becomes eligible for such button
after January 1, 1969, provided that, in the case of a deceased hrother
he was eligible for but had not received such button prior to his death,
and, in the case of an incompetent brother, that he is otherwise eligible."
Adopted 5/ 6 vote.
RECOMMENDATION No. i
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master has stated that most succe~sful and well organized businesses periodically survey their operations and procedures to
see if any improvement could be made and he has recommended that
the incoming Grand Master appoint a special committee, which committee shall report its recommendations at our next Annual Communication, as to any possible economies or improved efficiencies in the operation of our Grand Lodge. the Masonic Homes or Memorial Temple.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is cognizant that
on several occasions in past years a special committee has been created
to make a study of one or more of our entities to the same ends. Such
committees have, from time to time, produced valuable recommendations

to the Grand Lodge. So rapidly are improvements being made in mechanical and electronic devices for the storing of data, the reproduction of
documents and the performance of clerical tasks, that this committee
believes the time is ripe for the appointment of a special committee.
The Grand Master has further recommended that the incoming
Deputy Grand Master. Senior and Junior Grand Wardens be included
in the membership of this committee. The Committee on Policy and
General Purposes is cognizant that the ever increasing demands made
upon the time and energies of the Brethren occupying these stations
has been a matter of grave concern to them and to the Grand Lodge.
so much so that a study was made and as a result Resolution Number
Ten is on our agenda to relieve the Deputy Grand Master from serving
on the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes and to relieve both
the Senior and Junior Grand Wardens from serving on the Bomd of
Trustees of the Memorial Temple.
We believe the time required to serve on the proposed special
committee might exceed the time saved by the proposed relief. We recognize that the added familiarity with the operations of the Gra nd
Lodge and its entities which would be gained by service on the special
committee would be valuable to these officers.
We therefore believe that the best service to all would be rendered
by leaving it to the incoming Grand Master to find the best solution
in consultation with these other officers rather than to impose this task
upon them by naming them as members in the motion which will be
presented in a moment.
The Grand Master also stated: "I further recommend that provision be made in the budget for the necessary expenses of the committee." The Committee on Finance, to w hich this recommendation was
also referred, authorizes us to state that they have estimated the expense of the proposed special committee and a re prepared to include
such an item in the budget.
The Committee on Jurisprudence, to which the resolution was also
referred, authorizes us to state that as no legal question is involved
they will not make an additional report.
To implement Recommendation Number Four. but without imposing a burden upon the Deputy Grand Master and Grand Wardens
which they would then be obliga ted to carry and to get the matter
before the house :
I move that the incoming Grand Master appoint a special committee to make an in-depth study of the administration and operation of
our Grand Lodge and its entities toward effecting any possible economy or increased efficiency.
The Committee on Finance indicated its concurrence in the recommendation.
Adopted as amended.

YOUTH ORDERS WEEK-M ARCH 17-22, 1969
"It is with youth as with plants, from the first fruits
they bear we learn what may be expected in future." -Demop hilus
In a day of grave peril for our democratic institutions, in an hour
when social change by insurrect ion, anarchy and 'civil disobedience"
is challenging the very cornersto nes of civilization, we as Freemas ons
should reflect on the causes and individually unite to protect, defend
and preserve our heritage for ourselves and posterity .
One of the best ways of insuring a brighter future is the support
we can give to the young men and women of our great characte r building youth orders. the Internati onal Orders of DeMolay, Job's Daughers and R ainbow for Girls.
"Fifty Years of Young Men on the· Go" is the theme for the Golden
Annivers ary of the Order of DeMolay . which was founded by Frank
S. Land on March 18, 191 9. DeMola y's constant slogan is that no D eMolay shall ever fail as a Citizen, a Leader or a Man. The record is
markedly clear that our D eMolay boys live up to this motto.
Love, Religion, Nature, Immorta lity, Fidelity, Patriotis m and Service are the tene ts of the Interna tional Order of Rainbow for Girls.
Founded in April. 1922 by the Reveren d William Mark Sexson. a distinguished Oklahom a Freemas on, Rainbow for Girls fosters a love for
humanity and our ·Rainbow girls possess the finest attribute s of womanhood.
.
Job's Daughte rs bands together young girls, between the ages of 12
and 20 with M asonic relations hip, for the purpose of building characte r
through moral and spiritual development, by teaching a greater reverenc e
for God and the H oly Scripture s; loyalty to our flag and the coµntry for
which it stands; and respect for parents and guardian s. To quote from
the scriptures. " In all the land there were no women found so fair as the
daughter s of Job."
I hereby proclaim the week of March 17 through March 22 as
Masonic Youth Orders Week througho ut the Jurisdiction of this
Grand Lodge. Each Lodge is requeste d to give due notice of this
Proclama tion in its bulletin and I direct that this Proclama tion shall
be read at the March Stated M eeting of each Lodge in this Jurisdiction.
I further request that every Lodge during the month of March schedule an appropriate program in recognition and apprecia tion of the work
of our Youth Orders.

PROCLAMATION
PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK-APRIL 21 ST THROUGH 25TH, 1969
In 1920, Grand Master Charles Albert Adams stated, "A crisis
is now confronting the Public School system in America." He proclaimed Public Schools Week and called on all Masons to take an
active interest in all matters effecting our Public Schools. Because of
this action, our system of Public Schools has become the largest and
best in all the world.
Today, a different crisis is confronting the Public School system in
America. As Masons, and as exemplary citizens, we have a sacred
trust, duty and obligation to maintain and support our Public Schools,
Freedom's Foundation Stone.
I. therefore, proclaim the week of April 21 through 25, 1969 to be
Public Schools Week and call on every Mason in California and Hawaii to let his voice and his actions be heard. As concerned citizens,
we cannot remain silent. Apathy must be replaced with energetic resolution. I further direct:
That all Constituent Lodges in California and Hawaii actively participate in an appropriate Public Schools Program.
That the suggestions offered by the Public Schools Committee be
followed whenever possible.
That no Lodge programs or meetings be held during this period for
purposes other than this observance with the exception of Stated
Meetings.
That publicity be given Public Schools Week in the Trestleboard of
Constituent Lodges.
That this proclamation be read at each of the Stated Meetings for
March and April
Dated: February 11, 1969

Memorial Day, Flag Day and the Fourth of July-each has a special niche on the calendar because they emphasize preservation of
freedom at home and abroad.
Lethal influences are currently at work, endeavoring to undermine
the American Way of Life.
Freedoms Foundation at Valley Forge calls our attention to this
and invites participation in a program called OPERATION "CLOSE
RANKS." This urges all Americans to join in a positive expression
or reaffirmation of loyalty to God and Country.

I have informed Freedoms Foundation that the Grand Lodge of Free
and Accepted Masons of the State of California endorses this program.

PROCLAMATION
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE MONTH

One of the truly magnificent moments in recorded history took
place on September 17, 1787, when thirty-nine delegates from thirteen
struggling states signed the Constitution of the United States of
America.
My Brethren, we must never forget that it is this document which
delivers into the hands of the citizens . .. all of the citizens . . . the
right of democratic self-determination and guarantees to each citizen
basic rights desired by all, and at the same time, reserves to the people
the power and responsibility for government.
At this moment in America's history, it is essential that all of us,
including the "silent majority" be reminded of what has thus far been
accomplished and that the future depends upon our continued dedication to those principles set forth in the Constitution.
For nearly three decades the Masons of California and H awaii
have sponsored patriotic programs to stimulate thought and endeavor
on the part of all citizens to maintain and preserve the blessings of
liberty. This year, we join with our fellow citizens in celebrating the
one hundred eighty-second anniversary. Let us do so with an equal
measure of reverence and enthusiasm.
I, therefore. proclaim September to be Constitution Observance
Month, and direct every Lodge in this jurisdiction to commemorate
our Constitution with a public observance held on a date as close as
possible to the Anniversary date of September 17th.
This proclamation shall be read at the September Stated Meetings of every constituent Lodge, and wherever possible, it shall be
reprinted in the Lodge bulletin.
Dated: August 11, 1969
Sincerely and Fraternally.
ROBERT A. CRIGLER
Grand Master

Attest :
EDWARD H. SIEMS
Grand Secretary

MONIES RECEIVED

In accordance with Code provisions your Grand Secretary is required
to give an account of monies received during the year at each Annual
Communication. I refer you to the Grand Treasurer's Report, audited
by Certified Public Accountants. This report will be included in the
Advance Reports as well as the printed Proceedings of the communication. It reflects the detail of receipts and disbursements recorded by the
Office of the Grand Secretary.
The Grand Treasurer's report reflects again the recording of all
moneys received and credited to his account. The detail of disbursements
made by Grand Lodge during the year has been made available to the
Committee on Finance as required by law. Supporting books, papers and
vouchers are on file in the accounting office. All records of a financial
nature have been audited, and the records will be published in the Proceedings. The summarization of consolidated receipts and disbursements
for the year ending June 30, 1969-including Grand Lodge, Masonic
Homes, Endowments and Trust Funds. California Masonic Memorial
Temple, bequests, capital gains and others~ntails a tremendous volume
of paper work. These are carefully segregated into the appropriate
accounts by entity: The convenience and practicability of such a centralized accounting program, which has been in effect throughout the
years, continues to be confirmed daily through the ease of handling the
increased volume of recording required in the accounting office. Efforts
continue to be made to keep abreast of and to practice proven, modern
accounting techniques. Following prior consultation with our professional auditors, certain mechanical improvements in our systems have
been carefully installed and simplifications instituted which have made
our accounting more flexible and capable of absorbing even greater
demands. We have made much progress and continue to strive for further
improvements. The "team" effort on the part of our constituent Lodge
Officers. particularly the 711 dedicated Secretaries, the Inspectors, and
our loyal office staff, has made these many accomplishments possible. It
is a privilege to be a part of that team.

This is the fourth successive year that we have shown a net loss in
membership. In 1966 we recorded our first net loss since 1941. The
Lodges accepted 754 fewer applications that year than in the preceding
year. In 1967 there were 274 fewer applications accepted, 38 less in 1968
and 711 fewer for the fiscal year ended June 30. 1969. This large decrease may be significant. Only time will tell.
In 1966 I reported the average number of deaths for the prior ten
years had increased by about 140 per year. Comparable figures for the
period since 1959 indicate the average increase in number of deaths has
been abou t l 08 per year.
Suspension for non-payment of dues for the year ended June 30.
1969, totaled 1834, which was the largest number since the depression
days in the 1930's. This represents 421 more suspensions than for the
same period ten years ago, but more alarming is the fact that it also
represents an increase of 170 over one year ago.
A careful study of the Membership Summary in this report should
give concern to each Master. There is a job to be done. It is said that
a man begins to die when he stops learning. This could also apply to
Lodges.
If the members. officers and committeemen of each Lodge. and of the
Grand Lodge, took this admonition seriously, a new goal of achievement
in the direction of greater learning could be translated into reality.
