Section 150, C.M.C., duties of Grand Secretary. Paragraph 14th,
reads as follows : " To act as Grand Librarian and take charge of the
library of Grand Lodge . under such regulations as it may prescribe."
During the past nine years I have worked closely with the Board of
Library Commissioners under the immediate direction of the several
Grand Masters.
Much has been accomplished, especially when we consider the
Board of Library Commissioners has very little space in which to func-

78

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

tion. Frankly. it has resulted in much frustration. Shelf space is limited.
We have more books in storage in the morgue than we have in the
Library.
In 1967 Grand Master Laurence E. Dayton made the following
observation in his message to Grand Lodge : "In the years I have served
as a n Officer of Grand Lodge. I ha ve had the pleasure of visiting the
Libraries and Museums of a number of Grand Lodges, including those
in London, Edinburgh and Dublin. This h as been a stimulating experience. One is impressed with the quality and extent of both the Libraries
and the Masonic Museum s in these other jurisdictions and the great
importance a ttached to them.
"We take just pride in our beautiful Grand Lodge Temple, but the
space available for our Library and Muse um is meager indeed with the
result that these facil ities suffer by comparison. It is the one feature of
our Temple which leaves much to be desired. All books available to us
cannot be accommodated and items of historical interest cannot be
properly displayed. There is a real and present need for more adequate
facilities and this need can only grow as time goes on.
"I express the fervent hope that the Temple Board will explore and
in due course develop ways and mea ns of providing library and museum
facilities commensurate with our needs and our sta tus in the Masonic
world."
Grand Lodge approved Grand Master Dayton's recommendatio n, as
quoted above, last year.
In line with these observations of Past Grand Master Dayton there
is a growing need for the further development of a Library and Muse um.
There is property adjoining our present Temple that ca n be acquired.
Some positive steps in acquiring property have been taken. When it is
announced that the acquisition has been accomplished , additional funds
and bequests will be forthcoming to help make the Library and Museum
a reality. In the meantime the necessary planning can take shape so that,
when sufficient funds do become available, your then Grand Lodge
leadership can submit a complete proposal to this body for its final
approval before further expenditures are made.
My Brethren, to build the California Masonic Memorial Temple a
start had to be made. In 1951 the Grand Lodge exhibited faith and confidence by taking positive action to make the Memorial Temple a reality
and voted a modest 50¢ per capita tax. This was long before an architect
was employed to draw the plans. The first step was officially taken. In
1969 you are asked to renew that faith and confidence.

The Committe e on By-Laws:
The 1969 meeting of your Committee on By-Laws began at 9:30
a.m. on Saturday, October 11th. Again all seven members participate d.
Promptne ss in meeting at the appointed hour, full participati on by all,
diligence, competence, and experience of the members, and harmony
among them, made this a pleasant and rewarding assignme nt-greatly
lightening the burden.
Some one hundred six changes by constituen t Lodges were checked
and rechecked; to wit. ninety-five changes in by-laws and eleven changes
in place of meeting. In addition your Committe e has conferred with
the representa tives of a number of the Lodges whose by-laws were reviewed.
One hundred three of these changes are set out in Exhibit B of the
Grand Secretary 's preliminar y report, to which the members of this
Grand Lodge may refer. Three were approved by the Grand Master
after this preliminary report was prepared for the printer. Your Committee, finding them in order, moves that they be included in the Grand
Secretary' s report in the printed proceedings. These three are:
Changing date of stated meeting : Ocean Park No. 369.
Increasing dues to $20.00: Educator No. 554.

The following is not approved, because the record before your
Committee does not establish that after written notice at one stated
meeting. the vote was taken at the next succeedin g stated meeting. as
required by Section 365 of the California Masonic Code:
Vermont Square No. 515: Changing time of stated meeting.
It is indicative of our time that of the nine Lodges changing fees
for degrees, and the fifty-one Lodges changing dues. all adopted increases.
Five Lodges, as an inducemen t to sojourning Brethren, rescinded
their fees for affiliation.
Your Committee especially commends Clarence F. Smith Lodge
No. 482, Hunters Point Naval Lodge No. 706, and Palmdale Lodge
No. 769 for increasing the authority of their respective charity committees. Article X of the by-laws of many of our Lodges is completely
antiquated in this respect, and figuratively pleads for amendmen t to
an amount more in keeping with the times in which we live. These
three Lodges are thanked for their example.
It may assist the Lodges if we here point to some of the more common pitfalls encounter ed in amending by-laws or removing place of
meeting.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

84

85

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

One of the most frequent is the requirement of California Masonic
Code Section 365, which is Article XIII of the Uniform Code of By.
Laws, that written notice be given at the stated meeting next preceding
the stated meeting at which it is voted upon. The purpose of this is to
prevent dissension among the Brethren : to ensure that all Brethren are
told exactly what is to be voted on and have an opportunity to attend
and vote; that it is not "slipped through" by postponement, but rather
that of those desiring to attend, at least two-thirds are convinced that
the change is in the best interest of the Lodge. To this end. while the
proposal may be amended as much as desired at the meeting at which
it is proposed, yet when the written notice is given at the meeting. then
at the next succeeding stated meeting it must be voted on in that exact
form, and cannot be amended in any particular.
There are four important points respecting the date of the stated
meeting specified in Article III of the Uniform Code of By-Laws:
First, the only exceptions for which the Lodge may provide an
alternative date are: during the Annual Communicatio n of Grand
Lodge. and those meetings which fall on days which are legal holidays
in the state in which the Lodge meets. There are no other exceptions.
Lincoln's Birthday is not a legal holiday in Hawaii and cannot be excepted by Lodges there. Kamehameha Day is not a legal holiday in
California and cannot be excepted by Lodges in that state.
Second. the particular legal holidays for which a Lodge wishes to
provide an alternative date must be specifically and individually named.
This prevents argument or misunderstand ing as to whether a particular
day is or is not a legal holiday. The officers of a Lodge should not have
to consult an attorney in order to be certain of the date on which their
stated meeting should be held.
Third, the particular legal holiday excepted should be identified by
NAME and NOT by date; for example New Year's Day. not January 1st, Independence Day, not July 4th, Veterans Day, not November 11th. The reason is that when a named legal holiday falls on Sunday. it is by law celebrated on the next day. Monday, which then becomes that legal holiday; and in Hawaii a similar situation exists with
respect to Friday when a named legal holiday falls on Saturday. For
example, if July 4th falls on Sunday, then July 5th is a legal holiday,
being by law the date on which Independence Day is celebrated. If the
by-laws of a Monday Lodge except "Independence Day." then the
Lodge does not meet on July 5th when it is a holiday. But if the by-laws
except "July 4th," then the Lodge must meet on July 5th, holiday or
no. since the 4th was excepted but the 5th was not. Now this is the
privilege and prerogative of the Lodge. It can meet on any holiday
except Sunday if it so desires. But probably it does not so desire. and
most likely it did not so intend. The Grand Secretary's office has a form
especially for use by Monday Lodges, and will provide it on request.

Fourth. a Lodge which makes no other exception should still provide an alternative date should its stated meeting fall during the Annual
Communication of Grand Lodge. At present the only Lodges affected
are those whose stated meeting is during the second week. But the date
of the Annual Communicatio n may be changed for any year. This has
happened many times in the past. and undoubtedly will happen again.
The contingency should be provided for.
Lodges can avoid annoyance to themselves and unnecessary work
for Grand Lodge by remembering that the fees stated in Article VIII
of the by-laws are only the sums which the Lodge intends to keep for
itself. DO NOT include in these fees : the Masonic Hornes contribution. the George Washington Masonic National Memorial contribution. or the California Masonic Memorial Temple contribution, each
and all of which are in addition to the fees stated in Article VIII.
Much inconvenience, and often error. will be avoided if each Lodge
considering an amendment to its by-laws or a change in its meeting
place will obtain the forms available from the Grand Secretary's office
and read them before action is taken.
We report. happily, that the Lodges continue to adopt the entire
Uniform Code of By-Laws as it now stands. These are the by-laws of
each Lodge, whether adopted by it or not. By keeping them up-to-date
the Lodge makes certain that no conscientious officer is misled by reading by-laws no longer in effect.
We commend and thank the Grand Secretary and his staff for their
good work. their courtesy, and their cooperation.
Most Worshipful. we move that this Grand Lodge approve the
amendments and resolutions listed in Exhibit B of the Grand Secretary's report, with the exception hereinabove specified; that the three
additions heretofore stated be approved; and that the charters of the
two Lodges moving their respective places of meeting to another city
or place be amended in accordance with California Masonic Code
Section 373.
Respectfully submitted,
VIRL BENNEHOFF, Chairman

TRIAL RECORD No. 1958
The provisions of Section 732 C.M.C. were invoked against a member of Channel Lodge No. 757 after his conviction of grand theft in the
Superior Court of San Joaquin County. The member did not ask for a
trial and he was automati cally expelled pursuant to that section.
Section 732 C.M.C. provides for automati c expulsio n of a Mason
who ''shall suffer a final judgmen t of conviction of a crime classified
as a felony under the law, and be imprisoned in pursuanc e thereof."
The accused had been convicte d of grand theft which may be punished
by imprison ment in the state prison but in this case he was sentence d to
the county jail which to Californ ia law reduces the crime to a misdemeano r.
It is the belief of the Committ ee on Grievanc es that the classification
of a crime under Section 732 should be classification by sentencin g. In
this particula r case. the sentence having reduced the crime to a misdemeano r, the automati c expulsio n section was not applicable and the
Lodge should have proceede d under the broader Section 692.1 C.M.C.
We therefore off er the following resolutio n:
RESOL VED that the expulsio n of the member be reversed and the
Lodge be directed to proceed under Section 692.1 C.M.C. and the
appropri ate sections thereafte r.
Adopted .
TRIAL RECORD No. 1960
A member of Menorah Lodge No. 623 was convicte d of a crime
da5.>ified as a felony and was imprisoned. The forms used in the trial
were adopted from repealed sections of the Californ ia Masonic Code.
C.M.C. Section 689 provides in part that standard ized forms, maintaint d by the Grand Secretar y, shall be used for all Masonic penal proceedings .
The Gra nd Secretary has available the standard ized forms for the
three penal proceedi ngs authorize d by the C.M.C. The proceedi ng under
Section 732 on the conviction and imprison ment of a felony contains
four standard ized forms. The proceedi ngs under Sections 694 and 697,
trial by a commiss ion. contains twelve standard ized forms. The proceedings under Section 692.1 contains six standard ized forms.
Your Committ ee feels that in the orderly process of Masonic trials
the use of the standard ized forms is mandato ry. The failure to use the
standard ized forms requires a re-trial.
We, therefore , offer the following resolutio n :
RESOL VED that the judgmen t in Trial Record No. 1960 be reversed and remande d for re-trial accordin g to C.M.C. Sections 689 and
732.
Adopted .

TRIAL RECORD No. 1966
Your committee reports on Trial Record No. 1966 as follows:
A ~em~er of Glendale Lodge No. 544 was found not guilty after a
Masonic trial on charges of committing sexual acts with an eight year
old girl.
The accused had pleaded not guilty to the Masonic charges but did
not appear at the trial nor offer any evidence.
He had been convicte d by a jury of a violation of Section 6i7a of the
Californi a Penal Code. The only evidence introduc ed at the Masonic
trial consisted of the criminal trial transcrip t. It was properly received in
evidence under Section 7 I 8 Masonic Code. The transcrip t clearly shows
his guilt and your committee is of the opinion that the finding of not
guilty should be set aside, the accused declared guilty and expelled.
We, therefore , off er the following resolutio n:
RESOL YEO, that the finding of not guilty by the Trial Commissioners in Trial Record No. 1966 be reversed , that the judgmen t be
changed to guilty of unmason ic conduct in committing sexual acts with
a minor girl and that he be expelled from all of the rights and privileges
of Masonry .
Adopted .

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
According to the California Masonic Code, it is incumbent upon the
Grand Lecturer to render a full and detailed account of his services and
activities during the year and set forth therein a report of the condition
of the Lodges throughout the jurisdiction at each Annual Communica~
tion. This report, in addition, however, will also include certain activities
of the Ritual Committee and the lnspectoral Corps, which fall under the
direction of the Grand Lecturer.
RITUAL

Conformity, uniformity, and excellence in the ritualistic work through~
out the jurisdiction, have been the goals of this Grand Lodge since its
inception. The Ritual provides the candidate with his first exposure to
the principles and tenents of Freemasonry and, while the candidate may
not remember much regarding the sequence of the ·c eremonies of the
degrees, he will remember the manner in which the Ritual is rendered
by the officers and the dignity in which it is performed. Our present
system of instruction in the Ritual through the Grand Lecturer and Ritual
Committee to the lnspectoral Corps, and then in turn taught to the
officers of our constituent Lodges by the Inspectors, has been followed
for many years and the results of our present system are most gratifying.
In order to maintain and improve our level of proficiency at the con~
stituent Lodge level, the following series of activities were performed.
1. The Ritual Committee met at Mill Valley for the review of our
Ritual under the direction of the Grand Lecturer on November 29-30,

99

~968. At thi~ annual meeting, also, many plans were made toward the
1mplementahon of the Grand Master's proposed program of activities.

of the R~t~a_I, with the members of the Ritual Committee present:

CANDID ATE COACHI NG

In the Grand Lecture r's Report at our last Commu nication concern
was express ed in regard to our Candid ate Coachin g program . This
concern was directed , not at the Candid ate's lecture portion, but specifically at the educatio n and indoctri nation element s of the program .
This concern was prompte d by the results of an analysi s of the Inspectors' annual reports, the commen ts of many of our Inspecto rs, and the
relative ly small number of our membership who have been certified by
the Inspect ors as qualifyi ng as Candid ate Coache s with a thoroug h
knowle dge of the content s and informa tion contain ed within the pages
of the Handbo ok for Candid ates Coache s.
Some Lodges have develop ed very effective program s. based on the
use of the Handbo ok for Candid ates Coache s and the impartin g of
knowle dge and informa tion to the Candid ate during the periods between
his degrees . Also, there are Inspect ors who have develop ed program s
designe d to accomp lish the aims of the program through an organiz ed
District effort.
The Ritual Commi ttee has directed its attentio n to this serious
problem and is in the process of studyin g the possible means to bring
about a more universal adheren ce to the spirit of the adopted program .
Howeve r, any move toward improve ment must be execute d at the Lodge
level, through the co-oper ative efforts of the Inspect or a nd the Master,
irrespec tive of any propose d format develop ed by the Ritual Commit tee.
A great step forward would be for each Master to see to it that
each newly raised Mason is informe d, educate d, and trained to qua lify
as a Certified Candid ate Coach. We submit that this should be a primary
goal of every Master a nd Warden .
LoDGE ACTIVIT IES

Most of our Lodges are reported as having particip ated in the
primary Grand Lodge program s, such as Public Schools Week, Constitution Observa nce, and achieved greater results in our Homes Endow ment program . These achieve ments indicate some semblan ce of Lodge
activity , and in many instanc es meritorious results have been noted, and
these will be reported on in further detail by the Grand Lodge Committees involve d.

The Inspect ors' annual reports indicate a large number of Lodges do

Many Inspect ors have commen ted that too many of our member s
are not willing to commi t themselves to the years o f service required to
serve through the chairs of the Lodge. This thought is not new. Several
of our Grand Masters through the years, even back in the 19th century.
express ed their concern over this matter. In 1963 the Special C ommission
on Masonic Practice s suggest ed, as Grand Masters had done in the
past, that the lower s tations be filled on a one-yea r appoint ment basis
and that the progres sive line start at not lower than the Junior Deacon 's
station. This is a matter that must be resolved at the Lodge level and it
is highly recomm ended for conside ration, especia lly in those Lodges
that have difficulty in enlistin g the members, particul arly the younge r
member s, into the corps of officers.
INSPECT ORAL CORPS

The duties of the,lnsp ector are set forth in Section 161 of the California Masoni c Code. How ever, over the years addition al duties have
been added to the Inspect or's responsibilities and. as the Gra nd Lodge
represe ntative in the District to which he is assigne d, his activities cover
a broad spectru m of authori ty. This hardy band o f dedicat ed Masons
has done yeoman work through out our jurisdiction year after year and
this year has been no exceptio n. W ith each passing year, in addition
to already prescrib ed duties, the Inspect or is charged with the responsib ilities of arrange ments for the increasi ng number of Grand
Lodge ceremonies, receptio ns for the Grand Master, and other special
meeting s in which Grand Lodge is involved. Their's is an indispen sible
service to Masonr y and no praise is too great for their unselfis h contributio ns of time and talent to our great Fratern ity and its work.
The Ritual Commi ttee joins me in this gratefu l word of thanks, and
our commen dation and praise for their outstan ding service.
There ha ve been twenty- three new lnspecto ral appoint ments during
the year. The new Inspect ors a re called upon to pick up the reins from
their compet ent predecessors and are distingu ishing themselves by that
same quality of service exemplified by the Inspect oral Corps through
the years. During the year, we were saddene d by the loss of three

During the year several complaints were received that Masters.
Officers, and the Brethren were not fulfilling their Masonic duties in
regard to funerals. First, Masters were not contacting and visiting the
widow or family of the departed Brother and. secondly, that the Lodge
members were negligent in their duty to attend the final rites for the
Brother. These points require careful consideration on the part of
Masters and Officers who have been negligent in the past.

A SSISTANT GRAND LECTURERS

As former Inspectors, the Assistant Grand Lecturers are well
schooled in those qualities of service and leadership required to supervise the activities, duties and responsibilities of the Inspectors under
their command. They have distinguished themselves by their conscientious attention to their assignments. their helpfulness to the Inspectors in their respective Divisions and their outstanding devotion to
Freemasonry.
I am particularly grateful for their thoughful deliberations, their
willingness to accept assignments and, above all, for their treasured
friendship. Their qualities of leadership constitute one of the outstanding
assets of our Grand Lodge.

FUNERAL SERVICE

In last year's report the Grand Lecturer pointed out the mounting
wave of criticism that ha d developed in recent years beca use of the
manner our Masonic Funeral Service was being rendered in various
parts of our jurisdiction. Subsequently, in January of this year, a directive was addressed to the Inspectors reiterating the policy submitted to
this Grand Lodge by the then Grand Lecturer, Chester H. Warlow.
and adopted at that time, requiring Masters-elect, as a part of their
qualifying examinations, to be proficient in the Masonic Funeral Service.
This policy, incidentally, was again referred to in the 1950 Proceedings
of the Annual Communication.
The directive also stipulated that the Inspector would ascertain that
at least two or more qualified brothers were not only qualified but available to perform the Funeral Service in a proficient manner and that he
would ascertain the proficiency of the Master, or any other brother

REPORT OF TRUSTEES OF THE

Covina to meet on the ground with our architects at a time when detailed
drawings were nearing completion.
At the request of the Board. Trustee Dayton made an historical
analysis of the quota system as to Decoto guests. Under rules adopted
by the Board in 1941 , Lodges of under 300 members were permitted two
residents without contribution by the lodge; between 500 and 600, one
for each 150 members, with larger Lodges in a decreasing ratio. It now
appears that the age of the Lodge being reflected in the age of its members is more of a determining factor in admissions than size. Furthe r.
many of our older Lodges are both smaller in the number of members
and in their income than younger and perhaps larger Lodges. Seeking
justice for our applicants and for the Lodges from which they may come,
the Board. after conscientious and soul-searching examination of the
conditions created by the quota system, has decided to rescind it eff ective October 1, 1969. This means that those Lodges heretofore contributing for residents in excess of the quota will no longer need to contribute. and that future applications will not be s ubject to quota. We are
certain that this meets with your approval.
The relaxation. or re-definition of entrance requirements by the
State Fire Mars hal and the establishment of a so-called non-ambulatory
section. has enabled the Board to approve the admission of many into
the Decato Home who would have previously not been eligible. There
are, however, distinct limitations to these expanded rules. Bedfast persons and persons requiring assistance in dressing and caring for personal needs still cannot be admitted. Persons mentally confused and
incapable of leaving the buildings cannot be admitted. \Ve caution
Masters and investigating committees by Lodges to carefully weigh the
possibility of misunderstanding on the part of applicants and their
families if applications facing a lmost certain non-approval are submitted. For the sake of the applying member and his family, we ask you
not to ask the Board to bear the brunt of a case which you can clearly
forsee as ineligible under State Welfare Department rules. Preliminary
investigation should always be made by the Lodge prior to formal application. The Inspector of your Masonic District can be most helpful in
advising you in these matters.
In consequence of the Board's decision in I 967, after thorough investigation of possible alternatives, to maintain the Home for Children In
its present site and the master plan of re-development reported to you
at the 1968 Communication, your Board has proceeded to develop final
plans for, and to proceed with construction. The site plan, floor plan
and elevation of a typical cottage were reported to the Craft through
the California Freemason in its Summer issue.

worth in handling the many problems involved in real estate donated
to the Homes. His evident love of the Fraternity and his fellowman
have led to service beyond the call of duty.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF SUPERINTENDENT-COVINA HOME
It is with pleasure that I submit my annual report for the year 196869. At year's end our population consisted of fifty-three children, thirtythree boys and twenty girls. Elementary school children numbered
twenty-five, Junior High numbered twenty, and High School children
numbered thirteen.
The year 1969 saw five groups of children reunited with their families or next of kin, indicating that the services for the Home were no
longer needed. These five groups consisted of the Moore boys, Sojourners of Benton, Illinois, the Knauer children, Ashlar No. 306, Colton,
the Crane children from Highland Park No. 382. Los Angeles, the
Mayo boys from Bear Mountain Lodge No. 76. Angels Camp. a~d the
Rogers children from Big Bear Lodge No. 617. Although we miss all
these children it is thrilling to know that the family situations have been
so resolved to the degree that the re-establishing of the family can be
accomplished. Meanwhile, all the children will have been able to remember their years a t Masonic as happy and meaning ful ones.
All four graduating seniors of June, 1969, will be attending college
on Fra ternity scholarships. Craig Gockley will be attending the ~an
Francisco Academy of Art. while Paulette Weddell. Walter Perkms,
and Dennis Cox will be attending Mt. San Antonio Junior College.
Our Home family has enjoyed good health this past year. The
notable exception was open heart surgery for Timmy Pedretti. As of
this writing Timmy has received the "go-ahead" so that he might engage
in any and all activities. From camp to hospital and back to camp consisted of a time lapse of five weeks.
On June 14. 1969. Grand Master Crigler broke ground for the first
phase of the Covina redevelopment program. Some 3,000 Brethren, their
wives, and children participated in this great occasion. Since the ceremony the grounds have been a beehive of activity with earthmovers,
trench-diggers, architects, contractors, and inspectors, seeing that the
necessary jobs are done and properly inspected so that the ensuing ten
months will insure the preparations of the eight new dormitories for our
children's use. These new dormitories will allow the children to enjoy
a more meaningful "family experience," and will be contructed so that
a brother and sister may live together, rather than be separated as they
now must be.
Many contributions have been received from individuals and groups
this past year. We express our sincere appreciation for this support
and continued interest in our children.
During the summer mon ths our children were housed at Camp
Masonic at Big Bear Lake, California. A mea ningful. comprehensive
program was carried out including "California History Tours" through
the Mother Lode country. Many special trips to art festiva ls. museums,
back-packing trips, and other activities were enjoyed.

ANNUAL REPORT OF THE
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
It is with a feeling of fraternal gratitude and appreciation to this
Grand Lodge that our Board presents the 37th Annual Report o f the
Masonic Homes Endowment Board, for the fiscal year of July 1. 1968
through June 30, 1969.
In the mainstream of productive M asonry, the 1968-69 campaign
chalked up several remarkable achievements.
The income from the Homes Endowment Fund this year was
$912.009.47 and that amount has been transferred to the operating
account of our Masonic Homes.
What makes this increase more significant is that the Board operated
on a reduced ann u al expenditure of $10.104.00, compared with
$20.071 .00 during last year. This measure of fraternal economy was advanced by our Grand M aster. With the wonderful support of our Board
members and everyone in connection with our annual effort. we were
able to achieve the record collection without the use of printed mailing
"stu.lfers" and "convenience" remittance envelopes. The savings over
the previous year amounted to nearly $10,000.00. We are, therefore,
thrilled that such a major saving was fin alized, while a t the same time
contributions increased.
BEQU ESTS

Gifts and bequests in the amount of $411.826.53 were received into
the Endowment Fund during the past year. In addition, $1 ,700,119.83
in bequests were received by the Homes direct, from estates wherein the
Endowment Fund was not specifically mentioned in the Will. Thus a
total of $2.111,946.36 was received in bequests during the fiscal year,
hence, my Brethren, the importance of stressing in our Lodge rooms and
meetings the value of bequests and wills for the benefit of our two wonderful Homes.
PERCENTACE OF PARTICIPATION

The report, if carefully read and thoughtfully studied, will reveal
that the Brethren-nearly one half of our 237,000 membership-are continuing to show an increasing interest in our great humanitarian cause.
Many Lodges had impressive increases in contributions which reflect
an accelerated amount of effort demonstrated by those Lodges in nearly
every sector of our State. The past year witnessed a reawakening by
many Lodges, via enthusiastic committees using personalized techniques
to get out the contributions. This "extra" effort of contact work was
responsible for many Lodges scoring higher totals than in several previous campaigns.
This year 111,745 Brethren made cash contributions to the Endowment Fund.

113

Statistically speaking. the percentage of participation has remained
at approximately 47%. Thus, it will be noted-much to our concernthat more than 50 % of the members of our Lodges are still not making
even small contributions to this most worthy cause. We hope that the
"Forgetful 50 % " will join us next year to materially increase the number of contributors.
The individual Board members. in their year-long associa tion with
Lodges in their areas. attempt to inform the Craft that " Masons T ake
Care of Their Own," not only during the fleeting present but for generations to come.
INDIVIDU AL CONTRIBUTIONS T HROUGH LODGES

A total of $886,120.14 was the record mark attained this year
through individual contributions, $22.780.32 up from $863,339.82 a year
ago.
The overall average per contributing member in all Lodges combined
was $7.93 compared to $7.57 per member a year ago. This represents a
new all-time average record considering our slightly reduced total membership and number of contributors.

Lodges. These Lodges deserve our sincere fraternal thanks and congra tulations. Of these, 465 who attained an average of $3.00 or more

CONGRATULATIONS TO O uR LODGES IN H AWAII
The ten Lodges over in the Isla nds, from the oldest (Hawaiian
No. 2 1) to the youngest (Koolau N o. 801) once again demonstr a ted
that they care a bout our two wonderful Masonic Homes by contributing generously for their support.
Gra teful appreciation is expressed to the M asters of t he Lodges for
spearheading the campaign, ably assisted by t h e Insp ectors of the 382nd,
384t h a nd 385th Districts, w hic h comprise t h e Island Lodges.
Of 3,198 members, th is year's con tributors numbered 1,434, or approximtely 45% - almost coinciding with the average percentage o f
contrib utors on the mainland. We are proud of o ur Lodges in the Islands
and look to them for consistent gains in years to come.

CAMPAIGN WORKSHOPS AND Ams
This year's drive demonstra ted the effectivene ss of personaliz ed contacts within the Lodges to get out the largest participati ng donors,
particular ly among the "Forgetfu l 50%." Lodges organized special
committee s who appealed to the members and supplemen ted their
program by screening, at special meetings or district gatherings , the
beautiful set of slides in color, of highlights at each Home. Board members also gave talks before Lodges and urged members to visit the two
Homes and obtain a first-hand view of what our Homes look like, what
they perform, how the people residing there are grateful and discussion
of future growth. Your Chairman set up four workshop s in every section
of the State and discussed regional problems and programs to cooperate
and assist the area Brethren in charge of the program. Such innovation s
proved s uccess ful. Greater emphasis is to be placed to reach the vast
number of potential givers in the Lodges.

SPOTLIGHT ON PERSONNEL
Your Chairman , called from the "sidelines " to direct the campaign.
found the current list of Board members interested . sincere and committed to the aims of the program. My personal thanks to each for the
help they gave during the year.
It is with the deepest fraternal regret that I announce the termination
of Board membersh ip of four "veteran" members; Kent Seymour, LeRoy
L. Ervin, Henry A. Allcock and M. J. Dungan. Their contributi ons
towards the cause will be long remember ed and we appreciate their interest "to insure the continuan ce of loving care."
Your Endowme nt Board is confident that the spirit of true charity
demonstra ted again this year through your donations will continue next

OUR GRATEFUL THANKS
Special appreciati on must go to our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Robert A . Crigler, who has been an inspiration to all of us. He has
proven an invaluable leader. During his hundreds of thousands of miles
of travel during this year, he has constantly reminded the Brethren of
their opportuni ty and privilege to help in the support of their Homes
for the Aged and the Children. Your Board wishes to personally acknowledg e the results of his intense interest.
In addition, mention mus t be made of the invaluable assistance provided the Board by members of the Grand Master's "official family"particular ly the Assistant Grand Lecturers and Inspectors .
During the past year no coercion or pressure in any way was used.
We have endeavore d individual ly and collectivel y to tell the story of the
necessity for support of our two Homes and the privelege that is given
to members of our 705 Lodges in California and Hawaii.
Our Masonic thanks, therefore, should go to 111,000 contributo rs
among the 237.000 members of our Craft. It is our fervent hope that
next year the number of contributo rs will materially increase.
My sincere thanks to the Brethren called on throughou t the yea r the Lodge Officers. Committe emen, "side-line rs," and especially the
Secretarie s who play an important role in our annual campaign.
My sincere thanks is extended to the Grand Lodge office staff. It is
a real joy to work with such a fine, loyal and dedicated group of employees.
Our work has been a great pleasure. First, because of the high and
lofty purpose, and, second. because of the unselfish devotion of so many
members cooperatin g with the Board. The two Masonic Homes are the
embodime nt of those truly Masonic tenets of Brotherly Love and Relief
and should be the source of our greatest satisfactio n as men and as
Masons.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF INVESTMENT COMMITTEE

CONSOLIDATED MARKET VALUE
OF SECURITIES AND INVESTADLE CASH*
(BY GROUPS AND TOTALS) and D OLLAR INCOME (In Parenthese•)

FOR FISCAL YEAR ENDING JUNE 30,

1969
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Investment Committee concludes its nineteenth year of activity,
and herewith renders its report for the twelve months ended June 30,
1969. Each year's report gives a certain amount of historical background
and basic information, which should be helpful to those attending Grand
Lodge for the first time.
The Prudent •Man Rule, in modified form, was adopted by and for
Grand Lodge at the 1950 Communication. For the Constituent Lodges
a Prudent Man Rule was adopted in 1951.
The Committee does not supervise the investments of Constituent
Lodges, but Grand Lodge makes the services of its investment advisor
available to the Lodges. Many Lodges are making use of this service.
The following is Moody's report of activities for Constituent Lodges
for the year ending June 30, 1969:
Constituent Lodge Activity Report-July 1, 1968 to June 30, 1969:
Number of Active Lodges at end of period........
91
Number of inactive Lodges ................................
218
Approximate portfolio value ............................ $9.432,150
Approximate average value of portfolios .......... $ 36,005
Lodge letters........................................................
121
Moody's letters ....................................................
127
Telephone contacts ..............................................
77
Office visits ..........................................................
12
The Investment Committee hopes that the Lodges are making full
and continuing use of this valuable service.
We would also like to call your attention to the fact that there is a
circular issued by Grand Lodge regarding the investment of funds by
Constituent Lodges, which is available at the Grand Secretary's office.
It is my understanding that a copy of this 'Circular or reprint of Section
403 with respect to investments by Constituent Lodges has been inserted in the new Lodge Manual.
Since its inception, the Investment Committee has met regularly
every three months. This has now been changed so that the Committee
will meet every two months. Between meetings the business of the Committee is conducted by correspondence or telephone. The Committee is
available at all times, should special meetings be advisable or necessary.
As stated, we have just completed nineteen years of operations. The
following is a summary of the consolidated market value of the securities owned, plus investable cash, together with a record of dollar income
on these investments, beginning with November 30, 1950, and for each
succeeding fiscal year, through June 30, 1969, including the percentage
income on the market value of each year:

During the past year securities were sold at prices yielding
$621 ,230.90 more than their cost, thereby increasing the total asset value.
Since the inauguration of the Prudent Man Rule in 1950, this total
amounts to $7,009,049.03. Sales always remain a part of capital assets
and are never included in income totals. With respect to the Endowment Fund, no capital assets are ever withdrawn.
Endowment Fund contributions made through the Lodges amounted
to $886,120.li for the year ended June 30, 1969. Other contributions to
the Endowment Fund were : Gifts and Bequests $411,826.53, Memorials
$23,351.09, and Dona tions from Organizations and Individuals
$7, 448.98. General Fund Gifts and Bequests amounted to $1.700.119.83
(which also includes real estate and items other than stocks and bonds).
The Masonic Homes Board of Trustees determines how these gifts and
bequests are allocated-such allocations are made in accordance with
specific bequests. or in the absence of such at the direction of the
Trustees. The Endowment Fund contributions remain in that fund, and
only the income is used.
May we also call attention to the fact that the consolidated portfolio,
after taking into account the several withdrawals listed above aggregating $3.276,535.94, has increased since November 1950 from $6,124,471
to $30,821.969, or about 403.26%. and at the same time the income has
increased from $120.598 to $1,408.929, or about 1068%.

These evidences of debt or certi.6cates are owned by the Masonic
Homes of California. It would be appreciated if negotiations were under·
taken by those Lodges or Temple Associations which could afford to
redeem these certificates. The Investment Committee would greatly
appreciate your consideration of this request. Just write to the Grand
Secretary for further information.
Grand Lodge owns 21 shares of Ramona Savings & Loan Associa·
tion, located in Fillmore, California, which stock regularly pays cash
dividends. The book value of the stock is now $1.298.00 per share. In
answer to our recent inquiry, the Association informed us that 9 shares
have recently sold at an average price of $650.00 per share. However,
we are holding the shares, and do not contemplate selling them at this
time. For the 7 months ended July 31 , 1969, Ramona Savings & Loan
showed a net profit of $111,758.00.
We also own 102 shares of Corona Foothill Lemon Company. the
market value of which is much too low as compared to its potential
value. Consequently these shares are being held. The territory in which
this property is located in Southern California is steadily improving in
value. These shares should also be an excellent growth situation. We
quote from a letter from the company, in response to our recent inquiry:
"Our formal report to shareholders for our fiscal year ending Oc·
tober 31. 1969, should be ready about January 1.
"The current year's crop was severely reduced both in size and
quality due to the freeze of last December. As a result our citrus income
is very low and we will show a substantial loss in this operation for the
current year.
"Our Canyon Lake project is going very well and it appears that
this venture will more than compensate for our farming losses. The
major part of the project should be completed by next spring and we will
be better able to analyze the situation then. Although we should show a
good profit. there are also certain contingent liabilities which must be
recognized. We have been looking for other projects to carry on our
business in this field but have not yet been successful."
The entire portfolio is listed in the Grand Treasurer's and the
Auditor's reports, and therefore is not included herein. The securities are
always held in safekeeping for account of Grand Lodge by the Trust
Department of the Crocker Citizens National Bank, at its One Mont·
gomery Street Office, San Francisco.
We have had excellent attendance at our Investment Committee
meetings during this year, as has been the case since this Committee was
organized. It was a pleasure to have Deputy Grand Master Chester R.
MacPhee at several of our meetings, as well as Junior Grand Warden
Lester S. McElwain, and P. G . M. Laurence E. Dayton representing the
Masonic Homes Board of Trustees. At the March 27, 1969 meeting
Judge Chamberlain dropped in for lunch.

Again we come to that portion of the Investment Committee t'eport
where we try to summarize in a few words our thoughts as to the
financial and investment outlook.
The investment outlook, as we see it at this time, continues to be one
of conservatism and caution. We are evidently going through a transi·
tion period, which causes us to maintain a more conservative approach.
In the meantime, the Prudent Man Rule continues to be our yard·
stick. We have an excellent and diversified list of investments, with
bonds and stocks , which are always under scrutiny.
Our Investment Counsel attends every meeting of the Committee,
and has always given us sound and conservative advice.
We again repeat that our course of action can be quite different
from that of an individual for a variety of reasons. This statement is
made so as not to unduly influence individuals in their personal invest•
ment programs.
Our thanks to the Grand Secretary and his staff. and to the Grand
Lodge officers who attended meetings from time to time. My thanks also
to the members of the Investment Committee for their wholehearted and
generous cooperation at all times.
Respectfully submitted on behalf of the Investment Committee:
PAUL A. PFLUEGER, Chairman

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. 6 A . M. of California:
The Grand Treasurer's Report in its entirety is referred to the
Committee on Finance with special attention to the items listed as expenditures for which no provision was made at the last Communication.

That portion relating to the changes of meeting places to the Committees on Charters and on By-Laws.
Those portions relating to the consolidation of Lodges and to the
replacement of a charter to the Committee on Charters.

which is accorded to the office of Grand Master.

REPORT OF TRUSTEES
CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. 6 A. M. of California:
The Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple
herewith submits its Fifteenth Annual Report.
· -At the close - of the 1968 Annual Communi~ti~n~Cthe Gr~d
Lodge. the Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial
Temple held its Annual Meeting. The President, Ralph H. Head, reported to the Board of Trustees the election of the Right Worshipful
Chester R. MacPhee as Deputy Grand Master, the Right Worship ful
Herbert A. Huebner as Senior Grand Warden and the Right Worshipful Lester S. McElwain as Junior Grand Warden. On motion duly made,
seconded and carried, they were duly elected members of the Board of
Trustees as provided in the California Masonic Code.
The Board of Trustees then proceeded to nominate and elect its
Officers to serve for the ensuing year until new ones were elected.
Our magnificent Masonic Memorial Temple atop Nob Hill is in its
eleventh year of use. It continues as an outstanding center for the cultural and civic activities of a great metropolitan community. It also serves
as an inspiring image of our pride as Masons and of the fine teachings
of our Fraternity.
The thousands of visitors who enter our Masonic Memorial Temple
need look no further for an example of Masonry's contribution to the
beautification and advancement of civilization. It shines as a beacon
of our determination to continue to build well a dynamic free and educated country for the generations yet to come.
It has no peer as an outstanding setting and showplace for business,
fraternal and professional meetings, for the dramatic exhibition of the
new creations of industry, for fine concerts, s timulating lectures and
premier performances of musical and dramatic compositions.
TOURS AND VISITATIONS

The Temple is open daily, except Sa turday and Sunday. for visitors
from 8:45 A.M. to 4:45 P.M. If there are other activities in the Temple
on Saturday or Sunday, then additional tours are arranged. We have
had guests from every one of the 50 States and from many of the countries of the world visiting our T emple. This year we were hosts to visitors
from the following countries:

Our Brethren from the 50 States and from the many countries seek
information to take home to their respective Lodges. They are amazed
at the beauty of our Temple, that it is debt free and the many faceted
activities of the Fraternity. We truly are a unique Grand Jurisdiction and
in the fore front of the growth of Freemasonry.
Many Senior Citizen groups. Rainbow for Girls, Job's Daughters ,
DeMolay Chapters and others continue to arrange for tours of our
beautiful building. Hundreds of school children visit our Temple and it
makes a lasting impres sion on them of our efforts to help them achieve
a better life through public school education.

INCOME

148

MAINTENANCE AND IMPROVEMENTS

Nothing less than the highest standards of maintenance will preserve
the classic beauty of our Temple. After eleven years of use and occupancy. some of the mechanical equipment of necessity will require replacement. Painting, stripping and waxing is a continual necessity to
not only preserve the charm and usefulness of our building but also the
surface from erosion through wear and tear. Most of this has been done
during the past year by our own staff to reduce the cost of operations.
PuBLIC RELATIONS AND Civic AFFAIRS

Membership in the Nob Hill Association, San Francisco Convention
and Visitors Bureau, the Press Club of San Francisco and the Greater
San Francisco Chamber of Commerce serves as a much needed contact
with prominent civic and business leaders from whom many rental
prospects and much useful information can be obtained.
Our staff has been instructed and is making every effort to give that
extra something in service and attention to our tenants. Their fine
cooperation will not only build a better image of our Fraternity but also
make the use of our .6.ne facilities more enjoyable for our tenants.
Some of the tenants who have used our premises h ave graciously
appreciated this extra service and have commented in letters as follows:
"Thanks so much for your help. In all my experience in the public
relations profession I have never experienced such a perfect setting for
our Annual Meeting." "Your efforts and personal contribution helped
to make this year's event successful and meaningful." "I want it to go
on record and let you know how much we appreciated your help in
connection with the Shareholders Meeting last month. Let us hope that
it will not be too long before we are working together again."

149

During the past year the income from the building and garage
reached an all time high of $214,778.00. The fiscal year of July 1. 1968
to June 30, 1969 shows a 7.2 % increase in building income over that
of the last fiscal period.
Through judicious supervision the operating expenses, salaries, supplies, repairs, maintenance, including real and personal taxes increased
only 5.6%.
The garage showed an increase of 3.6% over the previous fiscal
year. This income will always continue to fluctuate because it is largely
based on the occupancy created from the use of the Auditorium and
Exhibition space. Thus more use of space means more income from this
source.
For the third successive year we have with pride and pleasure made
a contribution of $10,000 to our Masonic Homes of California.
New hotel and convention facilities will soon be a reality as the
Building Department of the City of San Francisco approves new projects
from plans submitted to them.
The Hyatt House Hotel Corporation is planning three new buildings in San Francisco, one of them is to be built immediately adjacent
to our own Temple. It is said to be 28 stories in height with over 400
rooms and have a large revolving restaurant on the top floor. Another
hotel is contemplated on Sacramento Street atop Nob Hill and the third
project will replace the Plaza Hotel in Union Square. The St. Francis
Hotel has cleared land adjacent for the construction of a high rise
tower. When the ho!el adjacent to the Masonic Memorial Temple is
commenced. the digging for its foundations will require the expenditure
of considerable funds to protect our building from structural settling
because of the strain on the natural ground supporting our foundations.
An architect has already been engaged to formulate plans to protect our
property.
A new hotel is planned for the northeast corner of Powell and Sutter
Streets. The Stanford Court Apartments on Nob Hill have been vacated
of all tenants and the complete reconstruction of its inner facilities will
soon begin.
The South of Market Y erba Buena Center is still on the list for
future development. We must be cognizant that each new hotel or convention facility will eventually be competitive for our clientele insofar as
meeting space and convention business is concerned.

TEMPLE STAPP

OCCUPANCY

Our operation only requires a small, loyal. creative, capable and
dedicated staff. Without dedication from them, it will be impossible to
meet the many challenges and trying problems that continually arise
in the management of an edi.6.ce such as ours. We appreciate their past
services and helpful assistance.

The Trustees believe that it is most desira ble that they continue a
plan of diversified rental of the Auditorium and Exhibition Hall as a
protection against the lessening use of either one by the booking of only
one form of tenancy. Each new hotel will encourage and bring additional
convention business to San Francisco and increase its reputation as an

150

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

ideal place to hold meetings. Many conventions in the past did not
come to San Francisco because of the lack of ideal facilities required for
their use or type of meeting.
During the past year our Auditorium has been used for some of the
finest theatrical and concert type of performance s. With noted artists
such as the New York Philharmoni c Orchestra , Ballet Folklorico of
Mexico, Joan Sutherland. Vienna Boys Choir, Andres Segovia guitarist,
Grand Ka buki Theatre of Japan, Madrigal Chorus of Romania, Van
Cliburn internationa l pianist, N.D.R. Symphony of West Germany,
N.H.K. Symphony of Japan and Irina Arhipova, as performing artists,
the fine reputation of the Temple as a place of culture and refinement
befitting the admirable image of the Fraternity has been enhanced. The
Trustees believe that this type of tenancy and use of the premises
should be encouraged rather than the popular type of entertainme nt
which is of fleeting popularity and many times of questionable good
taste.
Our Auditorium is well adapted to all kinds of stockholder and
business meetings. The Standard Oil Company of New Jersey, the Bank
of America, Pacific Gas and Electric Company, Ford Company. The
League of California Cities, Radio Corporation of America and the
Pacific Telephone and Telegraph Company have used our Auditorium
this year. The Graduate School of Business of Stanford University
returned again this year.
Space does not permit a full recital of the many groups that have
used both the Auditorium and the Exhibition Hall for meetings of importance. The remainder of this year and all of 1970 are very heavily
booked for use of these facilities.
Japan occupied both the Auditorium and the Exhibition Hall for an
outstanding External Festival and Trade Fair celebrating "Japan
Week." In September the Internationa l Industrial Conference with
representati ves from over seventy countries used our premises for the
first time.
It is most satisfying that well known educational institutions continue
to hold their graduation exercises in our Auditorium because of the
beauty and impressive dignity that the setting contributes to the occasion.
These include the University of California M edical School, Hastings
Law School. and six San Francisco High Schools.
The State of California uses our Exhibition Hall for the examination s
conducted for Certified Public Accountant s and the State Bar of Cal~
ifornia holds its bar examination s in our premises.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TAXATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Since filing our report for 1968, there have been changes in the pay~
roll tax laws which apply to our various Masonic organizations.
As has been our custom in past years, we present, for reference
purposes, the usual schedule of tax rates and wage bases for the various
payroll taxes which will be in effect during the calendar year 1970 and
thereafter.
The Nixon Administration has recently recommended changes in
unemployment insurance laws which could alter information provided
herein. We will advise you if such recommendations are enacted.
FEDERAL WITHHOLDING (INCOME) TAX

All wages paid to employees of a Masonic Lodge are subject to
Federal income tax withholding. In order to determine the amount of
income tax which is to be withheld from wages paid to its employees,
the lodge should ask each employee to complete and file with the
Secretary of the lodge a Federal Form W~4. "Employee's Withholding
Exemption Certificate." Reference to withholding tax tables furnished
by the Treasury Department will enable the Secretary to determine the
amount to be withheld. The 10% surtax is scheduled to expire on Jan~
uary 1, 1970. There should be ample notice and publicity to allow all
employers to obtain a supply of revised withholding tables should the
surtax expire as scheduled.
FEDERAL INSURANCE CONTRIBUTIONS ( SocrAL SECURITY}

As the law now stands, an employee of a Masonic Lodge is subject
to tax for each calendar quarter during which he earns $50.00 or more.
The tax rates shown below are applicable to the first $7,800.00 of wages
paid to each employee during the calendar year. These rates are to be
paid by both the employer and the employee.

FEDERAL UNEMPLOYMENT TAX

Masonic Lodges will be subject to this tax if they employ four or more
individuals who are paid $50.00 or more per calendar quarter, providing
they have first qualified as an "employer" by employing four or more
employees on at least one day in each of twenty or more weeks during
the calendar year. For this purpose, all paid employees of the lodge,
including the Secretary and those who are performing ritualistic services
(Tiler, Organist, Soloist), should be counted if they receive $50.00 or
more per calendar quarter. Federal Unemployment Tax at the rates
shown below will be applicable to the first $3,000.00 of wages paid to
each employee during the calendar year. However, lodges which are
subject to the California Unemployment Insurance Tax law, and which
meet certain requirements, will be entitled to a credit up to 2.7%. Only
the employer pays Federal Unemployment Tax.

CALIFORNIA UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE TAX

Masonic Lodges will be subject to this tax if the total wages paid
during a calendar quarter to taxable employees are in excess of $100.00.
For this purpose a taxable employee is one who is paid $50.00 or more
per calendar quarter. However, whether or not elected or appointed
officials of a lodge are to be counted as taxable employees will depend
upon whether or not the Lodge is subject to the Federal Unemployment
Tax Act.
If the lodge is not subject to the Federal Unemployment Tax Act,
then the wages paid to an elected or appointed official will be exempt
from California Unemployment Insurance Tax unless the wages paid
to these officials exceed $100.00 per month.
If the lodge is subject to the Federal Unemployment Tax Act, then
the wages paid to an elected or appointed official will be subject to Cali~
fornia Unemployment Insurance Tax if the wages paid to these officials
amount to $50.00 or more, per calendar quarter.
For purposes of this tax, the term "elected or appointed official" will
include any official of the lodge who is compensated for his services.
Those usually compensated for their services are the Secretary, Tiler,
Organist, and Soloist.
If the lodge is subject to California Unemployment Insurance Tax,
the rate shown below will be applicable to a $3,800.00 base paid to each
employee during the calendar year 1970. In other years this base may
fluctuate between $3,800.00 and $4, l 00.00.
Only the employer pays the tax. Rates are based on employment

REPORT OF CALIFORNIA FREEMASON
PUBLICATION BOARD
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The publication and distribution of the California Freemason is
administered by a board comprised of the Grand Master, the Grand
Secereta ry and the Editor-in-Chief who is appointed by the Grand
Master.
During its sixteenth year of publication the magazine has continued
to inform our membership concerning the activities of Grand Lodge and
to present ma terial explaining M asonic thought and to a dvance M asonic
principles. Each issue is diversified to supply both information and inspiration. Long scholarly articles, excellent in themselves, are avoided because they lack appeal for many of our quarter million readers. A
quarterly cannot be a news magazine but with the help of letters from
readers we are able to report a few oustanding events having sta te-wide
interest.
Each member of a California Lodge receives a copy automatically.
There has also been a gratifying number of paid subscriptions from
sojourners and from interested persons in other states and countries.
The present per capita of 35 cents has been just sufficient to cover
the cost of preparing, printing, distributing and mailing. This will suffice
for the future until such time as rising costs ove.r take us.

The financial figures for the past year will be found in the auditor's
report.
Respectfully submitted,
NEWCOMB Co NDEE, Editor-in-Chief

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC I-llSTORY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your C ommittee on Masonic History presents the following report:
The members of the Committee wish to express their appreciation
to the Grand Lodge and especially to our Grand Master, Robert A.
Crigler, for the privilege of serving. The cooperation of the Grand
Master and Grand Lodge has again made this year a pleasure.
Your Committee this year has expanded its studies on all of the
Masonic buildings, past and present, in California and Hawaii. More
and more Lodges are sending in material on their past and present homes.
All of this material is being compiled into a complete history of the meeting places used by the Lodges of this jurisdiction.
During the past year there have been man y dedications, cornerstone
layings. and other events of historical interest. Your Committee on
Masonic H istory h• s tried to be at as many of these events as possible.
The recording of these Masonic occurances is important as a part of the
history that binds us together from one generation to the next.
This Committee has been requested to study several historical sites .
Brother Darrell D. Hull of this Committee journeyed to "Masonic
Cave," the first meeting place of V olcano Lodge No. 56. This is one of
the interesting sites of our early California history. Brother Hull made
a survey and has made several suggestions for improvement of the site.
Other s ites are being studied at the present time. As the findings are
recorded they will be placed in the proper ha nds in Grand Lodge.
We are still getting calls to show our slide lecture, "Some Came by
Land and Some Came by Sea." This interesting lecture depicts pioneer
Masonry here in California . W e are in the process of expanding this
slide lecture and dividing it into different locales. Any Lodge or M asonic
group wanting this lecture for an interesting and educational even ing
may contact the Chairma n of the Committee and he will see that it is
available to you.
In order that your Committee may continue its work for the coming
y ear we submit the following budget:

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Report of the Committee on Correspondence covers the fiscal
year 1968-1969.
Ed Siems, Grand Secretary. forwards to the Committee on Correspondence of the California Masonic Grand Lodge, all annual proceedings of Grand Lodges who publish their proceedings, including those of
the United States, as well as foreign jurisdictions, who are recognized
by the California Masonic Grand Lodge.
The reviews for many years have been restricted to the 49 Masonic
Jurisdictions of the United States, including the District of Columbia.
The State of Alaska is a member of the Jurisdiction of the State of
Washington and the State of Hawaii is a member, as you know, of the
State of California.

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

These proceedings contain a great deal of Masonic information
which is primarily of interest to the constituent Lodges of the Jurisdiction
publishing a given report, but it is also instructive so far as California
Masons are concerned in that it is informative to the members of our
Grand Lodge as to Masonic problems and developments in other
Masonic jurisdictions.

AFTERNOON SESSION-Tuesday, October 14, 1969

158

Various jurisdictions are making a sincere effort to build and solidify
the individual Mason's interest in Masonry in general.
We have at all times kept in mind the traditional function of the
Correspondence Committee, which is to inform the members of our
Grand Lodge as to what is being done in sister jurisdictions to further
the interests of Masonry. In this way they may be better informed and
prepared to reach intelligent opinions on Masonic matters.
Accordingly, the Committee has reviewed 49 annual reports of Masonic Jurisdictions in the United States, including the District of Columbia . Separate reports are not published for the States of Alaska and
Hawaii as these states are members of the Grand Jurisdictions of Washing ton and California respectively.
These reviews in turn are submitted to the Editorial staff of California
Freemason. While these reports may not measure up to what you expect
in reviews, yet we are constantly endeavoring to make them more readable, and to this end we solicit your suggestions.
We have for a number of years followed a uniform style disclosed
by the reviews published in the California Freemason in its quarterly
issues. Editorial comment is minimized and is placed in italics. All other
matter is printed without quotation marks, its sources being clearly
indicated.
Included in this report is an estimated budget for the ensuing Masonic year in the sum of $400.00. This sum includes disbursements of
the Committee; plus reimbursement for travel. hotel accommodations
and meals during Grand Lodge of the individual members of the
Committee.
Respectfully submitted,
GEORGE W. BURCH, JR., Chairman

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON LODGE FINANCING
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F. & A. M. of California:
In submitting its annual report for the 1968-1969 Grand Lodge year,
the Committee on Lodge Financing wishes, first, to take note of the predominantly healthy condition of T emple properties throughout the
jurisdiction and, second, to suggest certain precautions resulting from
experience with those situations where financial difficulties are being
experienced.
The most rewarding aspect of this C ommittee's task, which involves
consultation with Lodges and Temple Associations on real estate matters, is the almost daily evidence of the strength of Masonry in California
and Hawaii. It is indeed a privilege, through the functioning of this Committee, to see Masons in action and to work with the builders of Masonic
Temples; to see Masons finding a way to acquire property and erect a
Masonic edifice without incurring a penny of debt; to see Lodges and
Temple Associations finding a way to build or improve a Temple through
the commitment of donated material, volunteer labor, and willing
pledges; and to see the devotion and pride of the brethren involved in
creating or improving a Masonic Temple.
There are, however, as in any large organization, certain areas of
concern. These involve situations where a Lodge or Temple Association
may have overbuilt and incurred burdensome and excessive debt; where
a Temple project may have been undertaken prematurely; where the
initial forecas t of operating income and expense may have been too
optimistic; where it has been considered necessary to resort to a heavy
dues increase to raise funds for increased rental or heavy loan payments
and taxes; and where physical depreciation and obsolescence are occurring with no financial reserves existing for replacements and repairs.
The Committee on Lodge Financing is admonished to withhold approval of applications it receives from Lodges or Temple Associations
where any of the foregoing conditions are likely to develop and it therefore urges the constituent Lodges and the Temple A ssociations to keep
the following recommendations in mind:
1. M ake every effort to avoid going into debt.
2. Defer a property acquisition or building project. if at all possible,
until a thorough and conservative feasibility study indicates that it is
prudent to proceed.

160

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

3. Fund the depreciation reserves to cover repairs, replacements and
rehabilitation when needed.
4. Consider going together with another Lodge or Lodges where the
combined resources will make a Temple possible and where a single
Temple can serve a given community.
5. Keep insurance programs under constant review to provide full
and adequate protection.
6. Endeavor to keep the rental rates charged our three youth groups
at a minimum. While this Committee does not exercise control over rental
rates charged, it is aware of certain cases where it would appear that the
youth groups are being overcharged, and it has discussed this in a joint
meeting with the Committee on Youth Orders, sharing that Committee's
concern.
The formal actions taken by this Committe~ during the past year are
listed in the attached Appendix. In addition, Committee members have
met throughout the jurisdiction with Lodge and Temple Association
representatives when called upon for advice and counsel. Also. we are
endeavoring to develop an up~to~date inventory of Temple property
ownerships and locations in California and Hawaii, and will be seeking
the coopera tion of Lodges and Temple Associations in answering a
questionnaire now being prepared.

APPENDIX

Lastly, while acknowledging the help and cooperation of so many of
the brethren during the year, the Committee wishes to express special
appreciation to the following: to the Grand M aster, Most Worshipful
Robert A. Crigler, for his interest and strong support; to the Deputy
Grand Master, Right Worshipful Chester R. MacPhee, who has served
in a liaison capacity between the Committee and the elective Grand
Lodge line; to the Grand Secretary, Assistant Grand Secretary. and
their staff for cooperation and assistance; and to former Chairman Mark
A. Green for excellent help during a period of transition a year ago.
It has been a busy and rewarding year for the Committee member~
ship, and we hope and trust that our work has been acceptable. At this
time we request of the Grand Lodge an appropriation of $2,000.00 for
the operating expenses of the Committee on Lodge Financing during the
ensuing year.
Respectfully submitted.
J oHN F. P ORTER, Chairman

REPORT OF DIRECTORS
CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & AM. of California:
California Masonic Foundation was organized a nd is now in existence as a charitable. non-profit corporation, the date of incorporation
having been March 5, 1969. Tax exemption has been granted to the
Foundation by both the Federal and State Governments.
The Board of Directors, which is designated as the Board of Trus-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

165

tees, consists of 15 persons whose na mes are attached to this report and
will be available for the inspection of any Brother desiring to do so. In
choosing the members of the Board of Trustees, attention has been given
to as wide a geographical distribution of the members as is practicable so
tha t each a rea under the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge will have
representation.
The primary purposes for which the corporation is organized are
to receive gifts, devises, bequests, and contributions o f every kind and
nature and to hold, use. administer and disburse the same in a manner
not in conflict with the laws , rules, and regulations of Grand Lodge for
all phases of education , including scientific research.
The By-Laws require that the corporation's annual meeting be held
within thirty ( 30) days of the close of each annual communication of
Grand Lodge for the purposes. primarily, of receiving the nominations
of the Grand Master to fill vacancies on the Board of Trustees. to elect
them as Trustees, and to adopt the budget for the ensuing year as approved by Grand Lodge. The terms of office of the Trustees are staggered-5 to serve I year; 5 for 2 years; and 5 for 3 years.
An annual report in detail and a proposed budget for the ensuing
year are required to be fi led with Grand Lodge in sufficient time to be
considered at the Annual Communication. The offices, books. and operations of the corporation are open to the inspection of the Grand Master
or those designated to act for him at all convenient times.
Copies of the Articles of Incorporation and the By-Laws are available for inspection in the Office of the Grand Secretary.
Since the formation of the corporation, there have been two ( 2)
meetings of the entire Board of Trustees, and there have been numerous
meetings of various committees appointed by the Board. Standing committees have been established by the By-Laws as follows :
(a) Executive Committee

( d) Committee on Foundation Planning
In addition thereto, the President, with the advice and consent of
the Grand Master, is given power to appoint any other committees
deemed necessary or advisable, and each committee may appoint subcommittees or consultants at the committee's direction. Under this section , a committee on Public Rela tions has been appointed with Brother
Melvin A. P ixley as Chairman.
The original officers of the corporation were as follows: President,

area, consisting of forty-seven ( 4 7) high schools. An additional pilot
program is planned of comparable size in Southern California if additional fundi ng is available.
The Committee is recommending a budget of $10.000.00 to implement each phase of the pilot program above a nd beyond minimal anticipated adminis trative costs.
