PARAGU AY: A communic ation has been received from the Grand

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNI A

171

Lodge Symbolica del Paraguay, signed by Grand Master Ricardo
Frankel, in which he states that his Gra nd Lodge is very much concerned and greatly interested in intensifyin g their fraternal relations
with other Grand Lodges, and especially with the Grand Lodge of
California .
The Grand Lodge of Paraguay at present consists of five Lodges.
It meets our T ests for Recognitio n under the following principles:
It is an independe nt, self-gover ning. responsibl e organization, with
entirely undispute d and exclusive dogmatic and administra tive authority
over the Symbolic Lodges within its jurisdiction, who meet regularly
under the fundamen tal principles of the Three Lights, the Bible and
the Square and Compass .
It makes M asons of men only.
It requires conformit y and adherence to the acknowled gment and
belief of God, the Father of all men; secrecy; the Symbolism of Operative Masonry; the division of Symbolic M asonry into the three degrees;
and the Legend of the Third Degree.
Its dominant purposes are charitable, benevolen t, education al and
for the developm ent of a sincere reverence for God as Father of all
men; and it excludes controvers ial politics and sectarian religion from
all activities under its auspices.
It occupies exclusively its territorial jurisdiction, and does not presume to extend into or presume to establish Lodges in a territory occu~
pied by a lawful Grand Lodge.
The Grand Lodge of Paraguay has been recognized by the Grand
Lodge of Texas , the G€and Lodge of New York. the Grand Lodge of
Scotland; and since 1910 by the United Grand Lodge of England, together with many distinguis hed Grand Lodges around the world.
I therefore move that the Grand Lodge Symbolica del Paraguay .
whose seat is in the City of Asuncion, be recognized by the Grand
Lodge of California .
Since in the course of this report, your Committe e will recommen d
the recognitio n of three Grand Lodges in Brazil. we would now like
to direct the attention of Gra nd Lodge to a considerat ion of the history
of Masonry in that country.
It is believed that the first Masonic Lodge was establishe d in Pernambuco in 1796. and others followed, but all had a brief existence.
The Grand Orient of Brazil was founded May 28, 1822, and then,
immediate ly thereafter, ensued one of the strangest and most puzzling
events in Masonic history. Dom Pedro, soon to be Emperor of Brazil,
was initiated August 2, 1822; and at a meeting of the Grand Orient the
following month was elected Grand Master of the Grand Orient and
duly installed on Septembe r 14, 1822. Six weeks later, on the 27th of
October, the Emperor, in his capacity as Grand Master, sent a message
to the Senior Grand Warden, who was presiding over a regular meeting

172

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of the Grand Orient, ordering all work of the Grand Orient suspended,
as well as the work of its constituent Lodges. This was followed by
severe persecution of the Craft and Brethren-and Masonry was
driven underground until Dom Pedro abdicated. In 1832, ten years
later, the Grand O rient was reestablished but endured years of schisms
and factionalism. By 1883. however, we can say that Brazilian Masonry
was united in the Grand Orient and the Supreme Council. Contrary to
what we usually find when these two powers are in competition, the
Grand Orient controlled the Supreme Council and the Grand Master
became almost automatically the Sovereign Grand Commander.
In an attempt to restore the independence of the Supreme Council,
Grand Commander Mario Bhering. in 1925. renounced his position as
Grand Master and a Treaty was signed providing for the independent
status of each power. A succeeding Grand Master, Octavio Kelly by
name, unilaterally abrogated this Treaty and (at a General Assembly
of the Rite) insisted upon, and was. installed as Grand Commander
of the Supreme Council. The majority of the Supreme Council. led by
the legitimate Grand Commander, Mario Bhering, declared the Treaty
null and void, refused to recognize Grand Master Kelly as Grand Commander and moved the headquarters of the Supreme Council away
from the premises it had formerly shared with the Grand Orient.
Grand Commander Bhering then issued an edict authorizing the
Lodges. which held warrants or charters from the Supreme Council
(though holding obedience to the Grand Orient). to form themselves
into Grand Lodges. in accordance with universally recognized Masonic
principles.
This, then, my Brethren. was the origin and reason for the creation
of the State Grand Jurisdictions, of which there are now 19. and of
these we presently recognize 14.
The Grand Orient continued to function, and is numerically superior in the number of Lodges and in membership. It also has the respectability of recognition by the United Grand Lodge of England. The
Grand Lodges of the United States. however, have transferred recognition to the State Grand Lodge.
Those of you who have glanced over the past reports of this Committee will remember how difficult it has been to obtain information
from the Grand Lodges of Latin America who have applied for recognition, as to their position in respect to the Tests of Recognition which
this Grand Lodge adopted. These Tests for extending fraternal recognition to other Grand Bodies are to be found in the following Proceedings : 1913, at page 163; 1918. at page 159: 1948, at page 250:
and 1953, at page 216. At last, however, through the good offices of
the Commission on Information for Recognition of the Grand Masters'
Conference. and from information gleaned from reliable sources in
Brazil, your Committee is able to make the following recommendations:

BRASILIA : This Grand Lodge was erected in the Federal District,
formerly part of the State of Goias. It is in effect a successor to the
Grand Lodge which had jurisdiction of the Federal District when it
was located in the City of Rio de Janeiro, and which we now recognize
as the Grand Lodge of Guanabara. A Grand Lodge in this new territory. working closely to government circles, was grea tly desired by the
State Grand Lodges, and was recognized immediately by them. The
Grand Lodge of Goias chartered and consecrated the Grand Lodge
of Brasilia on February 16. 1963. It has 7 Lodges in its jurisdiction
which comprises only the City of Brasilia. We are informed it works
according to the Ancient Landmarks and in strict conformity to the
Tenets of regular Freemasonry.
We. therefore, move that the Serenissima Grande Loja Symbolica
de Brasilia be recognized by the Grand Lodge of California.
GOIAS : An application for the establishment of friendly relations
and mutual recognition has been received from the Grand Lodge of
th e State of Goias, signed by their Grand Secretary of Foreign Relations, Brother Roland Martin. The State of Goias is bounded by jurisdictions we recognize: Para to the North, Matto Grosso to the West,
Minas Gerais to the South and Bahia to the East. Information from
Brethren in Sao Paulo and from the Commission on Information for
Recognition confirm that this Grand Lodge can be regarded as meeting
our Tests for Recognition.
We, therefore. move that the Grande Loja Maconica do Estado de
Goias, whose address is Caixa Postal 332. Goiania, Estado de Goias,
Brazil. be recognized by the Grand Lodge of California.
PERNAMBUCO: As an example of the time involved in corresponding with our Brethren in South America. may I tell you that we
first received a request for recognition from the Grand Lodge of Perna mbuco on May 26. 1959. Both my predecessors as Chairmen o f this
Committee, Past G rand M asters John Moore and Phil Myers, in addition to myself, have sought factual informa tion from this Grand Lodge;
and, finally. we have enough knowledge to justify recommending recognition.
The State of Pernambuco is small for a Brazilian state. It stretches
along the Atlantic Seaboard. on the hump of South America, and states
whose Grand Lodges we recognize border it as follows: Ceara to the
North, Piaui to the West and Bahia to the South. It has been recognized by 10 American Grand Lodges and by all of its sister State Grand
Lodges in Bra zil. It is a leader in inter-Brazilian affairs and we believe
it to be regular in all respects.
We, therefore, move that the Grande Loja de Pernambuco, whose
address is Caixa Postal I 415, Recife, Pernambuco, Brazil, be recognized by the Grand Lodge of California.

IRAN: As proof of the ubiquity of Freemasonry, we will now turn
our attention from South America to Asia.
Regular Freemasonry has existed in Iran since the erection in 1918
of Lodge Light No. 1191 , of the Scottish Constitution. There are presently 27 Lodges in Iran, 14 chartered by the Grand Lodge of Scotland,
1O by the National Grand Lodge of France and 3 by the United Grand
Lodges of Germany.
Probably as a result of the increasing sense of nationalism in the
world, and particularly in Asia, the Shah of Iran let it be known that
the creation of the Grand Lodge of Iran would have his royal favor.
The Masonic membership in that country has been of the highest caliber, and the Grand Master. who is said to have been personally chosen
by the Shah, is the Most Worshipful Jafar Sharif Emami, President
of the Senate of Iran.
On March 1, 1969, the ceremonies of the Consecration and Erection
of the Grand Lodge, and installation of the Grnnd Master, were carried
out by the Grand Master Mason of Scotland, the Grand Master of the
National Grand Lodge of France and the Grand M aster of the United
Grand Lodges of Germany. Also in attendance was the Assistant Grand
Master of the United Grand Lodge of England.
This Grand Lodge has responded correctly to our Tests, and with
its distinguished sponsorship as a further recommendation, we move
that the Grand Lodge of Iran, located in the City of Tehran, be recognized by the Grand Lodge of California.

GRAND ORATION
"LET THERE BE LIGHT"
Grand Orator

WILLIAM J. WILLIAMS.

Most Worshipful Sir, Brother Grand Lodge Officers, Distinguished
Guests, My Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
This morning I am at once filled with pride and humility; proud of
being a member of our great Fraternity. humble in the knowledge and
memory of the great men of Masonry that have addressed you in previous communications as your Grand Orator.
This past year has been, for me, filled with inspiration as we have
participated in Masonic functions and ceremonies the length and breadth
of our Grand Jurisdiction and the courtesies and expressions of brotherly love will never be forgotten.
The greatest satisfaction has been to become well acquainted with
my brother officers of the Gra nd Lodge, and most particularly with our
Grand Master, the Most Worshipful Robert Arthur Crigler. He is a
pillar of strength when strength is so needed, a man of great dignity

176

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

and moral courage at a time when we seek men of these qualifications,
a man of personal warmth and great devotion to our Fraternity who
has exemplified the teachings and principles of Masonry in his constant
travels, his almost unbelievable number of meetings with his Brethren
in Freemasonry, and in his daily life. It has been truly. Most Worshipful
Sir, a great inspiration to serve as one of your Grand Lodge Officers
and I shall be eternally grateful for this opportunity.
LET THERE BE LIGHT!
"In the beginning. God created the heaven and the earth, and the
earth was without form and void, and darkness was upon the face of
the deep, and the spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters, and
God said, 'Let there be light,' and there was light." This passage from
the Bible. the first verse in the Book of Genesis, the Story of Creation,
is precious to all who revere the Bible, but particularly our Brethren in
Freemasonry. for it was in response to this command. " Let there be
light,'' that they first saw the Light by which Masons work.
From time immemorial. Masons, ancient and modern, have obeyed
this august command and have labored in bringing Light to the world,
much of which is still in darkness, devoid of the Light of Brotherly Love,
Relief. and Truth.
We cannot trace our Masonic heritage with exact definition to the
ancient builders of the pyramids. temples. and other great works of
antiquity, but we do know they used the same tools, the plumb, square
and level, for their operative work that we use today. and there is much
to indicate that these tools were also used to teach valuable lessons in
morality. life, and conduct, as we speculative Masons do at the present
time.
We can, however, start tracing our history in the Tenth Century
in the guilds of operative Masonry and in their building of the great

cathedrals of Europe. places of worship and the universities. the seats
of learning, and bringing to the world the great Lights of Religion and
Education. How well our ancient Brethren performed their tasks is selfevident in viewing these magnificent structures today. They wrought
not only in stone and timbers, but they wrought in the building of men,
and each succeeding generation has advanced the principles of Masonry.
Coincidentally with the labors of our ancient operative Brethren, the
Crusaders were, as they saw the truth, bringing the Light of Religion
to those areas of darkness. They carried the banners of the Christian
Religion and practiced the principles of our ancient Craft. In the walled
City of Rhodes, 800 years ago. the Knights of St. John built a great
monument to Brotherly Love, one of the first edifices for the relief of
human suffering, a hospital that still stands, tending the needs of the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

177

dtizens of Rhodes today. two hundred years later. the Knights of St.
John moved to the Island of Malta and adopted the name of their new
home and. as the Knights of Malta, continued their charitable and religious activities. Their counterparts on the continent, The Order of
Knights Templar, because of their role in bringing Light to their less
fortunate Brethren, earned the fear a nd enmity of the despotic spiritual
and temporal rulers of their time a nd their Order was decimated by the
horrors of the Inquisition and their last Grand Master, Jacques DeMolay, was burned at the stake. These names, the Knights of St. John,
the Knights of Malta, the Knights T emplar and DeMolay are revered
in Masonry today.
Over eight hundred years ago the barons stood before King John
on the fields of Runnymede with their demand that he sign the Magna
Carta, guaranteeing those rights to the people that have become the
basis for democracy since that time and so treasured throughout the
free world. There is little doubt that our Brethren of that day were in
the vanguard of those seeking for themselves and their fellowmen the
blessings of justice, equality. and freedom from oppression.
From our rich Masonic heritage, it was only natural that with the
formation of the Grand Lodge of England two hundred and fi fty-two
years ago that M asonry became a dominant force in the colonies and
that our early Masonic leaders were also the leaders, politically and
economically, in the birth and development of our country. We have
read of the relationship of St. Andrews Lodge and the Boston Tea Party,
where, in its minute book, only the large letter "T" appears for that
night's meeting. We 'know of its prominent members. P aul Revere and
John Hancock, and history is replete with the leaders hip provided by
those great Masons, Washington. Franklin, Madison. and scores of
others for whom Masonry is justly proud.
In the formation of the Constitution, one meets with the theory that
government not only derives its power from the people, but that it is
designed to protect the people from dictators and their greed. For the
first time we find the theory that leadership is elected from the people,
that while leaders should be followed faithfully and earnestly by the
members, the leaders would soon return to the ranks to serve as a common member with their brethren. Where, in the political or religious
thinking of that time, can that idea be found? Certainly not in English
or Scotch politics, although they were very liberal compared with the
rest of Europe. Neither can it be found in the Anglican, Congregational.
Presbyte rian or Methodist creeds, as they were then understood-and
those were the four predominating religions in the colonies. Neither the
Declaration of Independence nor the Constitution was based on credal
concepts, but upon the broader concept o f a Divine Designer, Creator
and Upholder of the U niverse, much broader than the creeds of that
day. Where, in the political and religious thinking of that period, can

179

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

you find a declaration for the separation of church and state, or a declaration in favor of the free exercise of religions? It is not found in our
Scotch background, for they believed in their own established church;
not in our English origins, for in most colonies they were strongly for
the established Church of England; not even can that theory be found
in Puritan New England, for they established a strict theocracy and
established the Congregational Church as the church of the several colonies. These ideas can be found in none of the dogmatic religions or
political philosophies of that day.

"To focus the attention of the Craft on existing conditions, I. as
Grand Master of Masons in the Jurisdiction of California, do now proclaim the week commencing Monday, September 27th, 1920, as 'Public
Schools Week' in the Masonic Lodges in this Jurisdiction; and I do earnestly request that, during that week, in every Lodge in this Jurisdiction,
some phase of the questions affecting the Public Schools be brought to
the attention of the members present by speakers appointed for that
purpose."
As is true of all great essays or proclamations, this one, too, is ageless. It is, with but the change of one word, "urban." instead of "rural,"
the exact statement of the condition of our Public Schools today. Today,
as then, needed bond issues are being defeated by the traditional enemies
of our Public School System, but more particularly by an apathetic public; now, as then, Boards of Trustees are seeking the best qualified men
and women of the community for members and often are disappointed
in their efforts; today, as then, teachers' salaries are too often below
that of common labor and today, as then, our children, the most precious
product of our society, are being taught by many teachers of less-thanthe-needed excellence, because many desirable candidates for the teaching profession are being attracted by more lucrative offers in commerce
and industry. Yes, my Brethren, we need to rededicate ourselves and
r~double ~ur efforts in behalf of our public schools, that they may contmue to bring to our people the great Light of Education.
Those cherished institutions of a free and democratic society-a
stable .a nd respons~ble system of government guaranteeing equal opportunity for all; a system of free public education; those fundamental
inalienable rights, the free exercise of religion, freedom of speech and of
th: press, the prohibition of deprivation of life, liberty, or property
without due process of law-are being threatened today as never before
in the history of our country. Never has our entire system of government
been so viciously attacked, never has our entire educational system been
threatened by such diverse elements from every economic and educational level. Classes are being closed, teachers beaten and abused, buildings damaged and destroyed. Demands are being made for reforms in
our ~ystems of education and government by individuals and groups
ranging from well-meaning, interested citizens to militants, revolutionaries, and anarchists who would destroy that which we have been centuries building.
It. is incumbent upon us, as Masons and good citizens, to closely
e~amme and analyze all of our public institutions in the light of our
times. Are they this day serving the needs of our people in the best
possible manner? Are reforms needed, and, if so, what are they? Surely
no documents or institutions or regulations conceived in the minds of
men are eternal. One of the best examples is the numerous resolutions
presented each year to this Grand Lodge, containing in them, in the

Where, then, in the political or religous thinking of that time can
those ideas be found? Only in the great Light of the teachings and practices of Freemasonry. As we delve deeply into our country's early history we realize that Masonry was the great unifying force, the catalyst
that welded the colonies with their diverse economics, political philophophies, predominant religions, and their geographical ba rriers, into one.
With this glorious heritage down through all ages, we, as Masons,
clearly recognize our responsibilities as citizens in maintaining for all
the people those principles of freedom, equality of opportunity and justice, for which our early brethren worked, and lived, and died, that they
might pass on to future generations a brighter and better world.
As Masonry has espoused these principles, it has recognized that
they can only be attained and assured by an educated and enlightened
citizenry. From the first public schools in the colonies in the mid sixteen
hundreds and the founding of our first public high school by that outstanding Mason, Past Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania Benjamin Franklin, Masonry has been the leader in bringing
the great Light of Education to our country. California Masonry has
achieved nationwide, and yes , even worldwide recognition, in establishing Public Schools W eek in California in 1920. Nearly fifty years ago
Past Grand Master Charles Albert Adams made the following proclamation, and I quote in part:
''As Masons, we unqualifiedly subscribe to the belief that an educated
and enlightened citizenship is the first great care of a progressive State;
and that upon our Public Schools depend the hope for the perpetuity
of a free and untrammeled democracy.
"The professions we make as Masons demand that as citizens of the
Commonwealth we take an active and intelligent interest in all matters
affecting our Public Schools.
"A crisis is now confronting the Public Schools System in America.
There is a dearth of competent teachers, schools are being dosed, children, particularly in the rural communities, are being denied the education to which they are entitled, and there is apparently a deplorable
apathy concerning remedial measures which have been proposed.

If reforms are needed, let us, as responsib le citizens. be the ones in a

Tomorro w, we have the opportun ity of visiting the Masonic Home
at Union City. I hope all. who can, will go for the first time. or as a previous visitor. It will be, in my opinion, the greatest experien ce you will
ever have in the fraternal spirit of Relief and Brotherl y Love. There, in
this beautiful Home for our less fortunate Brethren , their wives and
widows, is Masonry in action. It is one thing to relieve the body of
physical needs by welfare, but it is somethin g far apart to relieve the
minds of our aged and infirm Brethren of the worry and fear of providing for themselv es in their late years. To see the Light of love and appreciatio n for the Craft in the eyes of the residents of our Homes is
somethin g you will forever treasure. If every Californ ia Mason could
visit our Homes, we would never have to worry about the success of our
program for the support and maintena nce of our M asonic Homes, where
burns bright the Light of Relief and Brotherl y Love.
We hold in our hands, My Brethren , the future and the destiny of
Masonry in Californi a. It can be an awesome burden, or a stimulati ng
challeng e. This past year we had one of the greatest numerica l losses
of members and Lodges in the history of this Grand Jurisdiction. This,
in itself, need not be alarming , most other Grand Jurisdict ions also sustained net losses in members hips. as have other fraternal organiza tions.

181

So, we can say, complac ently, that it is the trend of the times and there
is nothing we can do about it. Many downtow n metropol itan Lodges,
in the past great towers of Masonic strength and activity, are suffering
severe declines in attendan ce and members hips; in many rural areas,
where towns are disappea ring due to better transpor tation and changes
in living habits, these small Lodges, too, are disappea ring. We hear
many reasons for the disturbin g conditio n-too many competin g activities. too much or too little discretio nary time available, commuti ng greater
distances to work, and that great destroye r of useful activity, television .
Or, is it a combina tion of these thlngs, or is it none of them, but a lack
of stimulati on? Yes, the latter perhaps. for running counter to the general trend are Lodges in Californ ia that are enjoying outstand ing activity, both socially and in their degree work. Let's look at some of them
and see if we can come up with any general observat ions or conclusio ns.
They generally are located in towns and cities near the residence , rather
than the place of business . of their members. They take pride in the excellence of their ritualisti c work and the attitudes and dress of their
officers in the performa nce of their duties. They never compromise with
the quality of their candidat es to get a new member. They give real support, not just lip service, to our Youth Orders, the Order of DeMola y,
Job's Daughte rs, and Order of Rainbow . Their observan ce of Public
Schools Week and Constitu tion Month Observa nce are well planned
and executed . They have good speakers and panels on subjects of Masonic interest and they make use of the service offered by the several Research Lodges. They have a well-bala nced social program , father and
son dinners, meetings where they can take that friend who you wish
was a Mason, and they have several nice affairs each year honoring
their wives. They have program s that are not peculiar unto large and
wealthy lodges, but program s that are possible and practical for every
Lodge in Californ ia.
These are not innovatio ns in the body of Masonry which we swore
we would not make when we were installed as Masters of our Lodges,
but are stimulati ng and complem enting program s to our basic Masonic
work of stated and degree meetings . Let us use all these proper means
that are possible and practical for our own Lodges and fill our Trestle
Boards and our Lodge Rooms with meaning ful Masonic activity.
If we do these things, then the ever-incr easing body of Masonry will
do credit to our stewards hip and will truly indicate our devotion and
service to those great Masonic Lights of Brotherl y Love, Relief and
Truth.
LET THERE BE LIGHT!

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
To the Most Wor shipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California:
Your Committee on Public Schools consisted of twenty-three members and two consultants, an increase of one member over last year,
making it the largest number of members in recent years.
Right Worshipful Herbert A. Huebner was chosen by the Grand
Master , Most Worshipful Robert A. Crigler, as liaison with the Committee. Brother Huebner, a former Chairman of the Grand Lodge
Committee on Public Schools, proved to be of great assistance to the
Committee.
Three meetings were held during the Masonic year: the first in San
Francisco on October 15 at which time there were 15 members in attendance, the second in Los Angeles on January 18 with 16 in attendance
and finally in San Francisco at the Grand Lodge on May 31 with 17
present. Many guests were welcomed at these meetings and included
Right Worshipful Herbert A. Huebner, Senior Grand Warden, Edward H. Siems. PGM. Grand Secretary, and Verne W. Hendrix, Assistant Grand Secretary. Brother Richard R. F. Lehman, a member of
Palestine Lodge No. 351 and a consultant to the Committee, attended
all meetings of the Committee and his efforts were again of invaluable
assistance.
MASONIC ORIENTATION MEETINGS

The Grand Master declared that a special Officers Association
meeting be held in each of the six divisions for the purpose of Masonic
Orientation. The Public Schools Committee was one of the committees
chosen to make a presentation at these meetings. In addition to the ,
Chairman, members who spoke at these six meetings were: Elroy Joyce,
Clyde Stine, Rolland Atwood, George Hiatt and Norbert Tester. The
general feeling of the representatives was that the idea of the meeting
was excellent and it was hoped that they would be continued.
PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK APRIL 21-25, 1969
The Grand M aster chose for this year's slogan " The Public School
- Freedom 's Foundation Stone. " The slogan was widely accepted
throughout California and Hawaii and was used extensively by both
Masonic and non-Masonic groups. The results of some of the Public
Schools Week activities follow:
Over six million milk cartons carried a panel urging visitations of
public schools during the week of April 21-25.
Billboards situated on major California highways carried the message to millions of motorists. This project was again sponsored by the
Scottish Rite.
The Committee again contacted all of the major food chains requesting tha t they use some space in their weekly food ads to publicize
Public Schools W eek. The response was good.

A letter was sent to all county superintendents of schools informing

Grand Lodge were received by the Chairman from these superintendents.
Proclamations were obtained from the vast majority of public officials and State legislators in both California and Hawaii declaring the
week of April 21-25 Public Schools Week and urging the citizenry to
visit their public schools.
Television and radio stations were again generous with their air
time and several committee members, Grand Lodge officers and other
prominent Masons appeared on radio and television.
The Yark Rite Bodies of California made it possible for us to have
more than 1,000 bus cards posted in buses throughout the State.
Over 27,000 "official" posters, printed at Los Angeles Trade Technical College, were distributed through the office of the Grand Secretary.
This represented an increase of approximately 10% over last year. The
Public Schools Committee was able to cut the price per package of 50
posters to $6.50 this year.
The pamphlet "The Masons of California and Hawaii Salute Their
School Administrators" was again widely accepted with over 25.000
copies distributed. The Committee has decided to update the pamphlet
and increase the printing from 25,000 to 30.000 this next year.
School systems and teacher groups assisted extensively by distributing publicity.

The Deputy Grand Master has announced the slogan "The Public

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON CEMETERIES
To the Most ·worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Cemeteries respectfully submits the following
report of their activities for the Masonic Year 1968-1969.
As in the past, we think it best to repeat for the benefit of those
attending Grand Lodge for the first time, a brief summary of the functions of this committee. It is the duty of this committee to care for the
three cemeteries owned by the Grand Lodge. To work with and counsel
those individual lodges where cemetery care problems exist. To see
that public cemeteries which set aside sections for the exclusive use of
Masons or their families do not deviate from our laws with respect to
commercialism. To study and inspect plans for any monuments to be
erected in such Masonic sections and make recommendations to the
Grand Master for his approval or disapproval.

Columbia and famestown: After a very severe wet winter, both the
St. James Masonic Cemetery in Jamestown, and the Columbia Masonic
Cemetery in Columbia State Park are in fairly good condition. It was
a continuous battle for the Future Farmers of America in Sonora to

185

Fiddletown Cemetery: T his year Brother Vincent V. Lake of Lodi
was appointed to the Cemeteries Committee. He was assigned to the
Fiddletown Cemetery and has done an outstanding job. He has made a
number of trips there and has personally done much land clearing and
repairing. In addition to the cleaning and repairing he has contacted
the Amador County Surveyor's Office and obtained a map showing the
layout of the cemetery and the location and names of those buried there.
He is at present working on some possible corrections and making an
attempt to find who is buried in some of the unknown graves.
Weed spraying at the Fiddletown Cemetery was done by Richard
D. Henderson, Agricultural C ommissioner of Amador County.
One burial was made this year. Brother Cecil Fisher, P.M. of Provident Lodge No. 609 of Sacramento, was laid to rest in March. A second
plot was sold to his wife for future use.
The entire Masonic section of this cemetery is in a very fine condition.
Michigan Bluff: Last year we were instructed to obtain title to the
Masonic Cemeter y in Michigan Bluff. This matter was assigned to Brother Leo J. Todd of Grass Valley. Because the necessary papers were not
received when expected and for other reasons, action to obtain this title
has been delayed. It is my understanding that the necessary filing has
now been done.
Peter Lassen Grave in Susanville: At the last session of Grand
Lodge we requested a sum of $250.00 to star t repairing and cleaning
the grave of Brother Peter Lassen. A considerable amount of work has
been done recently by some members of Lassen Lodge No. 149, but at
no cost to the Grand Lodge. It will, however, be necessary for us to
spend some money this year and we are making a request in our budget
for an amount we believe will be sufficient.
The area has been mowed and cleaned twice. Red cinder rock is to
be placed around the old marker this month. The remains of the huge
stump will be cut out and cement will be poured at the entry.
We request a budget in the amount of $2,075.00 for the ensuing
year as follows:

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
"PATRIOTIC PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE THOUGHT AND ENDEAVOR"

This, our One Hundred Twentieth Annual Communication, affords
each of us a wonderful opportunity to meet together and to share and
exchange information concerning all of the programs which, taken to~
gether, form the structure of Freemasonry in California and H awaii.
We have assembled this week to learn more about all the activities
and programs which are so vital to the successful conduct of our indi~
vidual Lodges.
Each and every Masonic activity and program (whether it be Ritual.

187

Endowment, Masonic Homes, California Masonic Foundation, Public
Schools, Masonic Education, Youth Orders or Constitution Observ~
ance) complements all the other activities and programs and the sue~
cess of any one of them is certain to assist the growth and development
of the others.
Some, of course, are indispensable, for without them there would
be no Masonry. And two sha re the unique distinction of being the only
programs which carry us as a Fraternity outside of the Lodge to join
with the citizens of our respective communities to promote general sup~
port for our Public Schools and for the Constitution of the United
States of America.
These two programs are both fraught with small and large dis~
appointments. They each possess a challenge of considerable magni~
tu de and constan tly demand our best efforts, and all too of ten our labors
are rewa rded with attendance far below expectations.
But, my Brethren, in spite of the difficulties and disappointments our
efforts are succeeding. We are individually and collectively hewing and
reshaping our talents to equal our task.
The Cons titution Observance programs for 1969 offer substantial
evidence tha t our sustained efforts over the past 29 years are meeting
with success.
Our Gra nd Master initiated and guided our endeavors this past year
and most eloquently and effectively conveyed our primary purpose in
his Proclama tion.
The reports submitted by you, my Brethren , offer assurance to our
Grand Master that his message was taken to heart. ·• ... Patriotic Pro~
grams to stimulate thought and endeavor ... "were observed throughout
the length and breadth of this Grand Jurisdiction.
It is a difficult if not an impossible task to select the best or most
outstanding observance programs. We shall not attempt to do this but
will share with you a random sampling taken from the first reports to
reach your Committee. We hasten to note that our purpose is to illustrate
the scope and variety of programs and failure to mention your Lodge,
or to give complete details for those programs included herein, is an
omission without significance.
Let us examine just a few reports:
1. The Orange County Committee on Constitution Observance
(sponsored by 20 Masonic Lodges. 2 Knights of Columbus Councils, 1
Elks Lodge and a Shrine Club) held its second annual parade and pro~
gram in Buena Park. A spectacular parade (comprised of nearly 2100
participants with the entire program attracting over 5000) concluded its
line~of~march at the front of the replica of Independence Hall at Knott's
Berry Fa rm where the official program was held in the most ideal
setting west of Philadelphia. The day~long. community~wide celebration
started with a Pancake Break£ ast at the Elks Club and from then on

Your Board, realizing that much knowledge of Board of Relief opera tions must be quickly gained, devised a form to be used by each Board
of Relief, reporting thereon, each request for Relief or Service. This

These forms asked for the name of the M ason in whose name the

the name and address of the person making the request: nature of the
request; what Relief or Service was furnished; with appropriate spaces

This request did not meet with enthusiastic support. Two of the

important information we sought.

REPORT OF BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
Your Board of Control presents herewith its report for the year
1968-69.
None of the statements of non-permissive activity or report of activity in this report are offered as criticism, but rather as a factual report
to you, the members of our Grand Lodge, to the state of deviation from
established Law. This condition has grown to alarming proportions.
The reason for a Board of Relief, with the single function covered
by Sect. 603 C.M.C., that of relieving the distress of sojourning Masons, their widows and orphans, is now a minor work of many Boards.
It is not here suggested that the present practices of the Boards
were instituted in intentional disregard for our Law. These actions have
grown, year by year, and though not permitted, have been overlooked
and condoned by previous Boards of Control with apparent full knowledge of the Officers of Grand Lodge. The Lodges, too, have permitted,
and in some cases encouraged, these actions to grow.
Your Board of Control on taking office October 18, 1968, and with
four new members, spent the first three weeks reviewing the files and
previous correspondence of the Board.
This detailed study of procedure and action, made clear the necessity of adopting a new policy of communication.
Previously, outgoing communications had been accomplished by
typing each letter, making five carbon copies, which many times were
not legible. Incoming communications might be directed to any one of
the five members.
From the personal knowledge of the present Board, it was noted
that many oral statements and direction had been made by former
members, and did not always follow a consistent pattern.

better treatment than the Lodge could or should properly provide for
its own members.
General directives and individual directives were issued to obtain
conformity within the framework of existing law.
The entire effort of your Board of Control this year has been directed toward bringing all Board of Relief operations within the framework of our present law, thus affording the sojourner the same measure
of relief and service in all parts of the state.

Your Board of Control visited this board on March 1, 1969, examining books, records and files. This examination disclosed the following
non-permissive activity:
1. Providing relief for non-Masons.
2. Making loans of board funds.
3. Furnishing relief without notification to or securing approval from
the sojourner's Lodge.
4. Holding personal funds of a sojourner. disbursing same in payment of life insurance premiums, and otherwise acting as fiduciary.
5. Storage of personal effects of a sojourner.
6. Listing in local telephone directory under "Local Masonic Information."
7. Performing non-sojourner services for member Lodges.
8. Lump sum auto allowance for secretary without accounting for
actual use.
9. It was noted that this board still listed a full time stenographer
in violation of direction from the Board of Control under date of June
18, 1968, to reduce this employee to a part time status.
10. Operation of a blood bank for member Lodges.
11. Operation of blood bank for non-member Lodges and other
organizations which included Eastern Star Chapters, Shrine Club and
Square Club.
12. Expending board funds for Christmas gifts.

and executive committee at Masters and Wardens functions and othe.r

MASONIC BOARD OF RELIEF OF SAN DIEGO

On January 20, 1969, the Chairman of your Board of Control received a call from an Inspector indicating that a forthcoming election
was adding to the disharmony which prevailed in this board.
The Chairman visited this office on January 23, 1969, checking
books, files and records and noted the following:
1. The books and records were not in proper condition and did no t
reflect proper activity.
2. Activity had been conducted for non-Masons.
3. The board had been disbursing relief funds on behalf of a concordant body.
3. Operation of a blood bank for member Lodges .
4. Operating a blood bank which included the Eastern Star, Amaranth. Scottish Rite, and Beauceants.
The Chairman attended a meeting of the representatives of the board
at which he endeavored to bring about a reconciliation. On January 29
a call was received from Board of Control member Jones giving details
of further deterioration of the harmony among members of the board.
Board of Control members were contacted by telephone and after consultation with the Grand Master. the San Diego Board was closed on
January 29.
The Inspectors of the area set to work with the Lodges and on April I
a plan of reorganization was approved by the Board of Control and the
San Diego Board reopened.
We can now report to ·y ou that harmony prevails and the San Diego
Boa.rd is operation within prescribed law.

STRUCTURE OF BOARDS OP R ELIEF

There is evidence that the Southern Alameda County and Richmond
Boards were formed for the sole purpose of gaining membership in a
blood ba nk and/ or to escape the higher per capita of the adjoining East
Bay Board.
There is evidence that other Lodges have joined, and are now asking

195

BLOOD BANKS

The operation of blood banks for either member or non-member
Lodges does not fall within the category of permissible activity of a
Board of Relief.
Many boards operate the blood bank as a commercial venture, accepting money for the purchase of blood, buying and selling, operating
on a debit, credit, deficit basis. Some very sizeable funds are held in
trust for blood purchase and are continually growing.
Your Board of Control on February I 0 recommended to the Grand
Master that the blood program be referred to a committee for study.
It is assumed that this Committee will submit for your approval a
recommendation for uniform blood bank operation.
PENSION PLAN

We call your attention to several interesting facts about the Grand
Lodge Pension Plan covering full time employees of the Board of Relief.
The San Francisco and Long Beach Boards had been directed by
the former Board of Control to cut stenographic employees to a part
time status. They requested reconsideration of the ruling on the ground
that the stenographers had one and two years respectively to be eligible
for the pension, and it was their feeling that full time employment should
be continued for that period, because we are a F raternal and not a commercial organization.
The Executive Secretary of the San Francisco Board has since
March 1, 1969 been receiving the sum of $60.86 per month pension,
under the plan, while continuing full time, full pay employment for that
period.
The Executive Secetary of the Los Angeles Board has been receiving the sum of $130.94 per month pension since January 1, 1965,
while continuing full time, full pay employment with the board. The
budget for the ensuing year reflects a raise in salary.
The Board of Control has no jurisdiction over the administration
of the Pension Plan, but deems it proper to bring this to the attention of
the Grand Lodge.

CONCLUSION AND OPINION REACHED PROM STUDY CONDUCTED
The Grand Master has directed this board to make an in-depth
study of Board of Relief operations . This prompts us to make the following conclusions. and express the following opinions.
In the discharge of the duties and responsibilities imposed by the
C.M.C. on your Board of Control. several dis turbing factors ha ve
been noted.
Some boards have encourage d donations to. and maintain funds
for. purposes inconsiste nt with their responsibilities under the law.
Some boards have actively solicited or encourage d endowmen ts
and bequests for like purposes.
This affluence has made possible some of the non-permi ssive activity.
When questioned , some boards have pointedly stated that their fu nds
•and actions are of no concern to your Board of Control. The Secretary
of the San Gabriel Board on one occasion made a public statement to
the effect that "It was none of the Board of Control's business how
their money was spent." Other boards have on occasion, in private.
made similar statement s to the same effect.
This accumulat ion of endowmen ts. estates, and other surplus funds
derived from per capita. has apparently tended to make some Boards
of Relief feel independe nt from control of the member Lodges, and
above supervision of Grand Lodge through your Board of Control.
Your Board of Control has according ly issued a written directive
that surplus funds of a Board of Relief may not exceed one year's ope~­
ating expense. To implement this directive, moratoriu ms have been directed to reduce surplus.
The co-operati on by many of the boards has been immediate and
complete. However, some of the problems found in the San Francisco
East Bay and San Gabriel boards have required much correspon dence,
necessitat ed action by the Grand Master, and to this date, all problems
have not been fully resolved. Others , too, have refused to heed the
"Good Counsel" given them. choosing to continue to circumvent or totally ignore the law.
It is our opinion that since many a gencies exist for the financial relief of the distressed , and because the administra tion of sojourner funer~
als under our present system is costly, that Board~ of Relief no longer
fill the need which once existed.
The contention by some Boards of Relief that operations be ex-

198

199

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

panded in order to justify their existence and to enhance the public
image is not in our opinion a valid one. but clearly indicates no further
need for the Board of Relief. Boards of Relief, in our opinion, should
not be operated as a public relations bureau.
O ver one-half of the Lodges in this Jurisdiction do not belong to
Boards of Relief. We have yet to find one case where such non-membership has caused the sojourner to receive less than proper attention.
In view of the contents of this report. and our experience and study
this year, it is our opinion that Boards of Relief should be discontinued.
We again repea t that nothing in this report has been stated as
criticism of any person. body, office, or officer but is made as a statement of facts as they appear recorded, with opinions clearly labeled
as such.

as members of Grand Lodge, to determine the proper work to be carried
on by all employees. boards and committees operating in the name of
Masonry in California.

Your Library's growth this year is almost triple that of the preceding
year. A mos t substantial gift was received from Brother Alfred R. Porterfield, who donated an extensive collection of val uable Masonic books
collected from all over the world. We now have in excess of 4600 volumes. of which 3620 are available on the shelves of the Library proper.
During the year of July 1. 1968. through June 30. 1969, your Commission has purchased 39 volumes of particular reference value. We
have also received gifts of 585 books. most of which are out of print
and some of which are true collector's item s.
Books necessarily stored in the downstairs vaults have been properly
accessed and shelved for their better preservation and availability. All
such books. of Masonic nature. are now catalogued and housed on steel
shelves in a dry. dark space, looking toward the day when the entire
library may be housed as a unit.
We have also received the entire library of the Berkeley Clubhouse.
but not in time to classi fy for this report. As yet there has been no decision of what to do with surplus Masonic encyclopedias or with nonMasonic books. fiction and otherwise.
We have the pleasure to report that the correspondence use of the
Library by the Brethren has grown this year to a new peak of 275 volumes.
Our visitors' book has less entries this yea r. Because it was found
advisable to close the Temple on weekends for security, the Library
and Museum are now open only five days a week. This has cut the
number of visitors as compared with last year. However. during Grand
Lodge Week, as usual. the facilities will be open every day. At that
time the registration of visitors is not officially kept.
Our volunteer Assistant Librarians, as dedicated a group of Brethren as you will find in this Jurisdiction. show a few changes in personnel
from last year. Our actives have been William H. Scott. William McMaster, Adolph Kiersch. Arthur Simpson. P aul Harasin, George Beard,
Morris Licin, Stanley A. Butera, Carroll Peake, Clinton Ross and H enry
Cardoza. These brethren are all well-acquainted with the cataloguing
and, regardless of whether you visit between Monday and Friday or
you write in for references, they will be of inestimable help in your
research.
This year we were permitted sufficient capital expenditure to purchase two new cases for Museum display. You will have noticed these
cases, which now use the last of the available space on the second floor
hallway, to give maximum display to our collections of memorabilia,
Masonic, early Californian and other.

The third meeting was held on September 6, 1969, at the Caledonia
Masonic Temple in Bakersfield at which time all matters considered at
the previous meetings were reviewed and finalized. It was decided to
present a Youth Order display in the Exhibit Hall during this Annual
Communicatio n. The above mentioned pamphlets and other pertinent
youth orders material are now on display and each of you is urged to
check this exhibit to see what our youth groups are doing.
All committee meetings were well attended and conducted in a
most friendly and harmonious manner.
In addition to the three Youth Orders Committee meetings, your
Chairman attended the two adult leaders conferences, held in Santa
Ana, as the representative of this Grand Lodge. At these meetings
numerous mutual problems affecting our three youth orders were discussed. These meetings afforded each of the orders an opportunity to
profit by the experiences of the others and to present alternate approaches to these mutual problems.
A thorough examination of records and reports obtained by the
Youth Orders Committee indicate the following problems as related to
our youth orders.
1. Rental rates
2. Adult attendance and support
3. Understanding of the California Masonic Code areas appertaining to Youth Orders fund-raising activities
Rental Rates: As indicated by many letters, visits and reports,
excessive rent continues to be a major problem. This is substantiated by
reports from the Grand Guardian, Supreme Deputy and Executive
Officers. These reports provide the following data:
Bethel No. 267, E ast 3rd St., Downey with 71 members pays $900.00
per year;
Bethel No. 62, 520 Main St., El Segundo with 38 members pays
$480.00 per year.
Bethel No. 4, W. Manchester, Playa Del Ray with 40 members pays
$480.00 per year.
John D . Spreckels chapter in the Southern Jurisdiction of DeMolay
with 30 members pays $720.00 per year and La Mirada chapter with 30
members pays $500.00 per year. Your Committee congratulates the San
Bernardino Temple Association for reducing the DeMolay Chapter rent
to $480.00 per year for the chapter. By their actions this chapter can
now continue to function and teach the young men of that city the
precepts of DeMolay.
One Rainbow Assembly was forced to pay the Long Beach Temple
Association $60.00 rent for a two- hour meeting and was told by the
secretary of the Association that he preferred not to rent to the girls
even though the temple would remain idle. It was also reported that

Southwest Chapter of DeMolay was forced to dose and relinquish its
Charter because of excessive rent by Fairview Masonic Temple Association. By the same token on the other side of the coin, those who don't
pay any rent are equally undesirable. This policy tends to undermine
the sense of self reliance and responsibility taught by the youth orders.
Your committee feels that rents should be charged but that they should
be commensurate with the youth groups' ability to pay. The Lodges
can contribute to the youth groups' treasuries by having these young
people prepare and serve dinners, by paying them to work on their
temples, etc. This will instill a sense of accomplishmen t and personal
pride within the youth order members. We recommend that each appropriate body review their rental policies concerning the youth orders
with the idea of establishing a more equitable rent rate if one is required.
Adult Support: Your Committee suggests a more diligent effort on
the part of every Mason to support the youth organizations. Adult
attendance at youth meetings and support of their activities promotes a
greater interest on the part of the youth and renders a rich reward to
each participating Mason. Such attendance and support also provides
direct communication with and results in better understanding between
all organizations concerned. The Masonic image will be greatly enlarged
and improved by your participation in our youths' activities and meetings.
Fund Raising: Problems relative to fund raising have often arisen due
to a lack of under.standing of the appropriate portion of C.M.C. :regulations governing commercialism and fund raising. Such regulations are
clea rly outlined in the 1968 Supplement to the C.M.C. beginning on
page 64. The contents of this section have been communicated to the
heads of the youth orders in this jurisdiction and it is recommended that
excerpts thereof be provided for distribution to the adult leader of each
DeMolay Chapter, Job's Daughters' Bethel and Rainbow Assembly.

R ecommendation
Your Committee recommends that a Standing Committee for Youth
Orders be appointed by the Masters of each constituent Lodge within
this jurisdiction. Such committee should consist of at least three members for each youth order meeting within their respective temple or, if no
youth groups meet within the temple, nearby vicinity. If no youth orders
exist within the area, it is recommended that action be initiated by these
standing committees to organize and have one or more of these youth
groups chartered. Such committee should also be charged with the
responsibility of having at least one of its members in attendance at all
Youth Order meetings and activities throughout the year. The Chairman
or his delegated representative should be required to report the activities of the youth orders directly to the Lodge at each Stated Meeting.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON INSURANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Insurance Committee of Grand Lxige is a special committee
appointed by the Grand Master and it is responsible to the Grand Master for such duties as the Grand Master may deem desirable or necessary. Under the instructions given to us we were instructed to analyze
all of the insurance policies for Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes at
Decoto and Covina as well as the coverages for the Constituent Lodges.
the Boards of Relief and the other Masonic entities. We were instructed
to report our findings and recommendations to the Grand Master.
The lnsur.ance Committee is composed of four full time insurance
men. One is a company manager and the other three are insurance brokers. We have met several times in discussions and we have utilized
our own experience to obtain what we believe to be minimum costs and
added coverage.

1. WORKMEN'S COMPENSATIO N
In 1968 the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes changed their
workmen's compensation to a retention form of coverage. It seemed
to us that the proper and logical course of action was to change the
other compensation policy. covering the employees of Grand Lodge.
the Constituent Lodges, Boards of Relief, etc., to a similar retention
form in the same company. In this way the premiums and loss could be
combined. This has been accomplished.
If the trend of losses in 1968 continues, and we believe that it will.
you can expect a refund of as much as $35,000 at the end of the three
year plan.

2. 3-D POLICY
This policy provides for losses of money, securities and checks due
to dishonesty, destruction or disappearance.
We prepared specifications and took bids from several companies.
The specifications called for a basic fidelity coverage of $10,000
for the Constituent Lodges. etc., with an excess coverage of $490,000
on the employees of Grand Lodge and Masonic Homes.

210

For those Lodges and Temple Associations that desired more than
$10,000 we provided it.
You will be pleased to know that all of this increased protection
only cost $255.00 additional over a three year period.
3. LIABILITY AND MATERIAL DAMAGE INSURANCE
Last year the li~bil'.ty coverage, fire insurance and. paraphernalia
coverages were carried m more than ten policies and by more than one
company.
. Wit~ th_e approv~I of o~r Grand Master bids were taken on a special lnst1tut1onal Policy. This combines all of our liability and material
dam~ge requirements in one policy. This policy provides all of the
previous coverages in the previous policies. In addition some new coverages have been added. One important coverage is the OFFICERS
!'-ND TRUSTEES LIABILITY PROTECTION. In addition we have
increased the coverage on the Valuable Papers from $500 to $5,000.
We are delighted to advise you that this revision will save about
$1.500 a year.
4. TRAVEL ACCIDENT POLICY
T~is policy provides coverage for medical expenses, accidental death
and dismemberment for certain Officers and Trustees when traveling
on Grand Lodge business.
C?ur Committee has carefully examined this policy and we find that it
~rov1des adequate coverage. and that the coverages provided are more
liberal than the average similar policy.
The poli~y pr?visions and exclusions are satisfactory. We recommend that this policy be renewed in its present form.
. The Insurance Committee is deeply grateful for the invaluable assistance of the Grand Master. He made our work very much easier
.
We have incurred no expenses to Grand Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,
SAMUEL C. LEVIN, Chairman

REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE
ON COMMERCIALI SM
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Commercialism herewith submits its Report for
the year just ending.
Infractions of our laws. rules and regulations under the jurisdiction
of this Committee have been of minor character during this year. No
Masonic Trial resulted from any matters under the jurisdiction of this

215

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Committee. Most violations were handled by a member of the Committee whispering good counsel into the ear of the offender. Most violations by individual members have been the result of ignorance. An
example of this type of violation is a calling card of a member on which
is imprinted the square and compass. The member using these calling
cards was not using them for business or commercial purposes. However, the right to use or authorize the use of the square and compass
is the sole prerogative of the Grand Lodge.
A more serious violation was that of an energetic salesman who
made use of a Masonic Roster in order to solicit sales of automobiles.
Needless to say, such solicitation was stopped by the offender immediately upon his being informed of our rules and regulations.
We have had no problems with the Shrine Temples or Shrine dubs.
Before commencing fund raising activities, these organizations have
sought our advice. Two examples are as follows . One, a proposed fund
raising program called a "Baseball Night." The plan contemplated
Shriners' Marching Units putting on a program before the game. In
order to raise money for the Shrine Hospital. the Shrine membership
would sell baseball tickets and the owner of the baseball club would
pay_ to the Shrine a percentage of the sales price of tickets sold by the
Shrme members only-the proceeds to be given to the Shrine Hospitals. This event would have been advertised as a "benefit for the Shriners'
Hospital for Crippled Children," This advertisement would have been
included in 4,000,000 brochures distributed by the owner of the baseball club. The Grand Master submitted this proposal to your Committee for recommendation. The Committee advised that while the purpose was laudable, the activity would be in violation of Sections 333
and 334 of the California Masonic Code, to wit: approval of this type
of fund raising activity would allow the Shrine to be lending its name
to the promotion of a commercial enterprise, a professional baseball club.
The other example was a proposal to have a DeMolay group, consisting of band and singers put on a single performance for the purpose
of raising money for the DeMolay chapter, Job's Daughters and Rainbow Girls. The sale of the tickets was to be made to the general public.
The Shrine club desiring to conduct this event requested advice from
our Grand Secretary as to whether the plan would be contrary to our
rules. The Grand Secretary submitted the matter to your Committee
and it advised that the performance would violate California Masonic
Code 333 and recommended that the request for authority to conduct
the program be denied.
Audited financial reports of the Shrine football games conducted
in California and ~awaii were submitted by the Most Worshipful
Grand Master to this C ommittee which examined the same, and reported its conclusions and recommendations to the Grand Master.
In general, all of these athletic activities have been well conducted,

the costs and expenses were within ·r eason, and the net proceeds have
been paid to the Shrine hospitals.
Your Committee does not initiate investigations. Our activities commence when complaints are referred to this Committee. As to each complaint, a member of the Committee makes an investigation and finally
a report. The lack of complaints during the last few years results from
the educational procedures of keeping the leaders of the appendant or
prerequisite organizations fully informed as to our regulations and to

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON STUDY
FOR THE COMMUNICAT ION OF THE
FUNDAMENTA LS OF FREEMASONRY
T o the. Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
At the One Hundred Nineteenth Annual Communication of this
Grand Lodge. the Most Worshipful Eugene S. Hopp, in his message
to the Grand Lodge, voiced his great concern in regard to the "importance of building Master Masons rather than merely initiating new
members in our great Fra ternity." Under this general heading of Ma~
sonic Knowledge and Education, he commented on the "laudable goal
of imparting more knowledge of Freemasonry to our Candidates and
to those who have received the degrees but failed to take advantage
of, or even to recognize, the great lessons.'' He then recommended that
the incoming Grand Master appoint a special committee to "study the
question of how best to implement the communication of the fundamentals of Freemasonry to every Master Mason."
Compliant to this recommenda tion, the Most Worshipful Robert A.
Crigler, Grand Master, appointed this Committee, charged with the
responsibility of making such a study, and with the responsibility to
report its findings and recommendations at our next Annual Communication.
The Committee met six times during the Masonic year, engaged in
research and study, consulted with many interested brothers throughout
the jurisdiction, and made inquiry into programs and activities of other
Grand Lodge jurisdictions, consistent with the purposes for which this

216

217

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Committee was appointed. The three members of the Special Committee
are unanimous in the comments, suggestions, observations, and recommendations contained herein, and are pleased to present the following Report:

part knowledge to our membership. These included the ?istrict m:etin.g
programs. the Regional Seminars. the Masonic Education Committee s
suggested programs, a nd the work of the Research Lodges and their
availability to assist.
The Committee also reviewed the Mentor, Intender , Counsellor
programs in use in various other Grand Jurisdictions, and the programs
in the area of Masonic education being followed in some of the Grand
Jurisdictions ref erred to.
During the entire period of the Committee's studies and deliberations it was recognized that the question as to how best to implement
the communication of the fundamentals of Freemasonry must be considered under two distinct headings. namely. ( 1 ) the indoctrination
of Master Masons, and ( 2) the indoctrination of C andidates for the
Degrees. Indoctrination would differ considerably both in subject ma tter and methods of communication. Further, it is recognized that the
Candidate indoctrination, insofar as the teachings of our Ritual. is mandatory, and the enhancement of his indoctrination through the introduction of other requirements during the period of his acceptance and
receiving of the degrees could properly be made a requirement during
this period when he is most enthusiastic and receptive to learn about
Masonry and what it stands for. On the other hand, the appeal :o the
mind and for the attention of the Master Mason must of necessity be
on a different basis, and any programs developed for this category
must be of a nature that will appeal to him, arouse his interest, and develop a sense of pride, enthusiasm and responsibility for bis Fraternity.
With this preamble to our thinking, we offer the following observations and conclusions as to courses of action to achieve the objectives
of Past Grand Master Eugene S. Hopp's recommendation.

INTRODUCTION

This concern in regard to the communication of the fundamentals
of Freemasonry to our members has been expressed from time to time
during the entire history of our Grand Lodge. Typical of this concern
is that expressed by Most Worshipful William H . Howard, Grand
Master, at the Sixth Annual Communication, in the year 1855, when
he said: "Masonry is seldom or never properly understood or duly
appreciated, without suitable proficiency in the degrees from which the
candidate advances; and this proficiency does not involve merely the
ritual and its correct recital, but involves an intimate acquaintance with
the sublime truths and precepts of the Order, and a knowledge of its
origin, history, and the purposes for which it was instituted, and has
thus far been maintained. I would suggest as a means of improvement.
the establishment of Lodges of Instruction, devoted not merely to the
Ritual. but to moral and scientific attainments, and the dissemination
of useful information among the Brotherhood."
Similar expressions have been made by our Grand Masters through
the years, and our Annual Proceedings record a variety of means employed from time to time to bring about a more meaningful indoctrination of our members.
The Committee's studies included a review of the methods now
employed or available, directed toward the goals desired, such as the
Degrees, the Candidate Coaching program , the Masonic Education
Committee program, the Research Lodge activities, the articles in the
California Freemason. the articles appearing in Lodge Trestleboards, and
the Grand Lodge programs such as Public Schools Week, Constitution
Observance, Homes Endowment, Youth Orders, etc. It was recognized that in some instances the activity and methods were mandatory.
some were optional, some limited in scope, some had their effect in an
indirect manner. We explored the problem attendant upon the execution of Masonic education or indoctrination programs; these included,
that with the exception of the Ritual and Candidate's Lectures, all endeavors in this direction were noncompulsory insofar as the individual
Mason was concerned; that in many areas there was a lack of leadership in quantity to engage in comprehensive programs; the lack of interest manifested among the membership of the Lodges; the lack of
detailed and well-planned programs directed toward established objectives; and the lack of printed material available to those interested
in pursuing such a program.
The Committee reviewed the endeavors of the past designed to im-

THE INDOCTRINATION OF MASTER MASONS

We recognize that much has been accomplished toward the goal
of communicating the fu ndamentals of Freemasonry in respect to Lodge
officers. past a nd present..and those faithful sideliners who are present
at most Lodge meetings. Our concern, therefore, is primarily for the
vast number of our members who seldom or never attend Lodge, or indicate an interest in the Fraternity.
In this regard, we recognize that the successful communication of
the fundamentals of Freemasonry to the non-attender-successful in
that he would take a renewed interest in Masonry and live and act as
such-has been a long sought and seldom achieved goal in the annals
of Masonry. This Grand Lodge, and all Grand Lodges . have used
every conceivable idea to attract these Brethren back to Lodge and to
Masonry. and most will agree there has been a pronounced lack of
success in this regard.

219

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRA N D LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

We suggest that, first. there must be a well-rounded program of
activities designed to create in the mind of the individual Mason a spirit
of fraternalism with his fellow Lodge members as a starting point; and,
secondly, that a predetermined progra m of education and indoctrination be pursued through the various means available within the Lodge.
The former suggests those activities that will appeal to the interests of
the individual members, designed to encourage their attendance, and
motivate their participation. This calls for a comprehensive program
of activities under the direction of the Master, with competent committees to carry out the assig nments.
The second element suggests a program of Masonic education and
indoctrination, utilizing the following means of communication:
A . A Masonic education and information committee, charged with
the responsibility of adopting one of the three basic programs sug~ested
by our Grand Lodge Masonic Education Committee in the Lodge Manual. We strongly urge the use of Research Lodge Personnel. or other
qualified speakers on Masonic subjects. at Stated Meeting dinner programs, perhaps quarterly; the inclusion of a five to ten minute talk on a
selected Masonic subject at each Stated M eeting, Installation program.
Roll Call meeting, 50-year Veteran Button presentation meeting, and
other special occasions; and the presentation of Masonic plays, by qualified groups.

To summarize the foregoing in regard to the education and indoctrination of the Master Mason, the Committee is of the opinion that
the structure and operation of a great many of our Lodges would have
to undergo some changes in procedures, attitudes and philosophy of
Masters and Wardens, and a broadening of the scope of activities of
the Lodges.

218

B. The use of and encouragement of Masonic publications. The
Lodge Trestleboard affords an opportunity of communicating the fundamentals of Freemasonry, because short but well prepared articles
may, over a period of time, have effect, and the reporting and commenting on Masonic events and functions arouses interest. Also the
California Freemason is a valuable instrument for this purpose and its
use as a source of education and information should be encouraged.
Further, members should be encouraged to read and subscribe to other
Masonic publications and literature.

C. Other source materials are available in the Grand Lodge Library, and the Masonic Library of Southern California. Their use by
Lodges and members should be encouraged.
D. Participation in the affairs and activities of the Lodge is an invaluable means of indoctrination and education of the individual member. The means of inducing participation of the member a t the Lodge
level include the following: (a) Indoctrina te and appoint member to
serve on Investigating Committee; ( b) Encourage degree participa tion ;
( c) Assign committee responsibilities; (cl) Encourage Candidate Coaching b?' the. member; ( e) Attendan~e and participation in Grand Lodge
functions m the area; a nd ( f) Bnng about exposure to programs and
functions of the Lodge that will appeal to the wife of the member,
and/or his family.

THE INDOCT RINATION OF CANDIDATES

In this area, the Committee believes, after long and careful study,
that efforts directed toward the education and indoctrination of the
candidate will produce the most notable results. It is during the period
of the candidate's travels through the Blue Lodge degrees that he is
more attentive and receptive to a program of indoctrination in the elements of Freemasonry that would be beneficial to both the candidate
and Masonry in general. The background for this, of course. is in the
fact that by our regulations he must give his attention to the coaching
necessary to attaining his proficiency in the candidate's lectures of the
three degrees. It was on this basis that our present candidate's coaching
program, during which, theoretically. he is indoctrinated with the contents of the valuable material contained within the Handbook for Candidates Coaches. was instituted. If the candidate coaching program,
augmented by the program originally designed to be used in conjunction with the Handbook for Candidates Coaches , were to be diligently
and effectively presented to the candidate. then we would make great
strides in achieving the goal of building Master Masons rather than
merely initiating new members in our great Fraternity.
The candidate coaching program, adopted by our Grand Lodge
in 1962, wherein the candidate is exposed to the various facets of F reemasonry by his coach during the period of his coaching sessions for
the next degree, is a laudable one. However, in practice, the fact that
it was made flexible in order to be adapted to the several ty pes of situations existing in our far-flung jurisdiction has in many instances worked
to the detriment of the program. In some instances it has been completely ignored, in others it has been followed ineffectively through lack
of dedication and interest on the part of the officers and the coaches,
despite the fact that it has been a very effective program in many Lodges
and in many districts. The Committee is of the opinion that our present
program has great potential. and that with serious application and
imagina tion on the part of those in whose hands it is entrusted at both
Lodge and District levels, it has the means to effectuate the objectives
desired.
In our search for causes of failures of the past and possible solutions
to direct our future efforts in this field, the Committee sought information in regard to like programs being carried on by other Grand Lodge
Jurisdictions. We found that their program of instruction to the candi-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

dates followed a generally uniform pattern, based on four or five printed
booklets, in most cases imparted or reviewed with the candidate by a
brother assigned to the candidate for that purpose. We found that
their programs, like ours, suffered from not being mandatory. The absorption of information by the candidate was not compulsory and further. that those assigned to instruct the candidates were not required
to pass any given proficiency before being certified to instruct the candidates. The information gleaned from other Grand Jurisdictions indicates that our present program of coaching and indoctrination parallels
the efforts of the other Grand Lodges, having the same opportunities
for success, but being plagued by obvious shortcomings due to the fact
that i~ both instances a strict adherence to and execution of the program is not mandatory by the Grand Lodge regulations.
Fundamentally, the education and indoctrination of the candidate
begins with the contents of the three degrees. efficiently exemplified.
~!so, the requirement that the candidate commit to memory those portions of the degree termed "The Candidate's Lecture" is a prime manner of imparting fundamentals and principles of Masonry to the candidate. While we recognize that the mere memorizing of the words of
the candidate's lecture does not make him a well-informed and knowledgeable Mason, we recognize that the knowledge •r eceived from mouth
to ear leaves a lasting imprint upon the mind of the candidate who
receives it in the receptive mood usually prevalent during the period
of his receiving the degrees.
The contents of the booklets prepared by our Grand Lodge for
prese~tation. t~ the candidate and the many facets of Freemasonry

contamed w1thm the Handbook for Candidates' Coaches constitute a
fund of information well calculated to impress upon the candidate the
origin, the history, the principles, the teachings, and the purposes of
Freemasonry. It is with such tools as these, with a well planned procedure and a dedication on the part of the officers and coaches to fulfill
their purposes that this phase of the candidate's progress in Masonary
will be enhanced .
Another area in which the candidate may become imbued with the
fund~mentals of Freemasonry is participation in Lodge activities and
f?nctions. that h_e _may be eligible to participate in during the course of
time o_f h~s rece1vmg the degrees. His attendance at Lodge dinners, at
Constitution Observance programs, at Public Schools Week Observance, at th~ ~nnual installation of officers, at a Cornerstone Laying Ceremony, a v1s1t to one or both of our Masonic homes, attendance at a

m the candidate coaching program, and assisting in the indoctrination
