221

After receiving the third degree, the candidate should become involved in the Lodge and its activities at once. Many avenues of endeavor are open to him, namely (a) Qualifying for his Third Degree Proficiency Certificate; (b) Assisting in t.h e ritualistic work and coaching
program; ( c ) Working on Lodge Committees; ( d) Working with one
of the Youth Groups; ( e) Attending Grand Lodge functions in the
area ; ( f) Serving on Investigating Committees; and the many other
activities and programs of the Lodge.
The Committee believes that exposure to the foregoing Masonic
experiences will give him further insight into what Masonry is all about
at the time when he is most interested and receptive. These experiences ,
together with the Ritual instruction, should make him a fairly knowledgeable Mason.
RECOMMENDATIONS FOR FUTURE CONSIDERATION OR STUDY

1. The Committee believes this Grand Lodge should give consideration to making it mandatory that a course of indoctrination be required
in each Lodge, or at the District or area level. Such course to be prescribed, and include Masonic information and education, and it be
audited by every candidate before he may become eligible to receive the
next degree. This cou.r se of instruction should include a preliminary
meeting for the candidate, to a cquaint him with the Fraternity and
what it stands for. and prepare him for a proper attitude in his approach
to receiving the degrees. It is suggested that the recommenders should
accompany the applicant tQ such a meeting, and consideration be given
to the advisability of the candidate's wife attending also. Further
sessions for the candidate's benefit would precede and follow each of
the three degrees, guided by a prescribed course of instruction based
on our available resource materials, or formats to be developed for this
purpose.
2. The program of education and indoctrination of the candidate
we envisage will necessarily slow down the frequency of the candidate's advancement through the three degrees. We submit that in
order that any such program be effective, sufficient time must be allowed
between each degree to permit the candidate's receiving the benefit of
the knowledge and information ofiered. Therefore, consideration should
be given to prescribing a waiting period between the degrees, such as
some foreign jurisdictions require, in order to obviate rushing the candidate through the degrees and short cutting this phase of his Masonic
ex perience.
3. The development of a more consistent and active program of
candidate education and indoctrination in every Lodge would necessarily result in more administrative duties and respo·n sibilities upon the

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The report of the Committee for the Study for the Communication
of the Fundamentals of Freemasonry has been referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes because it contains discussions
of numerous ma tters of presently existing policies, a number of plans
which the Deputy Grand Master has announced he intends to inaugurate through the Committee on Masonic Education, as renamed, and
the enumeration of some things which are being done in other jurisdictions which are not done in ours.
The report is fifteen pages in length and it is not practical to make
now the favorable comments which the report warrants. The report
will appear in the printed Proceedings and every Warden of a Lodge
should read it. We feel none can read without gaining information or
being stimulated to realization of some answers to local problems.

224

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

The report recommends the inauguration of meetings to the same
or similar ends of meetings already scheduled by the Deputy Grand
Master. We do not believe the Special Committee intended duplication.
We do note an important difference. We understand the program envisioned by the Deputy Grand Master will be voluntary as to attendance,
whereas several of the programs recommended by the Special Committee would be mandatory as to attendance by Inspectors. officers or
others. Our Committee quite firmly believes that if the meetings cannot be made sufficiently interesting to command support on a voluntary
basis no service to Masonry will be rendered by making attendance
mandatory for some or all of those whose attendance is desired.
The report suggests that a solution to some problems might be to
have each Inspector appoint a chairman in general areas of ( 1 ) ritual,
( 2) candidate education, ( 3) candidate ·c oaching. ( 4) Lodge administration and ( 5) activities. Your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes does not favor the appointment of committee chairmen in
Lodges by other than the Master.
The report recommends that two special committees be appointed
for the ensuing year, one to many of the same ends as the special committee whose report we are considering and another special committee
to be composed of "representatives from the Masonic Education Committee. the Ritual Committee and such other personnel as may be
deemed necessary."

IN GRAND LODGE

It appears to your Committee on Policy and General Purposes
that such a procedure would result in having three committees working
in the areas in which one of them has already been charged to plow
new ground and to plow deep. One plow working in a field can make
straight furrows from one end to the other. but three plows cannot get
comparable results unless two merely follow the leader. Further. we
would question making further demands upon the time and energies
of members of the two committees suggested as the sources of part of
one of the proposed special committees.
On behalf of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes. I
move that the report of this special committee be referred to the Committee on Masonic Information and Responsibility, that this Grand
Lodge expresses its deep appreciation to the special committee for the
study and report which it has made in depth and that the reading of
the report by the officers of our constituent Lodges be recommended.
The Committees on Finance and on Ritual indicated their concurrence in the report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
Adopted.

REPORT OF SPECIAL CODE REVISION COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M . of California:
Upon the installation of The Most Worshipful Robert A. Crigler as
Grand Master, he appointed a Special Committee known as the Special
Code Revision Committee, pursuant to approval by Grand Lodge of
the previous Grand Master's Recommendation No. 6.
The committee has been charged with the responsibility of preparing
a revision of the existing California Masonic Code for presentation to
Grand Lodge. The members of the committee, after due consideration
of the past work of other Revision Committees. a meeting with the
elective line Grand Lodge officers and the counsel of Bill Davis, Past
Grand Lecturer, concluded that an entire rewriting of the Code was
not necessary. It has been the efforts of this committee during the last
year to review the Code, edit. delete, and made as few substantive
changes as necessary.
Our committee has met once a month since November 1968, working on the Code, with an additional meeting with the Grand Lodge
officers. Also, each of the members has done substantial individual
work in the intervals between meetings . The work has been painstaking and therefore slow, but we are pleased to report that of the
approximately 436 sections. plus annotations. a substantial portion of
the final work has been completed. As the committee continues to work,
greater efficiency is achieved, and it is projected that the revision of the
Code may be submitted to Grand Lodge at the 1970 Annual Communication.
Your committee is also proposing that the new Code be prepared
in a loose-leaf form suitable for substitution of pages, making the

yearly amendments easier to refer to than the present Supplement.
A budget allowance of $1.500.00 is requested, which request has
been transmitted to the Committee on Finance.
We wish to thank the Grand Master and all of the members of

GRANO LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

Grand Lodge for the patience, understanding and assistance which
have been rendered the Committee during the last year.

PERMIT SERVING LIQUOR AT SOCIAL AND OTHE R
GATHERINGS AND MEETINGS
1968 RESOLUTION (5)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge P. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS. there is a great deal of confusion as to whether or not
Lodges and other Masonic organizations can hold dinners, dinner dances
and other meetings and gatherings of a social nature in hotels. restaurants, clubs, picnic grounds and similar locations, and as to whether or
not Masonic groups may follow the usual and generally accepted social
customs at such affairs; and
WHEREAS, prior to 1964 there were no restrictions on the holding
of such gatherings in the normal American way and there will be presented to th is Grand Lodge at its 1968 Communication a statement by
the Grand Master that Masons cannot use liquor a t any dinner dance
or other social gathering which they attend in a public hotel or other
public place, which is the same as the Prohibition Amendment of the
1920's which proved to be unworkable and unenforceable and therefore
was repealed by the American people;
NOW. THEREFORE. BE IT RESO LVED: That the following
section be added to the California Masonic Cade:
Section 324.2. Social and other gatherings and meetings. A Masonic
Lodge, or an organization the prerequisite of membership wherein is
that a person be a Master Mason, may hold social gatherings, dinners.
dinner dances, picnics, and other meetings of a social nature or other
social events in a hotel restaurant, dining room, club. convention hall,
picnic area or other establishment at which liquor, wine or beer ma y be
used or served.
Respectfully submitted,
DoN H. ScHwIMLEY, P.M..

(NOTE: The Chairman of the Committee on Jurisprudence read the
language of the 1968 report of the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes, including the proposed legislation. pp. 246, 217 1968 Proceedings. which follows.}
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes :
We are advised by a proponent of this Resolution No. 5 that it is
designed to permit the serving and use of liquor only at social functions
and events which are sponsored by Masonic Lodqes or by o ne of the
so-called "prerequisite" bodies and which are held outside of any Masonic Temple or any building owned or operated by one or more of
the "prerequisite" bodies. We are in accord with that intent. We believe, however. that the following language will best accomplish the
purpose, without chang ing any of the other provisions of our Masonic
Code relating to the use and serving of liquor:
"Section 324.2. Serving of liquor at social functions . A Masonic
Lodge, or an organization the prerequisite of membership wherein is that
a person be a Master Mason, may hold social gatherings. dinners, dinner

229

dances. picnics and other meetings of a social nature or other social
events at w hich liquor, wine or beer may be used or served. in a hotel,
restaurant, dining room. club, convention ha ll, picnic area or other establishment; provided, however, that, except for ritualistic purposes, no
liquor. wine or beer may be served in a M asonic Temple or in any building or structure owned or operated by a M asonic Lodge or any organization a prerequisite of membership wherein is that a person be a Master
M ason; a nd provided, further. that this section shall not require a
Masonic Lodge or Masonic-related organization to vacate leased premises prior to expiration of leases made in good faith. or to violate leases,
or to refuse to accept buildings so received from an estate or by gift; but
such building so received must be sold or otherwise disposed of. or
the offending use must be terminated. within a reasonable time."
In our opinion the adoption of the foregoing proposal will eliminate
any a ura of uncertainty or hypocrisy about the propriety of serving
alcoholic beverages at purely social functions held outside of Masonic
premises.
We therefore move that Resolution No. 5 be amended to read as
above indicated; that if it is so amended, the resolution be adopted; and
in that case the Committee recommends a "yes" vote upon the resolution
as amended.
The Committee on Jurisprudence indicated that the amendment to the
resolution would accomplish its intent.
The amendment to the resolution was adopted.
Adopted 2/ 3rds vote.

SPECIAL FINANCE STUDY
1967 AND 1968 GRAND MASTERS' RECOMMENDATIONS No. 3

REPORT OF SPECIAL FINANCE STUDY COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The report of the Special Finance Study Committee (as then constituted) was adopted in principle at the October. 1968, Annual Communication of Grand Lodge ( 1968 proceedings, page 212).
In the present report, we will first call attention to certain provisions
which will apply to attendance at the Annual Communication of Grand
Lodge in October, 1969.
PAY OF MEMBERS ATIENDING ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
The "pay of members" practice in accordance with C.M.C.. Section
171. ( 1968 Supp.), remains applicable to the officers and the representatives (one person only) of each Lodge, and to Past Grand Masters,
C.M.C., Section 176. provided they are not eligible under the new
policy for reimbursement of hotel and meal expenses incurred in attending.
In other words, a n officer or representative of a Lodge or a Past
Grand Master attending Grand Lodge only in that capacity, receives
his nileage, but no other reimbursement from Grand Lodge.
'Che rate for California residents has been increased from 7 cents
to 10 cents per mile. Residents of Hawaii continue to receive flrst class
air fare. etc. ( C.M.C., Section 171, 1968 Supp.)

'
EXPENSE REIMBURSEMENT FOR GRAND LooGE APPOINTIVc
OFFICERS, INSPECTORS AND COMMITTEEMEN
There is a group formerly entitled to "pay of members" (C.M.C.,
Section 176) who are now entitled to transportation, hotel and meals
in attending the annual communication.
These are appointed Grand Officers, Inspectors, Chairmen of
Standing Committees and the Members of the Jurisprudence, Policy
and General Purposes, Grievances. Finance, Credentials. Lodge Financing, Pay of Members, Code Commission. Charters. Correspondence
and By-Laws Committees.
Also included are newly appointed Grand Officers, both from California and Hawaii, who attend for installation and remain for instruction.
Inasmuch as all those enumerated in the foregoing categories will
receive reimbursement on a reasonable and actual cost basis. they are
treated in a different "capacity" from the ones receiving only "pay of
members" mileage.
They may present claims and be reimbursed in due course upon
approval of their claims by the Audit Committee, for transportation,

232

233

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

lodging and meals on the basis defined in the 1968 Report ( 1968 Proceedings at page 222).
For convenience, the paragraph on transportation is here set out.
"Transportation for the person claiming. Minimum air fare, where
convenient airline schedules are available, from the closest principal
airport to destination's closest principal airport may be claimed: limousine or bus service to and from the airport may be included or parking
at the airport, and where required, car rental charges. Travel by
private automobile is optional to be reimbursed at 10 cents per mile
..., plus actual cost of tolls and parking. when the automobile is used
to transport two or more persons entitled to reimbursement, or because
no convenient airline schedule is available. Otherwise, anyone traveling
by automobile rather than by airline shall claim whichever amount is
less. If bus or train is used as an option, the minimum air fare is the
maximum allowable claim."
The allowance for lodging is the cost of the hotel or motel selected,
at single occupancy rate. which must be reasonable and actual consistent
with prices prevailing in San Francisco, or the immediate vicinity. There
is no arbitrary or fixed per diem. The Audit Committee (appointed by
the Grand Master) is conversant with the range of hotel prices in San
Francisco and whatever is reasonable and actually spent will be reimbursed.
Reimbursement for meals is on the same individual basis and will
be allowed for amounts which are reasonable in San Francisco or the
immediate vicinity, and which are actually spent by the person claiming.
The Inspectors qualify for the foregoing. both in attending the
Lodge of Instruction immediately preceding Grand Lodge, and for the
entire period during which they are in attendance at the Annual Communication.
Appointed Grand Lodge Officers are entitled also to reimbursement
for the cost of renting formal attire.
If the duties of any Chairman, Members and Consultants of Committees and Boards, not listed in C.M.C., 176, re.quire their presence
at the Annual Communication, they also are entitled to reimbursement
on the same basis for transportation. hotel and meals for the period
actually needed in the performance of their duties. If any fall in this
category it will be by direction of the Grand Master, and the Audit
Committee will be so informed. If any consider themselves required to
be present, they must be sure that it is pursuant to direction of the
Grand Master, otherwise, they will not be entitled to reimbursement.
Any Committee or Board meetings in San Francisco, immediately
preceding the Annual Communication or called after the closing thereof.
when required by the C.M.C .. or approved in advance by the Grand
Master, are subject to the reimbursement provisions. Reference may
be made to the Report, 1968 Proceedings, page 221. An example is the

required organizational meeting of the Memorial Temple Board of
Trustees "at the close of the Annual Communication." Such a meeting
is a requirement in the C.M.C.
Anyone attending such meeting will be entitled to reimbursement
to the extent only that there is no duplication of reimbursement to him
in some other capacity.
CONTRIBUTION O F LoDGES TO EXPENSES OF
INSPECTORS D ISCONTINUED

Inasmuch as Inspectors will be reimbursed by Grand Lodge for
their transportation, hotel and meals in attending the Lodge and I nstruction and on through the entire session of Grand Lodge, so long
as they remain, the action taken by Grand Lodge prohibits the constituent Lodges from contributing . and Inspectors from accepting from
the Lodges, any sums intended to apply toward the expenses of an
Inspector.
This does not prevent any Lodge from contributing through its
officers or representatives, if desired, to the actual pro rata cost of a
special breakfast or luncheon hosted by the Inspector during the Annual
Communication.
METHOD OF SECURING REIMBURSEMENT

Those entitled to transportation under the formula of "pay of
members," as set forth above in this report, including both California
and Hawaii residents, will receive checks for the appropriate amounts
upon calling as u~ual at the counter of the "Pay of Members" Committee.
All other reimbursements will be upon presentation of claims upon
the proper forms, supported by reasonably available written memoranda
or data and subject to approval by the Audit Committee.
New forms for presenting claims for reimbursement may be avail~
able, with instructions printed on the reverse s ide, but in the event they
are not, the old forms provided by the Grand Secretary's Office may be
utilized.
BOOKLET OF INSTRUCTIONS AND REGULATIONS

In accordance with the intent of the 1968 Report and consona nt
therewith, the present Committee has prepared a booklet of instructions
(rules) and regulations pertaining to expense claims, a draft of which
is annexed to this Report as an exhibit. The Audit Committee is already
working under the system set forth. However, it is intended that upon
approval by Grand Lodge, the booklet be printed and given general
distribution.
We have endeavored to keep it in harmony with the 1968 Report,
with one minor exception. The 1968 Report required (Proceedings,
page 222) that for reimbursement of travel it must be fifty miles or more
in any calendar month. Your Committee, with the advice and consent

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of the Audit Committee. based on experience during the year to date.
has concluded that this is an unimportant and sometimes confusing
restriction. We recommend that it be eliminated, and have omitted it
from the Instructions and Regulations.

For lack of complete information and because a full year's experience

EXPENSE CLAIMS

ALLOCATION OF EXPENSE REIMBURSEMENTS
Your Committee construes the adoption of the 1968 Report, and
the action of the Committee on Finance in establishing a per capita
calculated to provide the increased funds necessary to cover reimbursement for those attending the Annual Communication, as a mandate
that all reimbursement for such attendance be allocated and classified
in the general cost of the Annual Communication.
None of it should be charged against committee budgets. To do so
would in many cases create an imbalance, as at least some budgets did
not provide for this expense. It is better to make a single accounting
adjustment, if one be required, that of the cost of the Annual Com munication, than a plurality of adjustments in committee budgets.
PROPOSED LEGISLATION
Some of the recommendations adopted in principle at the 1968
Annual Communication should be, and certain ones necessarily must
be. adopted as legislation to become fully and perma nently effective.
Your present Committee, therefore, has drafted legislation which
it deems to be desirable to carry out the full intent of the 1968 Report.
a nd presents such proposed legislation as an exhibit to this present
Report, in the form of a Resolution, and recommends that it be adopted.
Respectfully submitted,

Audit Committee
The Grand Master, in accordance with the Special Finance Study
adopted at the 1968 Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, has
appointed an Audit Committee empowered to approve, modify. or
disallow expense claims. The member requesting reimbursement of
expenses may request a review of the Audit Committee's decisions. The
Grand Master or an elective Grand Lodge officer designated by him will
review the member's request and the decision made by the Grand Master
or the Officer designated by him shall prevail. If the Audit Committee
be uncertain as to the correctness of requests for reimbursement, it
should request a review by the Grand Master or his designated Elective
Officer. Generally, the Audit Committee should satisfy itself that the
claim submitted is in accordance with the rules set forth herein and is
correctly computed.

Definitions:
"Necessary Expenses" as the term is used herein are de.fined as
follows:
1. They include:
(a) Transportation: for the person claiming. Minimum air fare,
where convenient airline schedules are available, from the closest principal airport to destination's closest principal airport may be claimed:
limousine or bus service to and from the airports may be included. or
parking at the airport, and where required, car rental charges.
Travel by private automobile, plus actual cost of tolls and parking,
is optional. when the auto is used to transport two or more persons
entitled to reimbursement OR because no convenient airline schedule is
available.
Otherwise, reimbursement shall be made on the basis of mileage or
airline fare, as previously described, whichever amount is less. If bus
or train is used as an option, the minimum air fare is the maximum allowable claim.
(b) Lodging: allowed when an overnight stay is essential to the
schedule of event attended, or prudence suggests by reason of adverse
flight or weather conditions, or when the lateness of adjournment hour
of the event would result in arrival at home after midnight. Allowance
shall be for reasonable and actual cost consistent with the location of
the function where the expense is incurred.
( c) Meals: allowed when the normal periods for meals occur while
away from home dl!ring the period required to complete the round trip.
The rules for reasonable and consistent costs apply as described in the
section referring to lodging.
( d) Long distance telephone calls essential to performance of duties,
and postage.
( e) Secretarial service and other expenses , only when previously
approved by the Grand Master or his designated liaison officer.
2. Necessary expenses do not include expenses incurred by reason
of unnecessary early arrival for any event or unnecessary stay after the
event.
3. Under special circumstances the Grand Master may authorize
deviation from the restrictions imposed by the foregoing definitions .

General Information
All requests for reimbursement of expenses from properly authorized
Grand Lodge Officers. Inspectors and Committee and Board Chairmen
and Members, should be submitted at least monthly.
Vouchers or receipts for expenses generally are available upon
request from those furnishing goods or services-such evidence should
accompany the request for reimbursement.
The rate of "mileage" is determined by Grand Lodge at the Annual
Communication. Until further action, the rate of 10 cents per mile fixed
at the 1968 Annual Communication will remain in effect.
Requests for reimbursement must be submitted on the forms supplied
by the Grand Lodge. All appropriate entries should be made legibly
and accurately.

NOTE: One column of the Travel Expense Voucher form is devoted
to defining the Grand Lodge activity which necessitated the expense.
It is necessary, in every case, to fill in this column. Failure to do so may
delay reimbursement.
All members of the Grand Lodge entitled to reimbursement of
expenses incurred in Grand Lodge business are, because of the very
nature of our Fraternity, expected to use reasonable judgement and
caution when creating expenses.
Unless authorized in advance by the Grand Master, expenses submitted by a member shall not include expenses for the member's wife.
If a member's wife accompany him, the member shall be entitled to
reimbursement for lodging, as hereinafter defined, on the basis of the
room rate for single occupancy.
Members of Committees which have no prescribed duties to perform
during the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge are not entitled to
travel reimbursement as committee members.

all other functions of his office, in such amount as the Deputy Grand
Master (incoming Grand Master) shall request. The Grand Maste.r
need render only a general account of expenses incurred by him.

It has been our standard policy under a system of reciprocity with
the other Grand Jurisdictions, that properly authorized monetary relief
to a Sojourner in need would be reimbursed to the local Lodge from the
Lodge of the Sojourner's membership upon notification of the amount
expended.
We have to remember that a Sojourner or visiting Mason is required
to be a regular Master Mason who is a member in good standing of a
Lodge under our Grand Jurisdiction or of another Grand Jurisdiction
which bas friendly relations with our Grand Lodge and who is residing
or sojourning beyond the jurisdiction of his own Lodge but within the
jurisdiction of the Board of Relief to whom he has appealed for assistance.
The Boards of Relief are authorized to furnish to the distressed
Sojourner, his widow or orphans necessary food, clothing. shelter and
those services which a Lodge would normally provide.
The temporary relief authorized between actual meetings is limited
to any one person not to exceed $25.00 unless the expenditure is made
or the indebtedness incurred in advance at the request of the Sojourner's
Blue Lodge, to be refunded to the local Lodge making the disbursement.
When a request is made for relief or a Masonic burial. the. Board
of Relief is required to communicate with the sojourner's or visiting
Brothers Lodge. verify his good standing and request permission to
furnish relief or a Masonic funeral with any incidental expenditure for
flowers. newspaper notices or any other required charges. All such
disbursements are to be billed and repaid by the sojourner's home Lodge.
The metropolitan areas have drawn the largest proportion of Sojourners, so the burden of satisfying their immediate needs in the past
has been the responsibility of the local Boards of Relief. There has
been, however, a continuous decline in the number of reques ts for
relief by Sojourners. This is attributed to the rapid growth and extension of local. state and federal governmental relief systems such as
Social Security, Disability Insurance and Unemployment Insurance
Benefits. Because of these modern social aids today, there has been an
almost lack of bona fide requests from Sojourners. Any request has
been for minor occasional temporary assistance payments, pending
arrangements for more permanent w elfare aid in some form. Thus in
our present affluent society, there is some type of assistance available
to nearly all persons in need from the "cradle to the grave."
Requests have been made to Boards of Relief and expenditures incurred by them without authority to persons not identifiable as Master
Masons. We do not believe that it was ever the intent of Grand Lodge
that Boards of Relief should: 1 ) Operate as a travelers aid for the

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
SOJOURNER RELIEF AND BOARDS OF RELIEF
1968 GRAND MAsTER's RECOMMENDATION No . 2
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In accordance with the recommendation of Grand Master Eugene
S. Hopp in his message to the 1968 Grand Lodge Communication, the
Most Worshipful Robert A. Crigler, Grand Master of Masons in
California and Hawaii in 1969, appointed a Special Committee to study
and evaluate Sojourner Relief. how it should be organized and how
Boards of Relief should be maintained. This Speci~l Committee was
instructed to make a thorough study and report to the 1969 Communication its conclusions and recommendations.
The Special Committee has held many meetings. visited all of the
larger metropolitan cities, examined the reports of all of the Boards of
Re~ief submitted to the Board of Control. and reviewed the history of
Soioumers and their relief in California and Hawaii.
.We have fou~d that fro~ the formation of our Grand Lodge a
policy was established to relieve the necessary. immediate distress of
Sojourning brethren and their families. Because there was little or no
assistan.c~ ~vailable from any source to strangers in the community, the
respons1b1ltty for this assistance was primarily that of the individual
Lodge to whom the Sojourner appealed for help.
In the large cities, the Lodges began to form a joint Board of Relief
as the most efficient manner to perform this service. The Boards of
Relief increased in number with the passing years. They operated

244

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

convenience of servicemen and tourists if they do not qualify as a
Master Mason in good standing, who being away from home and finding themselves in a position requiring temporary financial assistance
because of indiscreet dissipation of funds, 2) Compensate in an indirect
manner a Past Master or a Worshipful Master for expenses incurred
to officiate or conduct a funeral for a Sojourner at the request of a
mortuary, 3) Act as a fiduciary for a Sojourner, 4) Maintain cemetery
plots for future use of Sojourners. 5) Use Board of Relief funds for
unauthorized social events. 6) Give Christmas gifts, 7) Draw additional
compensation from other concordant bodies, 8) Have a Secretary who
draws a pension in addition to the regular Board of Relief salary, 9)
Have a Secretary who receives additional monetary benefits in addition to the regular salary, 10) Do acts which would be illegal for a
constituent Lodge to do.
In our opinion the matter of relief as it is being presently administered by the various Boards of Relief is too loose and uncoordinated.
Many unauthorized functions have been created as activities to justify
their existence.
Since Boards of Relief now have only a small administrative function, we believe that their existence and the burdening of Lodges with
their expense is a matter for serious consideration. Our investigation
has revealed that because of this small administrative function, and the
steadily declining legitimate requests for relief, we are of the opinion
that all Boards of Relief should be abolished. Our conclusions are
supported by the introductions of Resolutions No. 14 and 15 submitted by the Secretaries of two of the larger Boards of Relief in the
state - San Francisco and East Bay, asking you to increase greatly,
the expansion of their duties in order to justify the existence of Boards
of Relief. The expanded duties asked for extend far beyond those
now authorized in the California Masonic Code, would increase the
expenses of the Board of Relief and the name would have to be changed
to cover entirely new involvement of activities.
This Special Committee after prolonged investigation and mature
discussion, have concluded and do unanimously recommend as follows:
1. That all Boards of Relief be abolished.
2. That this be accomplished by June 30, 1970.
The undersigned are grateful to the Most Worshipful Robert A.
Crigler, Grand Master of Masons in California and Hawaii, for the
opportunity of service afforded them in this special assignment.
We move the adoption of this report and the recommendations
therein contained.
Respectfully submitted,
DE WALD BAUM. Chairman

JAMES E. WELLET

Referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The comprehensive and serious report of this Special Committee
has been referred to your Committee on Policy and ~eneral Pur~o~es.
Two basic ideas are contained in the report. The first is, that the original
purpose for which Boards of Relief were instituted no lo~ger exists.
The duty is performed by a variety of governmental ag~nci~s. If any
task remains at all for the Board of Relief in this area, 1t might be to
direct the Brother needing relief to the proper governmental agency.
The second idea in the report is that the Boards of Relief have
assumed a variety of duties which were never actually as.signed to t~em
by this Grand Lodge. These duties. include b_lood-~ankmg; ar.ra~~ 1~g .
in urban areas, Masonic funeral services for soJournmg Masons, v1s1t~ng
the sick, dispensing Masonic information, assisting in the preparation
of Masonic Homes applications for out-of-town Lodges and for other
Grand Jurisdictions, etc.
Your Committee agrees that. in the main, the original relief duty
of these Boards is gone. We also heartily approve of the efforts of this
Grand Lodge to establish a State-wide blood bank system. Your
Committee believes, however, that many of the other functions assumed
by Relief Boards are vital functions for Freemasonry and were p:rformed by the Boards because no other Masonic agency was performing
them and because they needed to be done. The problem of what to do
about these functions will not be solved by abolishing the Boards of
Relief. Amputation is radical treatment for a hang-nail.
your Committee feels tha t a determination should be made of those
activities of Boards uf Relief which are essential for Masonry and after
provision has been made for continuing those . activities. by whatever
name the Board may be given. then the continued existence of the
Board of Relief as such can be decided. Included in this study should
be the question of jurisdiction-wide support for activities that may be
centered in urban areas.
Your Committee therefore recommends that Boards of Relief be
continued until such time as the problems described above are resolved.
I so move.
Adopted.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
BLOOD BANK AND SOJOURNER RELIEF
1968 GRAND MASTER'S RECOMMENDATION No. 2

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In his message to the 1968 Grand Lodge Communication . the then
Grand Master Eugene S. Hopp. recommended that a Special Committ.ee
continue the study of Blood Banks. Sojourner Relief and the entire

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Board of Relief system with a particular view to recommend to Grand
Lodge at its annual Communication in 1969, ( 1) how Blood Banks
should be organized, ( 2) the manner of the organization of Relief,
( 3) what areas should be covered beyond those of Sojourner relief. if
any, and ( 4) how the Boards of Relief should be maintained financially.
. Pursuant to this recommendation, the Most Worshipful Robert A.

therefore have a current balance of all Lodge Blood Fund Accounts at
any given time.
The Blood Bank Chairman of each Lodge or his assistant designated
by the Worshipful Master, would be the person authorized to release
Blood Bank credits only upon the order of the Worshipful Master .
Withdrawals should be restricted to the "immediate family" and this
should be defined as the Lodge member, wife, widow and minor children of the Lodge member. Any person, whether a Lodge member, his
immediate family or a friend, should have the right to make a deposit
for the Lodges' account. This would permit replacement of withdrawals
by outsiders if a Lodge member is medically unable to make a deposit
in the Blood Bank.
We believe that the blood needs of a sojourner should be the responsibility of the Lodge within the jurisdiction of the sojourner's residence.
The Lodge's Blood Bank Chairman should through the Lodge's Secretary communicate with the Sojourner's Lodge and endeavor to procure
replacement of the blood used by its member.
If a Lodge member is medically unable to donate or secure donations
to replace any withdrawals used for his or his immediate family use, he
should have the right to make a cash donation to Grand Lodge who
shall immediately purchase blood credits covering the withdrawal. The
blood credits so purchased shall be for the credit and deposited in the
Blood Bank Account from which the withdrawal is made.
We have personally contacted all of the principal offices of the
American National Red Cross and the American Association of Blood
Banks in the States of California and Hawaii that now have a Masonic
Blood Bank account and they are of the unanimous opinion that this
plan for a Blood Bank for the entire Grand Jurisdiction is not only
feasible, easy to set up, but will secure more substantial donations
because of its opportunity for use by the 240.000 Masons in California
and Hawaii. With a Grand Jurisdiction Blood Bank, Grand Lodge
would be in a position to shift necessary credits in an emergency to the
place of need which could then be replaced. This system would also
present a unique opportunity for obtaining additional deposits for
Lodges now without a Blood Bank.
Under the system proposed there would be an awakening of
every member of each Lodge to the vital and growing need for voluntary
blood donations. The paperwork would be simple. Each time a
donation is made to a Lodge account, the Chairman will receive from
the Blood Bank a copy of the donor's receipt for the blood given. Each
month an activity report will be mailed to Grand Lodge on which will
be recorded the following information in condensed form :
1. The number of donations and to which Lodge Blood Account
they have been credited.

The Special Committee has made an exhaustive examination with
the assistance and cooperation of the American National Red Cross and
the American Association of Blood Banks in the States of California
and Hawaii (all Auxiliary Blood Banks being associated with either
~ne of these societies). of the inquiry imposed regarding the organization of Blood Banks. We herewith submit our report and our recommendations thereto:
. Every part of our body depends on blood for survival. Blood and
its use in medicine is incalculable in value. It has saved millions of lives
and the. demand for it has increased with the passage of each year.
Every six seconds in the United States a team of medical specialists
perform~ one of the most vital of all operating procedures - a blood
trans fusion. Som~ 20?0 gallons of blood are used daily for this purpose.
When a transfusion 1s needed, the existence of a blood bank is most
essential and necessary.
We recommend that a Grand Jurisdictional Masonic Blood Bank
for California and Hawaii should be established under the supervision
~f the Grand ..M~ster ..A Blood Bank functions in the same way as a
money bank with units of blood as the medium of exchange. Blood
for transfusions can come only from people. It cannot be manufactured.
When blood is needed, donors must give it. Although the need for
blood is. ~rowing in our State at a rate of 14 % a year, only 3%
of the eligible donors are now giving it. Blood is deposited in advance
of need and loaned to patients requiring transfusions. The borrowed
blood is then replaced in the Blood Bank for the necessary use of others.
The procedure for setting up such a Blood Bank should be as follows:
. . E ach Masonic Lodge in the Grand Jurisdiction should establish.
if 1~ .does not now have one, a Blood Bank Account with its local
aux1~1ary blood center. Each Lodge should appoint a Blood Bank
Chairman who.se responsibility it would be to release the proper credits
to members eligible to participate in the plan only upon the order of
the Worshipful Master of his Lodge. A copy of all deposits and withdrawals from the Blood Bank would be forwarded to Grand Lodge by
the local blood center at the end of each month. Grand Lodge would

2. The number of withdrawals from each Lodge Blood Account
and by and to whom given.
3. The number of credits, if any. transferred to either the Home
for the Aged at Decoto or the Home for Children at Covina.
4. The number of credits which will be expiring because of outdated
storage and not used.
5. The current balance of each Lodge.
6. Unusual blood types available to meet an emergency need.
\:Vhen a Lodge member or an immediate member of his family
reqmres blood, the Lodge member simply contacts the Lodge's Blood
Bank Chairman or his Assistant Chairman and tells him the name of
the patient, the patient's home address, where he is hospitalized and
how much blood is needed.
The Chairman or Assistant Chairman then notifies the Worshipful
Master of the Lodge of the need for a withdrawal from the Lodge's
Blood Bank and secures his consent to such withdrawal. The American
National Red Cross or the auxiliary of the American Association of
Blood Banks is then authorized to charge the Lodge's Blood Bank with
the necessary withdrawal and they will do the rest of the work to see
th_at ~he blood is delivered where needed and on time for use. They
will e1t~er replace the bl~~ that has been used in the hospital or arrange
to provide blood when 1t 1s needed. Your committee has an assent in
writing that they will so cooperate.
If the patient has been discharged from the hospital and has paid for
the blood used, his money will be refunded by the hospital upon notification that replacement from the Blood Bank has been made for the blood
used.
Blood that has to be purchased from commercial sources because
the Lodge member does not have a blood bank account costs today
from $25.00 to $75.00 per pint. The cost for some blood derivatives
c~n _be as much as $1 ~5.00 per unit. The great value of a Grand Jurisd1ct1onal ~lood Bank 1s clearly demonstrated. It is a vital necessity and
most advisable when the cost of blood is considered today.
Although there is no charge under our plan for the blood itself
there is a small charge by the American National Red Cross and th~
American Association of Blood Banks in California and Hawaii. for
the collection, processing and distribution of each pint which a patient
uses. Generally this charge is covered by the patient's insurance so the
cost of blood used is very small when compared with its purchase from
a commercial source when there is no Blood Bank to draw upon in
time of need.
It should be kept in mind that under our plan, it is possible to donate
blood locally and have the blood credit transferred for use to any of
the fifty states. Our Blood Banks have a reciprocity system with other

community blood banks as well as with blood programs whereby credits
may be transferred to patients in any part of the United States. thus.
whenever a member or his immediate family may travel. their blood
protection goes right along with them wherever they may be.
This protection is given twenty-four hours of the day for 365 days
of the year. E ach member receives dual credit for a donation of blood
to the Lodge's Blood Bank. One credit in the Lodge's Blood Bank and
a credit in a personal account, this latter account being under the complete control of the donor.
We recommend further that within our program provisions for the
securing of blood donations from entire families be it the Lodge membe r,
his wife. his widow. or children, or even friends be encouraged so that
additional credits to the Blood Bank account can be obtained .
Security and peace of mind comes fro m knowing that blood or its
derivatives will be immediately available when needed. The success or
failure of our Grand Jurisd ictional Blood Bank will be in direct proportion to the understanding of our members as to the tremendous beneflts
of our suggested program. A patient cannot wait for vital blood when
it is required. It can be a case of life or death.
Never forget someone's life depends on you. When you give blood.
you give life. The blood you give today may save some one very dear
to you many years from now. Science fiction not at all. Until recently,
bloods red cells could be kept only twenty-one days under ordinary
refrigeration. With the revoluntionary new science of extreme cold.
the red blood cells may retain their life-saving properties indefinitely.
This new breakthrough will make possible the storage of vast supplies
of blood so that even the rarest and most despera tely needed may never
again be in short supply when required to save a life.
Blood is today's most amazing medicine, a miracle worker-newer
in some respects than penicillin. It saves more lives than our wonder
drugs. If you would visit a hospital on any single day, you would see
that blood and the medicines made from it are fulfllling many needs.
In an accident ward, a quick injection of human serum albumin made
from blood would be used to save a person dying of shock. A newborn
baby may be given a complete new blood supply to halt a possible battle
with incompatible anti-bodies. In the children's ward, youngsters get
injections of gamma globulin, a blood fraction which saves them from
a serious bout with measles. These are only a few of the daily
uses of blood in any la rge hospital which one of your loved ones may
need. There is no substitute for blood! There is no substitute for you!
This special committee after much study a nd investigation, has
concluded and does unanimously recommend as follows:
1. That a Grand Jurisdictional Masonic Blood Bank for the States
of California and Hawaii be set up at once.

JAMES E. WELLET

Referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The report of the special committee to study the matter of blood
banks has been referred to the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes. The report is at some length. It is information as to the use
of blood in various types of therapy. The entire report leads to its
conclusion that a jurisdiction-wide blood bank be established by the
Grand Lodge.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes is persuaded that
the better policy will be to establish a single jurisdiction-wide or two
state-wide blood banks than to have scattered local banks. Because we
recommend the adoption of the broad suggestion of the special committee does not mean that we also recommend all the mechanics suggested in the report, for example, the limitation on the persons who
would be eligible to draw or the assignment of important decisions to
members other than the Masters of Lodges. The proposed program is
not crystalized yet to the point where directions as to details should be
attempted by this communication. To get the matter before the house.
I move:
That it shall be the policy of the Grand Lodge to move forward
toward the establishment of a jurisdiction-wide blood bank or two statewide blood banks and that the incoming Grand Master appoint a special
committee for study and such action as he may authorize.
Adopted,

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE FOR
STUDY OF 50-YEAR VETERAN PINS
1968 GRAND MASTER'S RECOMMENDATION No. 8

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In accordance with Recommendation No. 8 of the Grand Master's
message to the 1968 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, this
Committee was appointed by Most Worshipful Robert A . Crigler "to
study the entire problem of the material and the design of the 50-Y ear
Button . and present recommendations to Grand Lodge at its next Annual Communication."
The Committee reached the conclusion that the design of the pin
should be modernized and made more attractive. and has created and
recommends the design shown in the accompanying print. The small
print is the actual size-the large print is to illustrate details. The· gold
content is approximately the same as that of the pins presently in use.
It is recommended that the new design be adopted, to be made of
l 4K yellow gold from the hills of California with blue hard enamel,
using the new type thin push-on back.
Your Committee has located a reputable source which has made a
commitment. first, that gold is available, and, second, that it can supply
these pins currently to Grand Lodge at a price of approximately twothirds of the price being paid for the present pins. We recommend that
such source be utilized unless some other manufacturer on competitive
bids quotes lower for equal quality. The name and address of the committed source will be made available to the Grand Master and the
Grand Secretary.
We further recommend that a parchment similar in size and style
to the accompanying design, and suitable for framing, be obtained and
presented with each button, the cost of the parchment to be determined
on the basis of competitive bids.
We further recommend that a card suitable for carrying in the
wallet. and of similar design to the above parchment, be obtained and
presented with each button , the cost of the card to be determined on
the bas is of competitive bids .
It is recommended that implementation of the foregoing program
be undertaken forthwith upon adoption of this report by Grand Lodge,
but that the present supply of 50-Year Buttons be exhausted before
presentation of the new buttons and accompanying items be commenced.
The program recommended by this Committee is inspired and encouraged by the belief that all recognition possible should be shown our
50-year members, not only for their service to the Fraternity, but also
because these men who are in their retiring time of life feel deeply about
such tokens of appreciation.

PROCEDURE-COMMON DISASTER
(1)
To the M ost Worshipful Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, it is customary and sometimes incumbent on the Grand
Master. Deputy Grand Master, Senior and Junior Grand Wardens to
travel all together or several together in the performance of their duties,
and
WHEREAS, common disasters are possible and have occurred in
certain organizations, football teams and businesses. and
WHEREAS. the California Masonic Code is silent on procedure
to be adopted in the event of such a common disaster.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that a new section 32.l be
added to the California Masonic C ode as follows :
32.1. COMMON DISASTER. Should the offices of Grand
Master, Deputy Grand Master, Senior and Junior Grand Wardens become vacant by common disaster or otherwise. it shall be
the duty of the Grand Secretary or Assistant Grand Secretary
to convene a Special Communication within sixty ( 60) days of
said disaster wherein persons shall be elected and installed in the
manner provided for at an Annual Communication. Pending said
election and installation the immediate living Past Grand Master
shall discharge the duties of the Grand Master.
Respectfully submitted.

pos It is the other instance or time when a vote by ballot mii:Jht be requested that causes your Committee on Policy and General Purposes
to recommend that you vote "no" on this proposed amendment. That
is the instance when a vote is taken by voice, but the ayes and nays

The members of this Committee have observed the present requirement of only three requests in operation for many years. It seldom has
been requested after a voice vote and in no instance which could be
termed an abuse. Your Committee deems that it is more important to
achieve an accurate determination of a close vote than to merely make
it more difficult to obtain a written ballot.

would be necessary to achieve the change the proponent desires you to
make. After the legislation has been presented for that purpose. your
Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends that you vote
" no" as to its adoption.

CHANGE TIME OF STA TED MEETING
(6)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M . of California:
WHEREAS. the Great Light in Masonry is the Holy Bible and
within its pages are noted that the Passover Season has occurred each
ye~r, at which time all peoples were to pay homage to their Supreme
Bemg. Those that were Christians observed and still observe the rites
of the Last Supper or Communion on Holy or Maundy Thursday. Our
Jewish and other creeds also observe Maundy Thursday Rites , and
WHEREAS. it has occurred that the Grand Master has seen fit
to grant a dispensation to move the Stated Meeting of a Lodge from
one date in a month to another and then turned and denied another
Lodge who asked for the same right. The Grand Master claimed that
o.ne Lodge was predominantly Jewish and another predominantly Christian, but equal consideration should have been given to both faiths in
the observance of the Passover season, and the Maundy Thursday
Rites, and
~HEREAS, Masonry is religious but not a religion, advocating no
particular creed. but an allegiance to a Supreme Being, and
WHEREAS, many members of Lodges are Officers or active workers in their own place of worship and have a real obligation to be present at services;
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the following section
be added and made a part of Section 313 of the By Laws, relative to
the date of a Stated Meeting, giving a Lodge the right to change the
date; PROVIDED : that the change is desired by the Lodge, because

259

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 6 would give a Lodge the right to change the date
of its Stated Meeting should it conflict with a religious holiday. provided: that such change of date is adopted by a majority vote of the
Lodge two or three months before the date of the meeting to be changed,
and that notice of such change be given in writing to the members of
the Lodge and Grand Lodge at lea st three weeks in advance.
Our ritual clearly states that our obligation to Masonry will not
interfere with the.duty we owe to God, our families, or ourselves. Should
the majority of members of a Lodge wish to observe a certain religious
holiday. then they should be allowed to change the date of their Stated
Meeting if it interferes with that observance.
I move the adoption of this resolution and the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommends a "yes" vote.

in Section 365 of the California Masonic Code, except that said

The Committee on Ritual:
The Committee on Ritual. to which Resolution No. 8 was referred
proposing to amend Section l 61-4th of the California Masonic Code
allowing the appointment by the Inspector of more than one Officers'
Coach, has ca refully considered this proposal.
It is the unanimous opinion of th is Committee that the responsibility of the Officers' Coach to the Inspector should be vested in one
man, thereby avoiding the probability of division of authority and the
differences of opinion among several Officers' Coaches, and thus enabling the Inspector to insure the teaching of our lectures and ritual in
the uniform manner that is so necessary and desirable throughout our
jurisdiction.
This same resolution was presented at our last Annual Communication but was withdrawn when the proponents of the resolution were
advised that Section 161-4th of the California Masonic Code does not
prohibit, nor does the Ritual Committee oppose the use of one or more
assistants who ar~ directly responsible to the Officers' Coach appointed
by the Inspector. Therefore, this Committee believes that the purposes
desired by Resolution No. 8 can be accomplished without enacting legislation .
We, therefore, are opposed to the resolution and strongly urge a
" no" vote.
The Committe.e on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution would permit the appointment of more than one
Officers' Coach in a Lodge. Your Committee recognizes the advantages
of providing more labor for more Brethren and of making available
substitutes for the first team.
However, your Committee fears that providing for more than one
Officers' Coach may cause disagreement on matters of ritual and confusion in the Temple. Furthermore, there is at present a provision in our
law for an Inspector to provide needed assistance in a Lodge.
The Committee on Policy and G eneral Purposes moves the adoption of the resolution and recommends a "no" vote.
The Committee on furisprudence indicates that the language of the
resolution will accomplish the intent of the author.
A majority voted against the resolution.

CHANGE NAME OF MASONIC EDUCATION
COMMITTEE AND MAKE IT A

(9)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Masonic education should be for all Masons, and .not
for a select few scholars, and
WHEREAS. the existing Committee, possibly by virtue of its name
has had little relationship to Masonry as a whole, and
'
. WHEREAS, the function of disseminating Masonic information
differs from that of education, and
WHEREAS, informing a Brother has a different connotation and
acceptability than educating him, and
~HEREAS, it is not possible to set up a continuing function of
service to the Grand Lodge without assurance of a planned, well-developed and continuing program, and
. WHEREAS, a permanent program of recording and dissemination of Masonic information with understanding of Masonic responsibility would make better Masons and stronger Officers in our constituent Lodges, with a consequent strengthening of the whole fabric of
California Masonry,
NOW. THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT:
The Masonic Education Committee be henceforth known as the
Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic Information and Responsibility,
and that
. . ~he Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic Information and Respons1b1hty be constituted as a Standing Committee of the Grand Lodge
of California, to consist of not less than twenty, nor more than thirty
members, including the Master or a Warden of each Research Lodge.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
In considering Resolution No. 9, your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes is in accord with the purposes enumerated as to the
functions of the committee heretofore known as the Masonic Education
Committee, the proposed change in name to Committee on Masonic

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

263

Information and Responsibility and the proposed change in status from
that of a Special Committee to that of a Standing Committee.
The resolution also provides for the Committee to consist of not
less than twenty, nor more than thirty, members. It is the opinion of
the Committee on Policy and General Purposes that the provision of
a minimum of twenty members at the outset for a program yet to be
developed may not be necessary and we recommend that the membership of the Committee be established at a minimum of ten and a maximum of thirty members. This reduction in the minimum number of members on the Committee will not restrict any contemplated expansion
in the program or activities of the Committee but will be desirahle in
not requiring the appointment of more members than may be required.
The resolution further provides for the inclusion of the Master or
a Warden of each Research Lodge as members of the Committee. Inasmuch as officers of Research Lodges as such are not members of Grand
Lodge (see Section 385 C.M.C.), they cannot be appointed members
of Grand Lodge committees (see Section 192).
I move the adoption of a substitute resolution to read as follows:
RESOLVED. that the Masonic Education Committee be henceforth known as the Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic Information
and Responsibility, and that it be constituted as a Standing Committee
to consist of not less than ten nor more than thirty members.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a
"yes" vote on the substitute resolution.
The Committee on Finance indicated its concurrence in the recommendation of the. Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Resolution No. 9 proposes to change the name of the Special Committee on Masonic Education to "Masonic Information and Responsibility," and to make it a Standing Committee.
We note that the name of the Committee on Masonic Education was
changed in 1940 to the Committee on Masonic Information, and it was
so designated until it became the Committee on Masonic Research in
1955, and then the Committee on Masonic Education again in 1960.
The changes of name have not seemed to affect the results, or lack of
results, from the committee's endeavors.
To some degree the proposed name may conflict or be confused with
that of the Committee on Public Information. We do not think that
the proposed new name reflects what we assume to be the duties of
the committee.
To effect the intention of the proposal. however. we offer the follow~
ing resolution:
RESOLVED, that Section 192 of the C.M.C. be amended by
inserting after the first sentence a semicolon and the following
language: "and on Masonic Information and Responsibility, con-

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence presents the following Resolution
to carry out the intended purpose of the proposers of Resolution No. 10.
RESOLVED: That the first paragraph of Section 221 of the California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
"Sec. 221. Appointment and powers. The Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California shall be eleven in number. The Senior
Grand Warden and Junior Grand Warden shall be Trustees exofficio; the other nine Trustees shall be appointed by successive
Grand Masters. The term of appointive Trustees shall be three
years from the dose of the Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge. At all times four of the nine appointive Trustees shall be
residents in the vicinity of the Home at Union City and four shall
be residents in the vicinity of the Home at Covina. If a Trustee
shall serve three full consecutive terms, he shall be ineligible for
reappointment until the lapse of one year. To establish proper sequence, the terms of the three new appointees commencing on
October 17, 1969, shall be one for one year. one for two years,
and one for three years."
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED : That Section 226 be amended
to read as follows:
"Sec. 226. Appointment and Powers. The Trustees of the California Masonic Temple, a Corporation. shall be seven in number.
The Deputy Grand Master shall be a Trustee ex-officio. The other
six Trustees shall be appointed by the Grand Master for terms of
three years each, provided, however, that the terms of one-third
of said appointive Trustees shall expire at the close of the Annual
Communication of Grand Lodge each year. Where a vacancy occurs, the appointee shall serve for the remainder of the unexpired
term. The Grand Master may remove an appointive Trustee at
any time. The Grand Secretary shall always be the secretary of
the Board of Trustees."
For the purpose of putting the resolution before Grand Lodge we
move the adoption of the resolution.
Adopted 5/6 vote.

WHEREAS. at the Annual Communication of 1967, Grand Lodge

regarding the sale of the Berkeley and U.C.L.A. Clubhouses; and
WHEREAS, at the Annual Communication of 1968, Grand Lodge

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

267

ed Resolution No. 33, establishing the California Masonic Foun-

~~on to administer funds derived from the sale of said Clubhouses: and

WHEREAS. the Berkeley Clubhouse has been sold, and funds and
obligations of the purchaser have been transferred to the California
Masonic Foundation: and
WHEREAS, all of the assets of the U .C.L.A. Clubhouse have been
transferred to the California Masonic Foundation; and
WHEREAS, Sections 231. 232, 233, 234, 236 . 237, 238 and 239
f the California Masonic Code relate to Directors, Title to Property,

THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED: That Sections 231. 232, 233.

Respectfully submitted,
HARLAN P. HUEBNER, P.M., No. 445
RICHARD L. RIEMER, P.M..
JoHN B. WATTS, M .. No. 637
No. 778
ANDREW J. NocAs. P.M.,
ALLEN B. GRESHAM , P.M.,
No. 641
No. 348
Referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
This resolution proposes the repeal of Sections 231, 232, 233 and
234 pertaining to the appointment of directors. their service as the
Board of D irectors pf the Masonic Club at the University of California,
Berkeley, California, the way in which title to Club assets should be
held, the organization of the board and annual reports.
It also proposes the repeal of Sections 236, 237, 238 and 239 which
make similar provisions for the Masonic Club at U.C.L.A.
Because the two clubhouses have either been sold or assets transferred pursuant to Grand Lodge action, neither the Masonic Club at
Berkeley nor the Masonic Club at U .C.L.A. exists any longer, at least
in form to require these Code Sections. Therefore, it is appropriate to
eliminate from the Code sections pertaining to them.
In addition, Section 153 provides that the Grand Secretary shall
secure and maintain in force a blanket fidelity bond for certain named
officers, including officers of Masonic Clubhouses. This provision for
bond for Masonic Clubhouse officers may also be eliminated.
The following resolution would be appropriate:
RESOLVED. that Sections 231, 232, 233, 234 , 236, 237, 238 and
239 are hereby repealed and, further, that Section 153 is amended to
delete the words, "Masonic Clubhouses," therefrom.
The Committee moves the adoption of the resolution and recommends a "yes" vote.
Adopted 5/ 6 vote.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution requests that a special committee be appointed to
provide a Library and Museum, that a 50 cents per capita tax be levied
on the Lodges to develop this Library and Museum and that authorization be granted for the purchase of properties adjacent to this California
Masonic Memorial Temple.
Your Committee has been advised that the status of the property
adjacent to this Temple in the California, Taylor, Pine and Jones block
can now be made more generally known. Until now this information
has been restricted to avoid an increase in asking price should Grand

272

273

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Lodge interest in the purchase become known. Briefly. when the sale
of the property at the corner of California and Jones became imminent
and the possibility of a high-rise hotel being built on that corner became
an actuality. the Temple Board Trustees. foreseeing a structure that
could completely obstruct our magnificent, endomosaic, historical window, as well as destroy the view from the Temple, purchased two key
properties between the Temple and Pine Street. These have proved to
be excellent investments. They cost approximately $308,000.00. The
rental income for the year ending June 30, 1969, exceeded $33.000.00
with expenses (less depreciation) amounting to only about $15.000.00.
There are only two properties remaining on the window side behind
the Temple. Your Committee agrees that it is essential that they be purchased. In view of the revenue derived from the property Grand Lodge
now owns, there is every likelihood these two additional parcels will
also be self-supporting. For the future they could provide additional
garage space, so sorely needed. Our present garage gave us $82.835.00
in revenue last year.
The proposed purchase area would also provide additional meeting
space and an area for a Library and Museum commensurate with the
dignity of the remainder of this building and the stature of the Grand
Lodge of California.
Your Committee unanimously believes this Grand Lodge should
request the Temple Board Trustees to acquire the two properties and
then prepare plans for the development of the entire area to be presented
to Grand Lodge for approval prior to the initiation of any construction.
The plan proposed by your Committee would obviate the necessity for
a per capita tax at this time. We. therefore, offer the following substitute
resolution :
RESOLVED. that the Temple Board Trustees be requested to acquire at the most reasonable price the two properties needed to complete
the area behind the Temple window and that said Trustees prepare
plans for the development of the property which shall be presented to
Grand Lodge for approval prior to any construction.
I move the adoption of the substitute resolution and the Committee
on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "yes" vote.
The Committees on Jurisprudence and on Finance indicated their
concurrence in the recommendation .
Substitute resolution adopted.

CHANGE NAME OF MASONIC BOARDS OF RELIEF
(14)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS. The Masonic Boards of Relief were established in
California over 100 years ago at a time when Maso.nry o~er~d t~e only
source of relief available to the Master Mason or his family m distress;
and
WHEREAS. today there is some type of City. County. State or
Federal Welfare benefits available to nearly all needy citizens from
"The Cradle to the Grave"; and
WHEREAS. actual Masonic Relief has been reduced to occasional
temporary assistance payments pending arrangements for more permanent welfare aid; and
WHEREAS. the present day functions of the Boards of Relief include but are not limited to: The dispensing of all types of Masonic
information proper to be made known; the operation of the Masonic
Blood Bank by many California Boards; arranging Masonic funeral
services for sojourning Masons; visiting and comforting the sick; assisting with the preparation of Masonic Homes applicatio_n.s for out of ~o:vn
Lodges and other Grand Lodge jurisdictions; counc1lmg _and ~dv1~mg
Brethren who bring a multitude of problems to the Board; mveshgahons
of all types concerning Master Masons or their families from all _Pa~ts
of the world; processing applications for assistance, the great ma)onty
of which are taken care of by some branch of public welfare, resulting
in a very small part of our funds being expended on actual Masonic
relief.
NOW. THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED: That the name of
our California Masonic Boards of Relief be changed from BOARDS
OF RELIEF to MASONIC SERVICE BUREAUS.
Respectfully submitted,

EXPAND THE DUTIES OF BOARDS OF RELIEF
(15)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . ur A . M . o f C a [·t
•
1 orma:
1

. WHEREAS, the duties of our California Masonic Boards of
Relief. ~s ~et forth _in the California Masonic Code, are limited to ro _
:~IJ rehevmg the distress of visiting Masons, their widows and orpha!.
. WHERE~.S. thes~ rules were written at a time when there was
little o~no ava11ab~e assistance for distressed people, and
_W ERE~S. m our present day society there is some type of welfare
assistance .~vailabl~ to nearly everyone in need, from the "Cradle to
thhe Gfrave, ldand direct relief to sojourning Brethren or their families is
t ere ore se om called for, and
WHERE.~,.S. the activities of our Boards of Relief have evolved into
many ah.nd .vaned types of services to our Brethren, many of which are

WHEREAS. there is documentary evidence that the services being

California Masonic Code, need to be expanded.
NOW. THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 603 of
the California Masonic Code entitled Boards of Relief be amended by
eliminating the first sentence and in its place substituting the following
sentence: Lodges having concurrent jurisdiction may form a Board of
Relief for the purposes of: Properly relieving the distress of visiting
Masons. their widows and orphans; the administration of a Masonic
Blood Bank which may include in its membership Lodges which are not
members of the particular Board of Relief who by their participation
will benefit the general operation of the Blood Bank Account; arranging
for Masonic funeral services for sojourning Masons; visiting ill and
shut-in sojourning Brethren and providing for their needs, when possible; assisting with the preparation of Masonic Home applications; conducting investigations concerning Masons or their families from all parts
of the world; and performing other services for Masonry which are not
in conflict with the prescribed functions of other divisions or committees
of Grand Lodge or with other sections of the California Masonic Code:
under a compact to be agreed upon among themselves and approved
by the Grand Lodge or Grand Master before becoming effective, wherein they may provide. among other things. for paying the expenses of the
work in such manner as shall seem proper.

in explicit terms the duties presently ass umed to be implied in the words

other services for Masonry which are not in conflict with the prescribed
functions of other Divisions or Committees of the Grand Lodge or other
Sections of the California Masonic Code" may well include elements
of relief which can and should be performed by the local Lodge whose
responsibility it may be.

The Committe.e on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 16 proposes a renumbering of two sections in our
Code and the enactment of a new section to be numbered 265 dealing
with the withdrawal of Lodges from membership in Boards of Relief.
The resolution as originally presented also contained a proposed
lengthy addition to Code Section 603. It has been stated to us that the
proponent expressed an intention to withdraw that latter portion because of changed circumstances. He has not communicated such intention to our Committee but our report and request is not affected by withdrawal or retention of the second half.
The first half of the resolution purports to operate solely on
something which does not exist. The proposed amendment would authorize. and I quote : "The Board of Control may terminate its compact
with the Lodge or Lodges involved ." We are not aware of any compact
between the Board of Control and any Lodge. The compa cts which
create Boards of Relief are compacts between the Lodges which comprise the board. The termination of such a compact poses many problems as to assets. distribution and, in some instances. substantial testamentary trusts which name a Board of Relief as the beneficiary. It is
possible that the money coming from such a trust might be lost because
of one or several withdrawals and what is the best policy for the Grand
Lodge to adopt might depend upon the terms of such trusts. What is

COMMERCIALISM-POLICY MANUAL
(17)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
WHER~AS, there is much confusion existing among Lodges, concordant bodies, Ma~onic affiliated groups, women's organizations, and
youth orders. regardmg the various prohibitions related to fund raising
programs which may or may not be engaged in; and
'YHEREAS, there are various conflicting opinions which permit
certam .groups to do things which others cannot do under more .above
board circumstances; and
WHERE~~· it is possible to get around many of the prohibitions
by merely om1ttmg the name of the organization involved. which invites
these groups and individual Masons to violate the spirit, if not the letter,
of the law; and

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

279

WHEREAS. we are fast becoming an organization dedicated to
ulations that speak "thou shalt not," rather than an organization
re:·ch seeks to promote improved fraternal and public relations by en;:ragement of what "thou shalt" do; and
WHEREAS. relations between Grand Lodge and Masonic organif%ations have at times become strained unnecessarily because of misunderstanding or misinterpretation of existing Masonic law; and
WHEREAS, it may not be improper or un-Masonic to invite anyone to share in dignified activities which give full value for any payment
received if full disclosure is made of the intended use of funds derived;
and
WHEREAS. certain smaller lodges would benefit most by public
as well as fraternal support of projects to raise funds for new temples
or other.legitimate charitable purposes; and
WHEREAS. the committee reports in the 1961 proceedings of the
Grand Lodge related to commercialism, and in particular Exhibit XIII
on page 55, Proc 1961, are not generally available or even known to
the· current officers of our Lodges and other organizations; which regulations even seem to confuse rather than clarify the situation; and
WHEREAS, interest in joining the Masonic fraternity appears to
be lacking because there is presently little opportunity for public encounter and dialogue with Masons, thus the public remains generally ignorant
ol our aims and purposes;
NOW, THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED that sub-sections
326-d, 333-c, d. g. k, m, n, o, p. q, r, t, v, and 334-i of the C.M.C. be
repealed and the GraJ!d Lodge Committee on Commercialism, and the
Policy and General Purposes Committee prepare a clear and concise
policy manual intended to improve fraternal relations and permit specific
public participation in various fund raising programs of our Lodges and
Masonic related organizations. To comply with Section 333 C.M.C.,
the manual shall be approved by the Grand Master, and shall provide
the basis for compliance with the requirements of the law. Situations
not specifically contained in the manual shall be referred to the Grand
Master for specific approval as required by Section 333 C.M.C. Said
manual shall be widely distributed to all Lodges and to concordant bodies. women's organizations, Masonic youth groups. and shall be made
available to others with legitimate interest at nominal charge.
Respectfully submitted
FREDERICK BoLTE, P.M .. No. 21
